abstract: The new neural network classifier we propose transforms the classification problem into the coding theory problem of decoding a noisy codeword. An input vector in the feature space is transformed into an internal representation which is a codeword in the code space, and then error correction decoded in this space to classify the input feature vector to its class. Two classes of codes which give high performance are the Hadamard matrix code and the maximal length sequence code. We show that the number of classes stored in an N-neuron system is linear in N and significantly more than that obtainable by using the Hopfield type memory as a classifier.

paragraphs: The paper treats classification as an error-correction problem. An input begins as a vector of measured features, but the network transforms it into an internal representation in a code space. Classification then consists of decoding that representation as a noisy codeword to identify the corresponding class.

This separates the description of an input from the representation used to decide its class. Coding theory supplies the structure for the second stage: the decoder corrects discrepancies in the internal code instead of assigning a class directly from the original features. The paper identifies Hadamard matrix codes and maximal length sequence codes as two choices that give high performance.

The stated capacity result is that an N-neuron classifier can store a number of classes proportional to N. The authors report that this is substantially more than a Hopfield-type memory can provide when used as a classifier. The significance is a direct connection between class capacity and code design: the internal representation is an essential part of how the network performs classification.
summary.tldr: The classifier maps inputs into error-correcting codes, supporting a class count that grows linearly with neuron count.

title: A NEURAL NETWORK CLASSIFIER BASED ON CODING THEORY

Elevation is computed from the interaural difference in sound level. We present models and computer simula(cid:173) tions of two stages of level difference processing which qualitatively agree with known anatomy and physiology, and make several strik(cid:173) ing predictions.

paragraphs: The barn owl’s midbrain contains a map-like representation of where sounds originate, helping the animal turn its head toward a target. This paper focuses on the vertical component of that representation: how the nervous system determines a sound source’s elevation. The relevant sensory cue is the difference in sound level between the two ears.

The authors develop models and computer simulations of two stages that process these level differences. The aim is to connect a measurable acoustic cue with the neural processing that supports directional behavior. Dividing the computation into stages makes it possible to consider how intermediate processing contributes to the eventual representation of sound location.

The models agree qualitatively with known anatomical and physiological observations and generate further predictions. Qualitative agreement means that the modeled organization and behavior resemble the biological evidence at the level claimed by the authors. The result is a proposed computational account of elevation processing that can also guide additional investigation of the owl’s auditory system.
summary.tldr: Models of two auditory processing stages explain how ear-to-ear sound-level differences could encode elevation in barn owls.

title: The Computation of Sound Source Elevation in the Barn Owl

abstract: The Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN) algorithm represents the likeli(cid:173) hood function of a given class as the sum of identical, isotropic Gaussians. In practice, PNN is often an excellent pattern classifier, outperforming other classifiers including backpropagation. However, it. is not. robust with respect to affine transformations of feature space, and this can lead to poor performance on certain data. We have derived an extension of PNN called Weighted PNN (WPNN) which compensates for this flaw by allow(cid:173) ing anisotropic Gaussians, i.e. Gaussians whose covariance is not a mul(cid:173) tiple of the identity matrix. The covariance is optimized using a genetic algorithm, some interesting features of which are its redundant, logarith(cid:173) mic encoding and large population size. Experimental results validate our claims.

paragraphs: A probabilistic neural network represents each class using a sum of Gaussian components. In the standard version discussed here, these components are identical and isotropic, meaning their spread is the same in every direction. The paper identifies a weakness in this choice: changing the geometry of the feature space through an affine transformation can undermine classification performance.

The proposed Weighted Probabilistic Neural Network allows anisotropic Gaussian components. Their covariance can describe different spreads in different directions, giving the classifier more flexibility in how it measures the shape of a class. This directly addresses the restriction imposed by spherical components and makes the geometry of the probability model something that can be optimized.

The authors optimize the covariance with a genetic algorithm that uses a redundant logarithmic encoding and a large population. They report experiments supporting their claims. The contribution is a change to the probability model underlying classification: allowing directional structure gives the network a way to compensate for feature-space transformations that can cause trouble for the original formulation.
summary.tldr: Weighted PNN learns direction-dependent Gaussian shapes to address the standard classifier's sensitivity to affine feature transformations.

title: A Weighted Probabilistic Neural Network

abstract: A novel segmentation algorithm has been developed utilizing an absolute(cid:173) value smoothness penalty instead of the more common quadratic regu(cid:173) larizer. This functional imposes a piece-wise constant constraint on the segmented data. Since the minimized energy is guaranteed to be convex, there are no problems with local minima and no complex continuation methods are necessary to find the unique global minimum. By interpret(cid:173) ing the minimized energy as the generalized power of a nonlinear resistive network, a continuous-time analog segmentation circuit was constructed.

paragraphs: This paper develops a segmentation algorithm based on an absolute-value smoothness penalty. Such a penalty controls how neighboring values are encouraged to agree during optimization. The authors use it in place of the more common quadratic regularizer, obtaining a formulation that imposes a piecewise-constant structure on the segmented data.

The optimization energy is convex, and the paper reports a unique global minimum. This means the solution procedure avoids the problem of getting trapped in inferior local minima. The authors also state that complicated continuation methods are unnecessary. The choice of smoothness penalty thus affects both the form of the segmentation and the difficulty of finding its optimum.

The work connects this mathematical formulation to a physical implementation by interpreting the energy as generalized power in a nonlinear resistive network. Using that interpretation, the authors construct a continuous-time analog segmentation circuit. The contribution spans the objective and its implementation: a particular segmentation constraint is expressed through a convex optimization problem that can also be realized as circuit dynamics.
summary.tldr: An absolute-value smoothness penalty yields convex, piecewise-constant segmentation and supports a continuous-time analog circuit implementation.

title: Segmentation Circuits Using Constrained Optimization

abstract: We present the information-theoretic derivation of a learning algorithm that clusters unlabelled data with linear discriminants. In contrast to methods that try to preserve information about the input patterns, we maximize the information gained from observing the output of robust binary discriminators implemented with sigmoid nodes. We deri ve a local weight adaptation rule via gradient ascent in this objective, demonstrate its dynamics on some simple data sets, relate our approach to previous work and suggest directions in which it may be extended.
originalAbstract: We present the information-theoretic derivation of a learning algorithm that clusters unlabelled data with linear discriminants. We deri ve a local weight adaptation rule via gradient ascent in this objective, demonstrate its dynamics on some simple data sets, relate our approach to previous work and suggest directions in which it may be extended.

paragraphs: The paper derives a learning algorithm for separating unlabeled data into clusters using linear discriminants. With no supplied class labels, the learning objective must determine what constitutes a useful division. The authors choose an information-theoretic objective centered on what can be learned by observing a discriminator's output.

The discriminators are robust binary decision units implemented with sigmoid nodes. Training maximizes information gained from their outputs, directing learning toward informative distinctions in the data. This choice differs from objectives focused on preserving information about the full input patterns: the quantity being optimized is tied specifically to the binary decisions.

The authors derive a local weight-update rule by applying gradient ascent to this objective. They demonstrate how the resulting learning dynamics behave on simple datasets, relate the method to earlier work, and suggest possible extensions. The contribution combines a stated information objective with a corresponding adaptation rule, making the connection between the desired clustering behavior and the learning mechanism explicit.
summary.tldr: An information-gain objective yields a local learning rule for clustering unlabeled data with sigmoid-based linear discriminators.

title: Unsupervised Discrimination of Clustered Data via Optimization of Binary Information Gain

abstract: Online cursive handwriting recognition is currently one of the most intriguing challenges in pattern recognition. This study presents a novel approach to this problem which is composed of two comple(cid:173) mentary phases. The first is dynamic encoding of the writing tra(cid:173) jectory into a compact sequence of discrete motor control symbols. In this compact representation we largely remove the redundancy of the script, while preserving most of its intelligible components. In the second phase these control sequences are used to train adaptive probabilistic acyclic automata (PAA) for the important ingredients of the writing trajectories, e.g. letters. We present a new and effi(cid:173) cient learning algorithm for such stochastic automata, and demon(cid:173) strate its utility for spotting and segmentation of cursive scripts. Our experiments show that over 90% of the letters are correctly spotted and identified, prior to any higher level language model. Moreover, both the training and recognition algorithms are very efficient compared to other modeling methods, and the models are 'on-line' adaptable to other writers and styles.

paragraphs: The paper approaches online cursive handwriting recognition by first changing how the pen trajectory is represented. A dynamic encoding converts the recorded movement into a compact sequence of discrete motor-control symbols. This representation removes much of the script's redundancy while retaining most of the information needed to interpret it.

The second phase trains adaptive probabilistic acyclic automata on those symbol sequences. These models represent important components of writing trajectories, such as letters. The authors introduce an efficient learning algorithm for the automata and use the learned models to locate letter-like components and divide cursive writing into meaningful segments.

The experiments report that more than 90% of letters are correctly located and identified before applying a higher-level language model. That result attributes substantial recognition capability to the trajectory representation and learned component models themselves. The authors also report efficient training and recognition compared with other modeling methods, together with online adaptation to different writers and styles. The approach thus joins compact movement encoding with adaptable probabilistic recognition.
summary.tldr: Compact motor-control encoding and probabilistic automata identify over 90% of cursive letters before higher-level language modeling.

title: Decoding Cursive Scripts

abstract: The basic paradigm for learning in neural networks is 'learning from examples' where a training set of input-output examples is used to teach the network the target function. Learning from hints is a gen(cid:173) eralization of learning from examples where additional information about the target function can be incorporated in the same learning process. Such information can come from common sense rules or special expertise. In financial market applications where the train(cid:173) ing data is very noisy, the use of such hints can have a decisive advantage. We demonstrate the use of hints in foreign-exchange trading of the U.S. Dollar versus the British Pound, the German Mark, the Japanese Yen, and the Swiss Franc, over a period of 32 months. We explain the general method of learning from hints and how it can be applied to other markets. The learning model for this method is not restricted to neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper explores how a learning system can use knowledge beyond a collection of input-output examples. Its approach, learning from hints, incorporates additional information about the target relationship into the same learning process. The hints may express common-sense rules or specialist knowledge that would otherwise remain outside the training examples.

The motivation is financial market data, where noisy observations can make the intended relationship difficult to learn. Hints give the learner another source of guidance about that relationship. The idea is to make available knowledge part of training, allowing observed examples and other information about the target function to contribute together.

The authors demonstrate the approach in foreign-exchange trading involving the U.S. dollar against the British pound, German mark, Japanese yen, and Swiss franc over 32 months. They also explain how to apply the general method to other markets. Although neural networks provide the starting context, the learning model is not restricted to them. The contribution is a method for incorporating knowledge and a financial application demonstrating its use.
summary.tldr: Learning from hints incorporates expert or common-sense knowledge into training and is demonstrated on foreign-exchange trading.

title: FINANCIAL APPLICATIONS OF LEARNING FROM HINTS

abstract: This paper presents instance-based state identification, an approach to reinforcement learning and hidden state that builds disambiguating amounts of short-term memory on-line, and also learns with an order of magnitude fewer training steps than several previous approaches. Inspired by a key similarity between learning with hidden state and learning in continuous geometrical spaces, this approach uses instance-based (or "memory-based") learning, a method that has worked well in continuous spaces.
originalAbstract: This paper presents instance-based state identification, an approach to reinforcement learning and hidden state that builds disambiguating amounts of short-term memory on-line, and also learns with an order of magnitude fewer training steps than several previous approaches. paragraphs: This paper addresses reinforcement learning with hidden state, where the information currently available to the learner is insufficient to distinguish relevant situations. Its proposed method, instance-based state identification, builds short-term memory during learning. The purpose of that memory is to supply enough recent context to resolve ambiguity about the state.

The approach draws on a similarity between hidden-state learning and learning in continuous geometric spaces. It applies instance-based, or memory-based, learning, a method the abstract identifies as successful in continuous spaces. This choice connects the problem of identifying a hidden situation with a learning approach organized around individual instances.

The authors report learning with an order of magnitude fewer training steps than several previous approaches. The stated benefit combines efficiency with online construction of the memory needed for disambiguation. The contribution is therefore a way to learn a useful state representation as experience arrives, using short-term context to make hidden-state reinforcement learning more tractable.
summary.tldr: Instance-based state identification builds short-term memory online to resolve hidden states while reducing reported training requirements.

title: Instance-Based State Identification for Reinforcement Learning

paragraphs: This paper studies learning models whose parameter spaces contain singularities, including layered neural networks and Gaussian mixtures. In these models, the Fisher information matrix can be singular, and the usual asymptotic normality does not hold. That makes the geometry of the model directly relevant to understanding its behavior as more data become available.

The paper uses resolution of singularities, a method from algebraic geometry, to establish a rigorous asymptotic expression for stochastic complexity. It then examines how the choice of prior affects that expression. With a positive prior, the authors report substantially smaller stochastic complexity than the comparison criterion named in the abstract, together with smaller generalization error than regular statistical models. The claim also covers cases where the model does not contain the true distribution.

The second case concerns Jeffreys' prior, described as independent of coordinates and zero at singularities. This produces the comparison criterion's form of stochastic complexity. The paper distinguishes its usefulness for model selection from its usefulness for generalization, showing that prior choice changes the consequences of singular model geometry.
summary.tldr: Algebraic geometry explains how singularities and prior choice change stochastic complexity and generalization in hierarchical learning models.

title: Algebraic Information Geometry for Learning Machines with Singularities

abstract: The mystery of belief propagation (BP) decoder, especially of the turbo decoding, is studied from information geometrical viewpoint. The loopy belief network (BN) of turbo codes makes it difﬁcult to obtain the true “belief” by BP, and the characteristics of the algorithm and its equilib- rium are not clearly understood. Our study gives an intuitive understand- ing of the mechanism, and a new framework for the analysis. Based on the framework, we reveal basic properties of the turbo decoding.
originalAbstract: The mystery of belief propagation (BP) decoder, especially of the turbo decoding, is studied from information geometrical viewpoint. The loopy belief network (BN) of turbo codes makes it difﬁcult to obtain the true “belief” by BP, and the characteristics of the algorithm and its equilib- rium are not clearly understood. Our study gives an intuitive understand- ing of the mechanism, and a new framework for the analysis. Based on the framework, we reveal basic properties of the turbo decoding.

paragraphs: This paper studies belief propagation decoding, with particular attention to turbo decoding. The difficulty is that the belief network associated with turbo codes contains loops. In that setting, applying belief propagation does not make the true beliefs straightforward to obtain, and understanding the algorithm's behavior and equilibrium is itself a significant analytical problem.

The authors approach this problem through information geometry. This supplies a geometric viewpoint on probabilistic inference and a framework for examining what the decoder does. Their stated aim includes an intuitive account of the mechanism, so the framework is intended to clarify the decoding process as well as support formal analysis.

Using this viewpoint, the paper establishes basic properties of turbo decoding. The contribution is therefore an analytical explanation of an existing inference procedure and its equilibrium behavior. Its significance lies in making a difficult loopy decoding process more understandable and open to analysis; the abstract does not claim that the framework turns belief propagation into exact inference on these networks.
summary.tldr: Information geometry provides a framework for understanding belief propagation and basic properties of turbo decoding.

title: Information Geometrical Framework for Analyzing Belief Propagation Decoder

abstract: Several authors have suggested viewing boosting as a gradient descent search for a good ﬁt in function space. We apply gradient-based boosting methodology to the unsupervised learning problem of density estimation. We show convergence properties of the algorithm and prove that a strength of weak learnability prop- erty applies to this problem as well. We illustrate the potential of this approach through experiments with boosting Bayesian networks to learn density models.
originalAbstract: Several authors have suggested viewing boosting as a gradient descent search for a good ﬁt in function space. We apply gradient-based boosting methodology to the unsupervised learning problem of density estimation. We show convergence properties of the algorithm and prove that a strength of weak learnability prop- erty applies to this problem as well. We illustrate the potential of this approach through experiments with boosting Bayesian networks to learn density models.

paragraphs: The paper applies boosting to density estimation, an unsupervised task concerned with modeling how data are distributed. Its starting point is the view of boosting as gradient descent in a space of functions. From that perspective, successive learning steps search for a better-fitting function, and the authors adapt this methodology to learning a probability density.

The work includes theoretical analysis of the resulting algorithm. The authors establish convergence properties and prove that a form of weak learnability applies to density estimation as well. This connects the proposed procedure to the question of when relatively weak learning capability can support a stronger overall learning process.

The empirical illustration boosts Bayesian networks to learn density models. These experiments are presented as evidence of the approach's potential. Taken together, the theory and experiments broaden the setting in which gradient-based boosting can be used: the target is a model of the data distribution, with convergence and learnability serving as central questions about the method.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based boosting is extended to density estimation, with convergence analysis, a weak-learnability result, and Bayesian-network experiments.

title: Boosting Density Estimation

abstract: We propose a framework for classiﬁer design based on discriminative densities for representation of the differences of the class-conditional dis- tributions in a way that is optimal for classiﬁcation. The densities are selected from a parametrized set by constrained maximization of some objective function which measures the average (bounded) difference, i.e. the contrast between discriminative densities. We show that maximiza- tion of the contrast is equivalent to minimization of an approximation of the Bayes risk. Therefore using suitable classes of probability den- sity functions, the resulting maximum contrast classiﬁers (MCCs) can approximate the Bayes rule for the general multiclass case. In particular for a certain parametrization of the density functions we obtain MCCs which have the same functional form as the well-known Support Vec- tor Machines (SVMs). We show that MCC-training in general requires some nonlinear optimization but under certain conditions the problem is concave and can be tackled by a single linear program. We indicate the close relation between SVM- and MCC-training and in particular we show that Linear Programming Machines can be viewed as an approxi- mate realization of MCCs. In the experiments on benchmark data sets, the MCC shows a competitive classiﬁcation performance.

paragraphs: The paper designs classifiers using probability densities chosen to represent differences between classes that matter for classification. It selects these discriminative densities from a parameterized family by maximizing a constrained measure of their average bounded contrast. The objective emphasizes distinctions useful for making decisions.

The authors show that maximizing this contrast is equivalent to minimizing an approximation to Bayes risk, the risk associated with classification decisions. With suitable density families, maximum contrast classifiers can therefore approximate the Bayes decision rule for multiple classes. A particular density parameterization produces classifiers with the same functional form as support vector machines.

Training generally requires nonlinear optimization, although under certain conditions the problem is concave and can be handled by a single linear program. The paper also connects the training procedure to support vector machines and interprets Linear Programming Machines as approximate realizations of the framework. Benchmark experiments report competitive classification performance. Together, these results link a density-based classification objective to familiar classifier forms and, in specific cases, tractable training procedures.
summary.tldr: Maximum contrast estimation selects discriminative densities through an objective linked to approximate Bayes risk and connects the resulting classifiers to SVMs.

title: Discriminative Densities from Maximum Contrast Estimation

abstract: In models that deﬁne probabilities via energies, maximum likelihood learning typically involves using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to sample from the model’s distribution. If the Markov chain is started at the data distribution, learning often works well even if the chain is only run for a few time steps [3]. But if the data distribution contains modes separated by regions of very low density, brief MCMC will not ensure that different modes have the correct relative energies because it cannot move particles from one mode to another. We show how to improve brief MCMC by allowing long-range moves that are suggested by the data distribution. If the model is approximately correct, these long-range moves have a reasonable acceptance rate.
originalAbstract: In models that deﬁne probabilities via energies, maximum likelihood learning typically involves using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to sample from the model’s distribution. If the Markov chain is started at the data distribution, learning often works well even if the chain is only run for a few time steps [3]. But if the data distribution contains modes separated by regions of very low density, brief MCMC will not ensure that different modes have the correct relative energies because it cannot move particles from one mode to another. We show how to improve brief MCMC by allowing long-range moves that are suggested by the data distribution. If the model is approximately correct, these long-range moves have a reasonable acceptance rate.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a weakness of learning energy-based probability models using short Markov chain simulations. Starting a chain at the data and running it for only a few steps can work well, but separated concentrations of data create a particular difficulty for these brief sampling runs.

When regions of high probability are divided by very low-density regions, a short chain cannot readily move between them. As a result, learning may fail to establish the correct relative energies of different modes. The issue concerns how much probability the model assigns to separate regions, which cannot be reliably compared if sampled particles remain within their starting mode.

The authors improve brief sampling by introducing long-range moves suggested by the data distribution. These moves provide a route between otherwise separated modes. They state that such proposals have a reasonable acceptance rate when the model is approximately correct. The method therefore addresses the specific obstacle of crossing low-density gaps, with its acceptance claim explicitly depending on the quality of the current model.
summary.tldr: Data-guided long-range sampling moves help short Markov chains connect separated modes during energy-based model learning.

title: Wormholes Improve Contrastive Divergence

abstract: We show that anomaly detection can be interpreted as a binary classifi- cation problem. Using this interpretation we propose a support vector machine (SVM) for anomaly detection. We then present some theoret- ical results which include consistency and learning rates. Finally, we experimentally compare our SVM with the standard one-class SVM.
originalAbstract: We show that anomaly detection can be interpreted as a binary classifi- cation problem. Using this interpretation we propose a support vector machine (SVM) for anomaly detection. We then present some theoret- ical results which include consistency and learning rates. Finally, we experimentally compare our SVM with the standard one-class SVM.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection asks whether an observation belongs to the usual pattern of data or falls outside it. This paper shows that the task can be interpreted as binary classification. That interpretation connects the problem of identifying unusual observations to methods designed to distinguish between two categories.

The authors use this connection to propose a support vector machine for anomaly detection. The contribution is therefore both a reformulation of the learning problem and a method built from that reformulation. It gives a classification-based route to anomaly detection, with theoretical analysis accompanying the proposed algorithm.

The theoretical results include consistency and learning rates, addressing how the method behaves as more data become available and how rapidly learning progresses. The paper also compares the proposed method experimentally with the standard one-class SVM. Together, these contributions connect the classification interpretation to mathematical guarantees and an established practical alternative; the supplied abstract does not state which method performs better in that comparison.
summary.tldr: The paper recasts anomaly detection as binary classification and develops an SVM with consistency and learning-rate results.

title: Density Level Detection is Classification

abstract: In this paper, we aim at analyzing the characteristic of neuronal population responses to instantaneous or time-dependent inputs and the role of synapses in neural information processing. We have derived an evolution equation of the membrane potential density function with synaptic depression, and obtain the formulas for analytic computing the response of instantaneous re rate. Through a technical analysis, we arrive at several signi cant conclusions: The background inputs play an important role in information processing and act as a switch betwee temporal integration and coincidence detection. the role of synapses can be regarded as a spatio-temporal lter; it is important in neural information processing for the spatial distribution of synapses and the spatial and temporal relation of inputs. The instantaneous input frequency can affect the response amplitude and phase delay.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how neuronal populations respond to instantaneous inputs and inputs that change over time. It includes synaptic depression in its mathematical description, making synaptic behavior part of the response calculation. The aim is to understand both population firing and the contribution of synapses to processing incoming information.

The authors derive an evolution equation for the distribution of membrane potentials and obtain formulas for calculating instantaneous firing rates analytically. This population-level description supports an analysis of how input conditions affect the response. Their findings assign background inputs an important role: they can switch processing between accumulating signals over time and detecting signals that arrive together.

The analysis also describes synapses as filters operating across space and time. Both the locations of synapses and the spatial and temporal relationships among inputs matter in this account. In addition, instantaneous input frequency affects response amplitude and phase delay. Together, these conclusions show how the modeled population response depends on background activity, input timing, and spatial organization.
summary.tldr: An analytical population model with synaptic depression links background activity and input organization to different modes of neural response.

title: Response Analysis of Neuronal Population with Synaptic Depression

We (cid:2)rst analyze a one-pass algorithm in the setting of boosting with diverse base classi(cid:2)ers. Our guarantee is the same as the best proved for any boosting algo- rithm, but our one-pass algorithm is much faster than previous approaches. We next exhibit a random source of examples for which a (cid:147)picky(cid:148) variant of Ad- aBoost that skips poor base classi(cid:2)ers can outperform the standard AdaBoost al- gorithm, which uses every base classi(cid:2)er, by an exponential factor. Experiments with Reuters and synthetic data show that one-pass boosting can sub- stantially improve on the accuracy of Naive Bayes, and that picky boosting can sometimes lead to a further improvement in accuracy.

In the setting of diverse base classifiers, the authors analyze a one-pass algorithm whose guarantee matches the strongest previously proved for boosting, while being much faster than earlier approaches.

The paper also investigates whether a boosting procedure should use every available base classifier. It constructs a random source of examples where a selective variant of AdaBoost, which skips poor classifiers, can outperform the standard version by an exponential factor. This is a result for the exhibited source, establishing that rejecting some classifiers can have a substantial benefit under suitable conditions.

Experiments on Reuters and synthetic data show that one-pass boosting can substantially improve the accuracy of Naive Bayes. Selective boosting sometimes provides an additional improvement. The theoretical and experimental findings address complementary questions: whether a single pass can retain a strong guarantee, and whether choosing which classifiers to include can further improve the resulting predictor.
summary.tldr: One-pass boosting retains a strong theoretical guarantee, while selectively skipping poor classifiers can provide further benefits.

title: One-Pass Boosting

abstract: We consider the learning task consisting in predicting as well as the best function in a finite reference set G up to the smallest possible additive term. If R(g) denotes the generalization error of a prediction function g, under reasonable assumptions on the loss function (typically satisfied by the least square loss when the output is bounded), it is known that the progressive mixture rule g n satisfies E R(g n) < min_{g in G} R(g) + Cst (log|G|)/n where n denotes the size of the training set, E denotes the expectation wrt the training set distribution. This work shows that, surprisingly, for appropriate reference sets G, the deviation convergence rate of the progressive mixture rule is only no better than Cst / sqrt{n}, and not the expected Cst / n. It also provides an algorithm which does not suffer from this drawback.

paragraphs: The learning task is to predict nearly as well as the best function in a finite reference collection. Performance is measured by generalization error, with the goal of making the additional error as small as possible. The paper examines whether a favorable average guarantee for progressive mixture rules also implies favorable behavior across individual training samples.

Under suitable assumptions on the loss, the known expected-error guarantee has an additional term proportional to log|G|/n, where G is the reference set and n is the training-set size. These assumptions typically hold for squared loss with bounded outputs. The expectation averages over the random training set, which is central to understanding what this guarantee says.

The authors show that, for appropriate reference sets, the deviation convergence rate can be no better than order 1/√n rather than the anticipated 1/n. Thus, fast improvement in expected error can coexist with substantially weaker deviation behavior. The paper also supplies an algorithm that avoids this drawback, addressing the distinction between average performance and control of departures from that average.
summary.tldr: Progressive mixture rules can achieve fast expected-error rates while having slower deviation rates; the paper provides an algorithm that avoids this drawback.

title: Progressive mixture rules are deviation suboptimal

abstract: We consider the problem of efficiently encoding a signal by transforming it to a new representation whose components are statistically independent. A widely studied linear solution, independent components analysis (ICA), exists for the case when the signal is generated as a linear transformation of independent non- Gaussian sources. Here, we examine a complementary case, in which the source is non-Gaussian but elliptically symmetric. In this case, no linear transform suffices to properly decompose the signal into independent components, but we show that a simple nonlinear transformation, which we call radial Gaussianization (RG), is able to remove all dependencies. We then demonstrate this methodology in the context of natural signal statistics. We first show that the joint distributions of bandpass filter responses, for both sound and images, are better described as elliptical than linearly transformed independent sources. Consistent with this, we demonstrate that the reduction in dependency achieved by applying RG to either pairs or blocks of bandpass filter responses is significantly greater than that achieved by PCA or ICA.

paragraphs: The paper studies signal representations whose components are statistically independent, a goal relevant to efficient encoding. Independent component analysis addresses signals generated by linearly mixing independent non-Gaussian sources. The authors examine a complementary situation: a source distribution that is non-Gaussian and elliptically symmetric.

For that distributional case, a linear transformation cannot fully separate the signal into independent components. The paper shows that a simple nonlinear transformation, radial Gaussianization, can remove all dependencies. The complete-removal claim is tied to the stated elliptical setting, making the assumed distribution central to why this transformation succeeds where linear transformations do not.

The authors then examine bandpass-filter responses from natural sounds and images. Their joint distributions are better described by elliptical models than by linearly transformed independent sources. Consistent with this observation, radial Gaussianization reduces dependencies significantly more than PCA or ICA when applied to pairs or blocks of those responses. The theoretical result and empirical findings therefore support each other: a distributional model motivates the transformation, and natural-signal experiments show the value of that choice.
summary.tldr: Radial Gaussianization removes dependencies under an elliptical source model and reduces natural-signal dependencies more than PCA or ICA in the reported experiments.

title: Reducing statistical dependencies in natural signals using radial Gaussianization

abstract: In some stochastic environments the well-known reinforcement learning algorithm Q-learning performs very poorly. This poor performance is caused by large overestimations of action values. These overestimations result from a positive bias that is introduced because Q-learning uses the maximum action value as an approximation for the maximum expected action value. We introduce an alternative way to approximate the maximum expected value for any set of random variables. The obtained double estimator method is shown to sometimes underestimate rather than overestimate the maximum expected value. We apply the double estimator to Q-learning to construct Double Q-learning, a new off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. We show the new algorithm converges to the optimal policy and that it performs well in some settings in which Q-learning performs poorly due to its overestimation.

This poor performance is caused by large overestimations of action values. These overestimations result from a positive bias that is introduced because Q-learning uses the maximum action value as an approximation for the maximum expected action value. We introduce an alternative way to approximate the maximum expected value for any set of random variables. The obtained double estimator method is shown to sometimes underestimate rather than overestimate the maximum expected value. We apply the double estimator to Q-learning to construct Double Q-learning, a new off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. We show the new algorithm converges to the optimal policy and that it performs well in some settings in which Q-learning performs poorly due to its overestimation.

paragraphs: Q-learning estimates how valuable different actions are and uses the largest estimated value when learning. In stochastic environments, those estimates fluctuate. Taking their maximum can favor an estimate that happens to be too high, creating a positive bias. The paper identifies large overestimates from this mechanism as the cause of poor Q-learning performance in some environments.

The authors introduce a double-estimator method for approximating the largest expected value among a collection of random variables. This changes how the maximum is estimated and can sometimes produce underestimation instead of overestimation. The result is a different pattern of estimation error; the abstract does not claim that the new estimator eliminates every form of bias.

Applying this method to action-value learning produces Double Q-learning, an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. The paper proves convergence to the optimal policy and demonstrates good performance in some settings where ordinary Q-learning struggles because of overestimation. Its central contribution is to connect a specific statistical bias in value estimation to a concrete change in the learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Double Q-learning changes how maximum action values are estimated to address overestimation that harms Q-learning in some stochastic environments.

title: Double Q-learning

abstract: Many combinatorial problems arising in machine learning can be reduced to the problem of minimizing a submodular function. Submodular functions are a natural discrete analog of convex functions, and can be minimized in strongly polynomial time. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art algorithms for general submodular minimization are intractable for practical problems. In this paper, we introduce a novel subclass of submodular minimization problems that we call decomposable. Decomposable submodular functions are those that can be represented as sums of concave functions applied to linear functions. We develop an algorithm, SLG, that can efficiently minimize decomposable submodular functions with tens of thousands of variables. Our algorithm exploits recent results in smoothed convex minimization. We apply SLG to synthetic benchmarks and a joint classification-and-segmentation task, and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art general purpose submodular minimization algorithms by several orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Many discrete optimization problems in machine learning can be expressed as submodular minimization. Submodular functions play a role analogous to convex functions in continuous optimization, and general algorithms have strong polynomial-time guarantees. The practical problem is that those guarantees do not make the available general-purpose methods fast enough for many applications.

The paper identifies a more structured subclass called decomposable submodular functions. These functions can be written as sums in which a concave function is applied to a linear function. The proposed SLG algorithm uses that structure together with results from smoothed convex minimization to handle problems containing tens of thousands of variables.

Experiments cover synthetic benchmarks and a task combining classification with segmentation. On those problems, SLG outperforms general-purpose submodular minimization methods by several orders of magnitude. The contribution is therefore a substantial practical acceleration for the specified decomposable subclass: the additional mathematical structure makes it possible to solve large instances much more efficiently.
summary.tldr: SLG exploits decomposable submodular structure to solve large problems several orders of magnitude faster than general-purpose methods in reported experiments.

title: Efficient Minimization of Decomposable Submodular Functions

abstract: We consider the online binary classification problem, where we are given m classifiers. At each stage, the classifiers map the input to the probability that the input belongs to the positive class. An online classification meta-algorithm is an algorithm that combines the outputs of the classifiers in order to attain a certain goal, without having prior knowledge on the form and statistics of the input, and without prior knowledge on the performance of the given classifiers. In this paper, we use sensitivity and specificity as the performance metrics of the meta-algorithm. In particular, our goal is to design an algorithm which satisfies the following two properties (asymptotically): (i) its average false positive rate (fp-rate) is under some given threshold, and (ii) its average true positive rate (tp-rate) is not worse than the tp-rate of the best convex combination of the m given classifiers that satisfies fp-rate constraint, in hindsight. We show that this problem is in fact a special case of the regret minimization problem with constraints, and therefore the above goal is not attainable. Hence, we pose a relaxed goal and propose a corresponding practical online learning meta-algorithm that attains it. In the case of two classifiers, we show that this algorithm takes a very simple form. To our best knowledge, this is the first algorithm that addresses the problem of the average tp-rate maximization under average fp-rate constraints in the online setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online learner that combines probability predictions from several binary classifiers. It has no advance knowledge of the input distribution or the classifiers’ performance. The desired behavior is to identify positives effectively while keeping the average false-positive rate below a specified threshold.

The initial objective has two asymptotic requirements: respect the false-positive constraint and match the true-positive rate of the best feasible convex combination of classifiers chosen in hindsight. The authors connect this objective to regret minimization with constraints and show that the original goal is unattainable. This establishes an obstacle to demanding both guarantees together in the stated online setting.

They therefore formulate a relaxed objective and provide a practical online combination algorithm that achieves it. With two classifiers, the algorithm becomes especially simple. The contribution pairs an impossibility result with a usable alternative, clarifying why the original benchmark must be weakened. Its guarantee belongs to the relaxed objective, so it should not be read as achieving the two original requirements unchanged.
summary.tldr: An unattainable online classification objective motivates a practical relaxation for improving true-positive rates under false-positive constraints.

title: Online Classification with Specificity Constraints

abstract: Multi-structure model fitting has traditionally taken a two-stage approach: First, sample a (large) number of model hypotheses, then select the subset of hypotheses that optimise a joint fitting and model selection criterion. This disjoint two-stage approach is arguably suboptimal and inefficient - if the random sampling did not retrieve a good set of hypotheses, the optimised outcome will not represent a good fit. To overcome this weakness we propose a new multi-structure fitting approach based on Reversible Jump MCMC. Instrumental in raising the effectiveness of our method is an adaptive hypothesis generator, whose proposal distribution is learned incrementally and online. We prove that this adaptive proposal satisfies the diminishing adaptation property crucial for ensuring ergodicity in MCMC. Our method effectively conducts hypothesis sampling and optimisation simultaneously, and gives superior computational efficiency over other methods.

To overcome this weakness we propose a new multi-structure fitting approach based on Reversible Jump MCMC. paragraphs: Fitting several structures to data often starts by randomly generating many candidate models and then choosing a subset. The paper identifies a weakness in separating these stages: if sampling misses good candidates, later optimization cannot select them. The quality of the final fit is constrained by the hypotheses already available.

The proposed approach uses reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo to combine hypothesis sampling and optimization. Its hypothesis generator adapts during the process, learning a proposal distribution incrementally and online. Candidate generation can therefore develop alongside the search for a good collection of structures.

The authors prove that the adaptive proposal satisfies diminishing adaptation, a property crucial for ensuring ergodicity in MCMC. This gives theoretical support to changing the proposal while sampling, rather than treating adaptation solely as a computational heuristic. The method is reported to provide superior computational efficiency over other methods. The central contribution is the integration of candidate discovery and model fitting, supported by an analysis of the adaptive mechanism.
summary.tldr: Adaptive reversible jump MCMC combines hypothesis generation with multi-structure fitting and proves diminishing adaptation for its proposal mechanism.

title: Simultaneous Sampling and Multi-Structure Fitting with Adaptive Reversible Jump MCMC

abstract: Discriminative learning when training and test data belong to different distributions is a challenging and complex task. Often times we have very few or no labeled data from the test or target distribution but may have plenty of labeled data from multiple related sources with different distributions. The difference in distributions may be in both marginal and conditional probabilities. Most of the existing domain adaptation work focuses on the marginal probability distribution difference between the domains, assuming that the conditional probabilities are similar. However in many real world applications, conditional probability distribution differences are as commonplace as marginal probability differences. In this paper we propose a two-stage domain adaptation methodology which combines weighted data from multiple sources based on marginal probability differences (first stage) as well as conditional probability differences (second stage), with the target domain data. The weights for minimizing the marginal probability differences are estimated independently, while the weights for minimizing conditional probability differences are computed simultaneously by exploiting the potential interaction among multiple sources. We also provide a theoretical analysis on the generalization performance of the proposed multi-source domain adaptation formulation using the weighted Rademacher complexity measure. Empirical comparisons with existing state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods using three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Learning from several related datasets becomes difficult when the target data follow a different distribution and have few or no labels. Differences can concern both which inputs occur and how labels relate to those inputs. The paper addresses both forms of mismatch, rather than relying on the assumption that input-label relationships remain similar across domains.

The proposed framework combines source data with target data through two stages of weighting. First, it estimates weights independently to reduce differences in marginal distributions. Second, it computes weights jointly to address differences in conditional distributions. Joint computation in the second stage allows the method to exploit possible interactions among the available sources.

The authors analyze generalization using weighted Rademacher complexity, connecting the weighting formulation to its ability to perform beyond the training data. Comparisons with existing domain adaptation methods on three real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The central contribution is a framework that treats both kinds of distribution shift explicitly while coordinating how multiple sources contribute to learning.
summary.tldr: Two-stage weighting adapts multiple source datasets by addressing both input-distribution differences and changes in input-label relationships.

title: A Two-Stage Weighting Framework for Multi-Source Domain Adaptation

abstract: Reservoir computing is a new, powerful and flexible machine learning technique that is easily implemented in hardware. Recently, by using a time-multiplexed architecture, hardware reservoir computers have reached performance comparable to digital implementations. Operating speeds allowing for real time information operation have been reached using optoelectronic systems. At present the main performance bottleneck is the readout layer which uses slow, digital postprocessing. We have designed an analog readout suitable for time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers, capable of working in real time. The readout has been built and tested experimentally on a standard benchmark task. Its performance is better than non-reservoir methods, with ample room for further improvement. The present work thereby overcomes one of the major limitations for the future development of hardware reservoir computers.

At present the main performance bottleneck is the readout layer which uses slow, digital postprocessing. We have designed an analog readout suitable for time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers, capable of working in real time. The readout has been built and tested experimentally on a standard benchmark task. Its performance is better than non-reservoir methods, with ample room for further improvement. The present work thereby overcomes one of the major limitations for the future development of hardware reservoir computers.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a hardware bottleneck in reservoir computing: extracting the output quickly enough to benefit from fast internal processing. Time-multiplexed hardware reservoirs had already reached performance comparable to digital implementations, and optoelectronic systems had achieved speeds suitable for real-time operation. Slow digital processing in the readout layer remained an obstacle.

The authors design an analog readout specifically for time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers. Its purpose is to make the output stage operate in real time as well. This matters because accelerating the reservoir alone does not resolve a delay introduced when its activity is converted into the system’s usable output.

The readout is physically built and evaluated on a standard benchmark task. The authors report performance above non-reservoir methods, while noting room for further improvement. The result is an experimental demonstration that a major readout limitation can be overcome, helping connect fast reservoir hardware with an output mechanism capable of keeping pace.
summary.tldr: An experimentally tested analog readout enables real-time output from time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers.

title: Analog readout for optical reservoir computers

abstract: Bipartite matching problems characterize many situations, ranging from ranking in information retrieval to correspondence in vision. Exact inference in real-world applications of these problems is intractable, making efficient approximation methods essential for learning and inference. In this paper we propose a novel {\it sequential matching} sampler based on the generalization of the Plackett-Luce model, which can effectively make large moves in the space of matchings. This allows the sampler to match the difficult target distributions common in these problems: highly multimodal distributions with well separated modes. We present experimental results with bipartite matching problems - ranking and image correspondence - which show that the sequential matching sampler efficiently approximates the target distribution, significantly outperforming other sampling approaches.

paragraphs: Bipartite matching describes assignments between two sets, including ranking problems and correspondence between images. In the real-world applications considered here, exact probabilistic inference is intractable. The paper therefore focuses on sampling methods that approximate a distribution over possible matchings, supporting both learning and inference when direct computation is impractical.

The proposed sequential matching sampler generalizes the Plackett-Luce model. Its key property is the ability to make large moves through the space of matchings. This matters because the target distributions can have several well-separated modes: distinct groups of plausible solutions that a sampler must represent rather than concentrating on only one region.

Experiments on ranking and image correspondence show that the sampler efficiently approximates these target distributions and significantly outperforms the other sampling approaches evaluated. The contribution connects the structure of the sampling procedure to the shape of the distribution it needs to explore. Large moves provide a way to address the separated alternatives that make these matching problems difficult.
summary.tldr: A sequential matching sampler makes large moves between plausible assignments to approximate difficult multimodal matching distributions efficiently.

title: Efficient Sampling for Bipartite Matching Problems

abstract: We address the problem of deciding whether a causal or probabilistic query is estimable from data corrupted by missing entries, given a model of missingness process. We extend the results of Mohan et al, 2013 by presenting more general conditions for recovering probabilistic queries of the form P(y|x) and P(y,x) as well as causal queries of the form P(y|do(x)). We show that causal queries may be recoverable even when the factors in their identifying estimands are not recoverable. Specifically, we derive graphical conditions for recovering causal effects of the form P(y|do(x)) when Y and its missingness mechanism are not d-separable. Finally, we apply our results to problems of attrition and characterize the recovery of causal effects from data corrupted by attrition.

paragraphs: Missing entries can make a statistical or causal question impossible to answer from the observed data, but the answer depends on how missingness occurs. This paper assumes a model of that process and asks which queries remain recoverable. It covers conditional probabilities, joint probabilities, and causal effects expressed through interventions.

The authors derive more general graphical conditions for recovering these queries. A central finding is that a causal effect may be recoverable even when individual factors in an expression identifying that effect are not. Thus, inspecting the recoverability of every factor separately can miss cases in which the causal query as a whole can still be obtained.

The analysis includes conditions for recovering causal effects when the outcome and its missingness mechanism are not separated by the graph's d-separation criterion. The authors also apply their results to attrition, characterizing recovery of causal effects when observations are lost through that process. The contribution provides query-specific reasoning about missing data, with conclusions tied to the supplied model of missingness.
summary.tldr: Graphical conditions identify recoverable statistical and causal queries under missingness, including some effects whose identifying factors are unrecoverable.

title: Graphical Models for Recovering Probabilistic and Causal Queries from Missing Data

abstract: The degree of confidence in one's choice or decision is a critical aspect of perceptual decision making. Attempts to quantify a decision maker's confidence by measuring accuracy in a task have yielded limited success because confidence and accuracy are typically not equal. In this paper, we introduce a Bayesian framework to model confidence in perceptual decision making. We show that this model, based on partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), is able to predict confidence of a decision maker based only on the data available to the experimenter. We test our model on two experiments on confidence-based decision making involving the well-known random dots motion discrimination task. In both experiments, we show that our model's predictions closely match experimental data. Additionally, our model is also consistent with other phenomena such as the hard-easy effect in perceptual decision making.

Additionally, our model is also consistent with other phenomena such as the hard-easy effect in perceptual decision making.

paragraphs: A person's confidence in a perceptual choice does not necessarily match how often that choice is correct. This makes accuracy alone an incomplete way to explain confidence. The paper introduces a Bayesian framework that treats confidence as something to model within the decision process, rather than simply equating it with observed success.

The framework uses partially observable Markov decision processes, which represent decisions made with incomplete information about the underlying situation. A central contribution is that the model predicts confidence using only information available to the experimenter. This connects a model of the decision maker's uncertainty to observations that can actually be collected in an experiment.

The authors test the framework in two experiments involving judgments about the direction of moving random dots. In both, predicted confidence closely matches the experimental data. The model is also consistent with the hard-easy effect. Together, these findings support the framework as an explanation of confidence in the studied perceptual tasks, while preserving the distinction between confidence and accuracy.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model predicts perceptual decision confidence from experimenter-accessible data and closely matches two random-dot motion experiments.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Modeling Confidence in Perceptual Decision Making

abstract: Neural circuits contain heterogeneous groups of neurons that differ in type, location, connectivity, and basic response properties. However, traditional methods for dimensionality reduction and clustering are ill-suited to recovering the structure underlying the organization of neural circuits. In particular, they do not take advantage of the rich temporal dependencies in multi-neuron recordings and fail to account for the noise in neural spike trains. Here we describe new tools for inferring latent structure from simultaneously recorded spike train data using a hierarchical extension of a multi-neuron point process model commonly known as the generalized linear model (GLM). Our approach combines the GLM with flexible graph-theoretic priors governing the relationship between latent features and neural connectivity patterns. Fully Bayesian inference via Pólya-gamma augmentation of the resulting model allows us to classify neurons and infer latent dimensions of circuit organization from correlated spike trains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with applications to synthetic data and multi-neuron recordings in primate retina, revealing latent patterns of neural types and locations from spike trains alone.

The authors argue that conventional clustering and dimensionality-reduction methods are poorly matched to this problem because they do not adequately use temporal dependencies or account for noise in the recordings.

Their approach extends a multi-neuron point-process generalized linear model into a hierarchical model. Flexible graph-based priors connect hidden neuronal features with patterns of connectivity. This makes temporal activity and circuit organization parts of the same inference problem, rather than treating the recorded activity only as material for a separate clustering step.

The authors perform fully Bayesian inference using Pólya-gamma augmentation. The resulting method can classify neurons and infer latent dimensions of circuit organization from correlated spike trains. Applications to synthetic data and primate-retina recordings reveal patterns associated with neural types and locations using spike recordings alone, demonstrating the approach’s ability to recover meaningful hidden structure in those settings.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model infers latent neural types and locations from spike trains by linking temporal activity with connectivity structure.

title: Bayesian latent structure discovery from multi-neuron recordings

abstract: In this work, we present an additive model for space-time data that splits the data into a temporally correlated component and a spatially correlated component. We model the spatially correlated portion using a time-varying Gaussian graphical model. Under assumptions on the smoothness of changes in covariance matrices, we derive strong single sample convergence results, confirming our ability to estimate meaningful graphical structures as they evolve over time. We apply our methodology to the discovery of time-varying spatial structures in human brain fMRI signals.

We model the spatially correlated portion using a time-varying Gaussian graphical model. Under assumptions on the smoothness of changes in covariance matrices, we derive strong single sample convergence results, confirming our ability to estimate meaningful graphical structures as they evolve over time. We apply our methodology to the discovery of time-varying spatial structures in human brain fMRI signals.

paragraphs: Data recorded across locations and time can contain both temporal correlations and spatial relationships. This paper proposes an additive model that separates these into two components. One captures correlation over time, while the other represents spatial correlation. The separation provides a framework for studying how spatial relationships themselves evolve.

The spatial component uses a time-varying Gaussian graphical model. Its graphical structure represents relationships among spatial variables, and allowing it to change makes evolving patterns part of the model. This directly addresses the goal of estimating spatial structure over time, rather than summarizing the whole recording with a single fixed graph.

Under assumptions that covariance matrices change smoothly, the authors derive strong convergence results from a single sample. Those assumptions are part of the theoretical basis for recovering meaningful evolving structures. They apply the method to human brain fMRI signals to discover time-varying spatial patterns, connecting the statistical model and its guarantees to the analysis of changing brain measurements.
summary.tldr: An additive space-time model estimates evolving spatial graphs, with single-sample convergence guarantees under covariance-smoothness assumptions.

title: Time-dependent spatially varying graphical models, with application to brain fMRI data analysis

abstract: Deep neural networks are commonly developed and trained in 32-bit floating point format. Significant gains in performance and energy efficiency could be realized by training and inference in numerical formats optimized for deep learning. Despite advances in limited precision inference in recent years, training of neural networks in low bit-width remains a challenging problem. Here we present the Flexpoint data format, aiming at a complete replacement of 32-bit floating point format training and inference, designed to support modern deep network topologies without modifications. Flexpoint tensors have a shared exponent that is dynamically adjusted to minimize overflows and maximize available dynamic range. We validate Flexpoint by training AlexNet, a deep residual network and a generative adversarial network, using a simulator implemented with the \emph{neon} deep learning framework. We demonstrate that 16-bit Flexpoint closely matches 32-bit floating point in training all three models, without any need for tuning of model hyperparameters. Our results suggest Flexpoint as a promising numerical format for future hardware for training and inference.

Flexpoint is a numerical format intended to replace 32-bit floating-point arithmetic for both training and inference. Its design aims to support modern network architectures without requiring changes to their structure.

The key mechanism is a shared exponent for each tensor, adjusted dynamically to reduce overflow and make effective use of the available numerical range. This gives the format a way to adapt its representation as the values encountered during computation change. The approach addresses numerical representation directly while seeking to preserve existing model configurations.

The authors evaluate Flexpoint in a simulator built with the neon framework, training AlexNet, a deep residual network, and a generative adversarial network. Across these three models, 16-bit Flexpoint closely matches 32-bit floating-point training without model hyperparameter tuning. The findings support Flexpoint as a candidate for future training and inference hardware; the reported validation establishes simulated training behavior rather than measured hardware energy gains.
summary.tldr: Flexpoint dynamically adjusts shared tensor exponents so simulated 16-bit training closely matches 32-bit training on three networks.

title: Flexpoint: An Adaptive Numerical Format for Efficient Training of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We study a distributionally robust mean square error estimation problem over a nonconvex Wasserstein ambiguity set containing only normal distributions. We show that the optimal estimator and the least favorable distribution form a Nash equilibrium. Despite the non-convex nature of the ambiguity set, we prove that the estimation problem is equivalent to a tractable convex program. We further devise a Frank-Wolfe algorithm for this convex program whose direction-searching subproblem can be solved in a quasi-closed form. Using these ingredients, we introduce a distributionally robust Kalman filter that hedges against model risk.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation when the assumed probability distribution may be wrong. It minimizes mean squared estimation error while accounting for a collection of plausible distributions described using Wasserstein distance. The ambiguity set contains only normal distributions and is nonconvex, so the model uncertainty has a specific mathematical scope.

The authors prove that the optimal estimator and the least favorable distribution form a Nash equilibrium. This expresses a balance between choosing an estimator and choosing the most adverse distribution allowed by the uncertainty set. They also show that, despite the set's nonconvexity, the estimation problem has an equivalent tractable convex formulation.

To solve that formulation, the paper develops a Frank-Wolfe algorithm whose direction-search subproblem has a quasi-closed-form solution. These ingredients lead to a distributionally robust Kalman filter designed to hedge against model risk. The contribution combines a robust estimation formulation, a tractability result, and a computational method within the stated family of normal distributions.
summary.tldr: A tractable robust estimation formulation yields a Kalman filter that hedges against distributional uncertainty within a Wasserstein set of normal distributions.

title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Kalman Filtering

abstract: We study a simple variant of the von Neumann model of an expanding economy, in which multiple producers make goods according to their production function. The players trade their goods at the market and then use the bundles received as inputs for the production in the next round. The decision that players have to make is how to invest their money (i.e. bids) in each round. We show that a simple decentralized dynamic, where players update their bids on the goods in the market proportionally to how useful the investments were, leads to growth of the economy in the long term (whenever growth is possible) but also creates unbounded inequality, i.e. very rich and very poor players emerge. We analyze several other phenomena, such as how the relation of a player with others influences its development and the Gini index of the system.

paragraphs: This paper studies a simplified expanding economy in which producers repeatedly make goods, trade them, and use the goods they receive as inputs for the next production round. Each producer must decide how to distribute money among bids for available goods. Those repeated investment decisions connect individual behavior to the economy's long-term development.

The proposed decentralized rule updates bids in proportion to how useful earlier investments were. Producers therefore adjust their spending using the usefulness of their own purchases. The authors show that this simple dynamic leads to long-term economic growth whenever growth is possible within the model.

The same dynamic also produces unbounded inequality, with very rich and very poor participants emerging. Aggregate expansion therefore coexists with increasingly unequal outcomes in this setting. The paper further analyzes how a participant's relationships with others affect its development and examines the system's Gini index. These results describe the modeled production economy and its update rule, connecting a growth guarantee to a sharply unequal distribution of its benefits.
summary.tldr: In a simplified production economy, proportional bid updates achieve growth whenever possible while also generating unbounded inequality.

title: Universal Growth in Production Economies

abstract: Infants are experts at playing, with an amazing ability to generate novel structured behaviors in unstructured environments that lack clear extrinsic reward signals. We seek to mathematically formalize these abilities using a neural network that implements curiosity-driven intrinsic motivation. Using a simple but ecologically naturalistic simulated environment in which an agent can move and interact with objects it sees, we propose a "world-model" network that learns to predict the dynamic consequences of the agent's actions. Simultaneously, we train a separate explicit "self-model" that allows the agent to track the error map of its world-model. It then uses the self-model to adversarially challenge the developing world-model. We demonstrate that this policy causes the agent to explore novel and informative interactions with its environment, leading to the generation of a spectrum of complex behaviors, including ego-motion prediction, object attention, and object gathering. Moreover, the world-model that the agent learns supports improved performance on object dynamics prediction, detection, localization and recognition tasks. Taken together, our results are initial steps toward creating flexible autonomous agents that self-supervise in realistic physical environments.
