paragraphs: This paper investigates how an agent can develop useful behavior through curiosity when its environment provides no clear external reward. In a simulated setting, the agent can move and interact with visible objects. The learning system separates predicting the world from estimating where those predictions are likely to fail.

A world-model network learns the consequences of the agent's actions. Alongside it, an explicit self-model learns the pattern of errors made by the world model. The agent uses this second model to challenge its developing predictor, directing exploration toward novel and informative interactions. Here, self-awareness refers to tracking predictive errors through a separate learned model.

The resulting behavior includes ego-motion prediction, object attention, and object gathering. The learned world model also supports improved object-dynamics prediction, detection, localization, and recognition. These results connect curiosity-driven interaction with useful visual and physical representations. The authors present the work as an initial step toward flexible agents that can supervise their own learning in realistic physical environments.
summary.tldr: An agent learns to explore by modeling its own prediction errors, producing complex behaviors and more useful world representations.

title: Learning to Play With Intrinsically-Motivated, Self-Aware Agents

abstract: Knowledge graph reasoning, which aims at predicting missing facts through reasoning with observed facts, is critical for many applications. Such a problem has been widely explored by traditional logic rule-based approaches and recent knowledge graph embedding methods. A principled logic rule-based approach is the Markov Logic Network (MLN), which is able to leverage domain knowledge with first-order logic and meanwhile handle uncertainty. However, the inference in MLNs is usually very difficult due to the complicated graph structures. Different from MLNs, knowledge graph embedding methods (e.g. TransE, DistMult) learn effective entity and relation embeddings for reasoning, which are much more effective and efficient. However, they are unable to leverage domain knowledge. In this paper, we propose the probabilistic Logic Neural Network (pLogicNet), which combines the advantages of both methods. A pLogicNet defines the joint distribution of all possible triplets by using a Markov logic network with first-order logic, which can be efficiently optimized with the variational EM algorithm. Specifically, in the E-step, a knowledge graph embedding model is used for inferring the missing triplets, while in the M-step, the weights of the logic rules are updated according to both the observed and predicted triplets. Experiments on multiple knowledge graphs prove the effectiveness of pLogicNet over many competitive baselines.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph reasoning predicts missing facts from observed relationships. Logic-based methods can express domain rules and uncertainty, but inference in Markov Logic Networks can be difficult. Embedding methods learn useful numerical representations of entities and relations, yet the approaches discussed in the abstract do not incorporate domain knowledge. pLogicNet combines these two forms of reasoning.

The model uses a Markov Logic Network with first-order rules to define a joint distribution over possible triplets. It optimizes the model through variational expectation-maximization. In the expectation step, a knowledge graph embedding model infers missing triplets. In the maximization step, the system updates rule weights using both observed triplets and predicted ones.

This alternating procedure lets embedding-based predictions contribute to learning how strongly logical rules should influence the model. It also places those predictions within a framework that explicitly represents rule-based knowledge and uncertainty. Experiments on multiple knowledge graphs demonstrate effectiveness against many competitive baselines. The contribution is a coordinated learning procedure that brings these complementary modeling capabilities into one system.
summary.tldr: pLogicNet combines logical rules and knowledge graph embeddings through variational EM to infer missing facts and learn rule weights.

title: Probabilistic Logic Neural Networks for Reasoning

abstract: When approximating an integral by a weighted sum of function evaluations, determinantal point processes (DPPs) provide a way to enforce repulsion between the evaluation points. This negative dependence is encoded by a kernel. Fifteen years before the discovery of DPPs, Ermakov & Zolotukhin (EZ, 1960) had the intuition of sampling a DPP and solving a linear system to compute an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of the integral. In the absence of DPP machinery to derive an efficient sampler and analyze their estimator, the idea of Monte Carlo integration with DPPs was stored in the cellar of numerical integration. Recently, Bardenet & Hardy (BH, 2019) came up with a more natural estimator with a fast central limit theorem (CLT). In this paper, we first take the EZ estimator out of the cellar, and analyze it using modern arguments. Second, we provide an efficient implementation to sample exactly a particular multidimensional DPP called multivariate Jacobi ensemble. The latter satisfies the assumptions of the aforementioned CLT. Third, our new implementation lets us investigate the behavior of the two unbiased Monte Carlo estimators in yet unexplored regimes. We demonstrate experimentally good properties when the kernel is adapted to basis of functions in which the integrand is sparse or has fast-decaying coefficients. If such a basis and the level of sparsity are known (e.g., we integrate a linear combination of kernel eigenfunctions), the EZ estimator can be the right choice, but otherwise it can display an erratic behavior.

summary.tldr: The paper analyzes two DPP-based integration estimators and shows how their usefulness depends on matching kernels to integrand structure.

title: On two ways to use determinantal point processes for Monte Carlo integration

abstract: Evaluating novel contextual bandit policies using logged data is crucial in applications where exploration is costly, such as medicine. But it usually relies on the assumption of no unobserved confounders, which is bound to fail in practice. We study the question of policy evaluation when we instead have proxies for the latent confounders and develop an importance weighting method that avoids fitting a latent outcome regression model. Surprisingly, we show that there exist no single set of weights that give unbiased evaluation regardless of outcome model, unlike the case with no unobserved confounders where density ratios are sufficient. Instead, we propose an adversarial objective and weights that minimize it, ensuring sufficient balance in the latent confounders regardless of outcome model. We develop theory characterizing the consistency of our method and tractable algorithms for it. Empirical results validate the power of our method when confounders are latent.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new contextual bandit policy from logged data can avoid costly exploration, but standard approaches usually assume that no relevant confounders are unobserved. This paper considers a different setting: confounders remain latent, but proxies for them are available. The authors develop an importance-weighting method without fitting a latent outcome regression model.

A central theoretical finding explains why this setting is difficult. There is no single set of weights that yields unbiased policy evaluation for every outcome model. This differs from the unconfounded case, where density ratios are sufficient. The result identifies a boundary on what a universal weighting solution can accomplish when confounders are hidden.

The proposed method instead chooses weights by minimizing an adversarial objective designed to ensure sufficient balance in the latent confounders regardless of the outcome model. The paper characterizes consistency theoretically and provides tractable algorithms. Empirical results support the approach when confounders are latent. Its contribution combines an impossibility result with a constructive balancing strategy for evaluation using proxy information.
summary.tldr: Proxy-based adversarial balancing enables policy evaluation with latent confounders despite the absence of universally unbiased importance weights.

title: Policy Evaluation with Latent Confounders via Optimal Balance

abstract: In performative prediction, the choice of a model influences the distribution of future data, typically through actions taken based on the model's predictions. We initiate the study of stochastic optimization for performative prediction. What sets this setting apart from traditional stochastic optimization is the difference between merely updating model parameters and deploying the new model. The latter triggers a shift in the distribution that affects future data, while the former keeps the distribution as is. Assuming smoothness and strong convexity, we prove rates of convergence for both greedily deploying models after each stochastic update (greedy deploy) as well as for taking several updates before redeploying (lazy deploy). In both cases, our bounds smoothly recover the optimal $O(1/k)$ rate as the strength of performativity decreases. Furthermore, they illustrate how depending on the strength of performative effects, there exists a regime where either approach outperforms the other. We experimentally explore the trade-off on both synthetic data and a strategic classification simulator.

paragraphs: A predictive model can change the data it will later encounter because people or systems act on its predictions. In this performative setting, updating parameters and deploying those parameters are different events. An internal update leaves the current data distribution unchanged, while deployment can alter the distribution from which future observations arrive.

The paper analyzes two deployment schedules for stochastic optimization. Greedy deployment releases the model after every update; lazy deployment performs several updates before releasing a new version. Assuming smoothness and strong convexity, the authors prove convergence rates for both schedules. Their bounds approach the optimal O(1/k) rate as the strength of the model's effect on the data decreases.

The bounds also identify regimes where either schedule can outperform the other, depending on the strength of performative effects. Experiments with synthetic data and a strategic-classification simulator explore this trade-off. Deployment frequency thus becomes part of the optimization problem, with the analysis supporting conditional choices rather than one universally preferable schedule.
summary.tldr: Under smoothness and strong convexity, deployment frequency creates a quantifiable convergence trade-off when predictions influence future data.

title: Stochastic Optimization for Performative Prediction

abstract: Resource scheduling and coordination is an NP-hard optimization requiring an efficient allocation of agents to a set of tasks with upper- and lower bound temporal and resource constraints. Due to the large-scale and dynamic nature of resource coordination in hospitals and factories, human domain experts manually plan and adjust schedules on the fly. To perform this job, domain experts leverage heterogeneous strategies and rules-of-thumb honed over years of apprenticeship. What is critically needed is the ability to extract this domain knowledge in a heterogeneous and interpretable apprenticeship learning framework to scale beyond the power of a single human expert, a necessity in safety-critical domains. We propose a personalized and interpretable apprenticeship scheduling algorithm that infers an interpretable representation of all human task demonstrators by extracting decision-making criteria via an inferred, personalized embedding non-parametric in the number of demonstrator types. We achieve near-perfect LfD accuracy in synthetic domains and 88.22\% accuracy on a planning domain with real-world data, outperforming baselines. Finally, our user study showed our methodology produces more interpretable and easier-to-use models than neural networks ($p < 0.05$).

paragraphs: Scheduling in hospitals and factories requires allocating people or other agents to tasks while respecting time and resource constraints. Human experts handle changing conditions using strategies developed through experience. This paper aims to learn those strategies from demonstrations while preserving both differences among demonstrators and an understandable account of their decisions.

The proposed apprenticeship scheduling algorithm infers personalized embeddings and extracts decision-making criteria into an interpretable representation. Its formulation does not require fixing the number of demonstrator types in advance. This addresses the heterogeneity of expert behavior: the learning system can represent differing approaches within a shared scheduling framework.

The authors report near-perfect learning-from-demonstration accuracy in synthetic domains and 88.22% accuracy in a planning domain using real-world data, outperforming baselines. A user study also finds the resulting models more interpretable and easier to use than neural networks, with p below 0.05. The results support both accurate imitation of demonstrated decisions and improved usability in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A personalized scheduling learner extracts interpretable decision rules from heterogeneous demonstrations and reports strong imitation accuracy and usability.

title: Interpretable and Personalized Apprenticeship Scheduling: Learning Interpretable Scheduling Policies from Heterogeneous User Demonstrations

abstract: This work focuses on off-policy evaluation (OPE) with function approximation in infinite-horizon undiscounted Markov decision processes (MDPs). For MDPs that are ergodic and linear (i.e. where rewards and dynamics are linear in some known features), we provide the first finite-sample OPE error bound, extending the existing results beyond the episodic and discounted cases. In a more general setting, when the feature dynamics are approximately linear and for arbitrary rewards, we propose a new approach for estimating stationary distributions with function approximation. We formulate this problem as finding the maximum-entropy distribution subject to matching feature expectations under empirical dynamics. We show that this results in an exponential-family distribution whose sufficient statistics are the features, paralleling maximum-entropy approaches in supervised learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed OPE approaches in multiple environments.

In a more general setting, when the feature dynamics are approximately linear and for arbitrary rewards, we propose a new approach for estimating stationary distributions with function approximation. We formulate this problem as finding the maximum-entropy distribution subject to matching feature expectations under empirical dynamics. We show that this results in an exponential-family distribution whose sufficient statistics are the features, paralleling maximum-entropy approaches in supervised learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed OPE approaches in multiple environments.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using data collected under another policy. This paper studies that problem for systems that run indefinitely, measuring average reward without discounting future outcomes. It uses function approximation, so the evaluation can operate through features rather than a separate representation of every state.

For ergodic systems whose rewards and dynamics are linear in known features, the authors establish a finite-sample evaluation error bound. This extends the theoretical coverage beyond episodic and discounted settings. They also address a broader setting with approximately linear feature dynamics and arbitrary rewards by estimating the stationary distribution: the distribution describing long-run state occupancy.

Their estimator chooses the maximum-entropy distribution that matches feature expectations under dynamics estimated from data. This produces an exponential-family distribution defined by the features, connecting the approach to maximum-entropy methods in supervised learning. Experiments in multiple environments demonstrate the proposed approaches' effectiveness. The distinction between the settings matters: the finite-sample guarantee has stronger linearity assumptions than the broader distribution-estimation method.
summary.tldr: A maximum-entropy method estimates long-run policy performance, alongside finite-sample guarantees for ergodic MDPs with linear rewards and dynamics.

title: A Maximum-Entropy Approach to Off-Policy Evaluation in Average-Reward MDPs

abstract: Domains where supervised models are deployed often come with task-specific constraints, such as prior expert knowledge on the ground-truth function, or desiderata like safety and fairness. We introduce a novel probabilistic framework for reasoning with such constraints and formulate a prior that enables us to effectively incorporate them into Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), including a variant that can be amortized over tasks. The resulting Output-Constrained BNN (OC-BNN) is fully consistent with the Bayesian framework for uncertainty quantification and is amenable to black-box inference. Unlike typical BNN inference in uninterpretable parameter space, OC-BNNs widen the range of functional knowledge that can be incorporated, especially for model users without expertise in machine learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of OC-BNNs on real-world datasets, spanning multiple domains such as healthcare, criminal justice, and credit scoring.

That knowledge may come from domain expertise or requirements concerning safety and fairness. This paper develops a probabilistic way to incorporate such output-level constraints into Bayesian neural networks, making functional knowledge part of the modeling process.

The authors formulate a prior that produces an Output-Constrained Bayesian Neural Network. They also introduce a variant that can be amortized across tasks. The approach remains consistent with Bayesian uncertainty quantification and supports black-box inference, connecting interpretable constraints on model behavior to the machinery used to learn uncertain predictions.

The main practical appeal is that users can contribute knowledge about outputs without having to express it directly through difficult-to-interpret neural-network parameters. The authors demonstrate the framework on real-world datasets from healthcare, criminal justice, and credit scoring. These demonstrations support its usefulness for incorporating a wider range of functional knowledge; they do not turn safety or fairness desiderata into a universal guarantee about every deployment.
summary.tldr: Output-Constrained Bayesian Neural Networks encode interpretable knowledge about desired outputs through a prior while retaining Bayesian uncertainty quantification.

title: Incorporating Interpretable Output Constraints in Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the identifiability theory of probabilistic models and establish sufficient conditions under which the representations learnt by a very broad family of conditional energy-based models are unique in function space, up to a simple transformation. In our model family, the energy function is the dot-product between two feature extractors, one for the dependent variable, and one for the conditioning variable. We show that under mild conditions, the features are unique up to scaling and permutation. Our results extend recent developments in nonlinear ICA, and in fact, they lead to an important generalization of ICA models. In particular, we show that our model can be used for the estimation of the components in the framework of Independently Modulated Component Analysis (IMCA), a new generalization of nonlinear ICA that relaxes the independence assumption. A thorough empirical study show that representations learnt by our model from real-world image datasets are identifiable, and improve performance in transfer learning and semi-supervised learning tasks.

paragraphs: A learned representation is identifiable when the model determines its features uniquely apart from specified transformations. This paper establishes sufficient conditions for that property in a broad family of conditional energy-based models. The question concerns uniqueness of the learned functions, giving a precise meaning to when a representation is determined by the model.

The energy function is a dot product between two feature extractors: one processes the dependent variable and the other the conditioning variable. Under the stated mild conditions, the features are unique up to scaling and permutation. Thus, their magnitudes and ordering may change while the underlying representation remains equivalent in the sense established by the theory.

The results extend nonlinear independent component analysis and support Independently Modulated Component Analysis, a framework that relaxes the independence assumption. Experiments on real-world image datasets show identifiable representations and improvements in transfer and semi-supervised learning. Together, the theory and experiments connect a conditional uniqueness guarantee with useful learned features, without asserting identifiability outside the sufficient conditions.
summary.tldr: ICE-BeeM establishes sufficient conditions for identifiable conditional energy-based representations and reports benefits in transfer and semi-supervised learning.

title: ICE-BeeM: Identifiable Conditional Energy-Based Deep Models Based on Nonlinear ICA

abstract: In risk-sensitive learning, one aims to find a hypothesis that minimizes a risk-averse (or risk-seeking) measure of loss, instead of the standard expected loss. In this paper, we propose to study the generalization properties of risk-sensitive learning schemes whose optimand is described via optimized certainty equivalents (OCE): our general scheme can handle various known risks, e.g., the entropic risk, mean-variance, and conditional value-at-risk, as special cases. We provide two learning bounds on the performance of empirical OCE minimizer. The first result gives an OCE guarantee based on the Rademacher average of the hypothesis space, which generalizes and improves existing results on the expected loss and the conditional value-at-risk. The second result, based on a novel variance-based characterization of OCE, gives an expected loss guarantee with a suppressed dependence on the smoothness of the selected OCE. Finally, we demonstrate the practical implications of the proposed bounds via exploratory experiments on neural networks.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive learning chooses a model according to preferences about the distribution of losses, rather than simply their average. The paper studies how well such choices generalize from training data. It uses optimized certainty equivalents, or OCEs, as a common framework encompassing risks such as entropic risk, mean-variance objectives, and conditional value-at-risk.

The authors give two guarantees for a hypothesis that minimizes empirical OCE. The first directly bounds its OCE performance using the Rademacher average of the hypothesis space, a measure of that space's complexity. This extends and improves existing results for expected loss and conditional value-at-risk, connecting multiple risk objectives through one analysis.

The second guarantee concerns expected loss even though training optimizes a risk-sensitive objective. It uses a new variance-based characterization of OCE and reduces dependence on the chosen OCE's smoothness. The two bounds therefore address different questions: performance under the selected risk criterion and performance under average loss. Exploratory neural-network experiments illustrate practical implications of the theory, while the central contribution is the generalization analysis across these risk-sensitive learning schemes.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis gives risk-sensitive learners guarantees for both their chosen risk objective and expected loss.

title: Learning Bounds for Risk-sensitive Learning

abstract: Motivated by the problem of sampling from ill-conditioned log-concave distributions, we give a clean non-asymptotic convergence analysis of mirror-Langevin diffusions as introduced in Zhang et al. (2020). As a special case of this framework, we propose a class of diffusions called Newton-Langevin diffusions and prove that they converge to stationarity exponentially fast with a rate which not only is dimension-free, but also has no dependence on the target distribution. We give an application of this result to the problem of sampling from the uniform distribution on a convex body using a strategy inspired by interior-point methods. Our general approach follows the recent trend of linking sampling and optimization and highlights the role of the chi-squared divergence. In particular, it yields new results on the convergence of the vanilla Langevin diffusion in Wasserstein distance.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling from ill-conditioned log-concave distributions through mirror-Langevin diffusions. Its focus is a non-asymptotic convergence analysis: a quantitative account of how the sampling process approaches stationarity, rather than only a statement that convergence eventually occurs. This addresses the difficulty that motivates the work while connecting sampling to ideas from optimization.

Within the mirror-Langevin framework, the authors introduce Newton-Langevin diffusions. They prove exponential convergence to stationarity with a rate independent of both dimension and the target distribution. That independence is the striking theoretical finding: the stated rate avoids two sources of dependence that could otherwise make a convergence result less favorable as the sampling problem changes.

The authors apply the result to uniform sampling from a convex body using a strategy inspired by interior-point methods. Their broader analysis emphasizes chi-squared divergence as a way to study convergence and also yields new Wasserstein-distance results for ordinary Langevin diffusion. The claims concern convergence of the diffusions analyzed in the paper, giving a mathematical foundation for understanding these sampling processes.
summary.tldr: The paper proves exponential convergence for Newton-Langevin diffusions at a rate independent of dimension and target distribution.

title: Exponential ergodicity of mirror-Langevin diffusions

abstract: We propose a flexible gradient-based framework for learning linear programs from optimal decisions. Linear programs are often specified by hand, using prior knowledge of relevant costs and constraints. In some applications, linear programs must instead be learned from observations of optimal decisions. Learning from optimal decisions is a particularly challenging bilevel problem, and much of the related inverse optimization literature is dedicated to special cases. We tackle the general problem, learning all parameters jointly while allowing flexible parameterizations of costs, constraints, and loss functions. We also address challenges specific to learning linear programs, such as empty feasible regions and non-unique optimal decisions. Experiments show that our method successfully learns synthetic linear programs and minimum-cost multi-commodity flow instances for which previous methods are not directly applicable. We also provide a fast batch-mode PyTorch implementation of the homogeneous interior point algorithm, which supports gradients by implicit differentiation or backpropagation.

paragraphs: Linear programs are usually specified through known costs and constraints. In inverse settings, only examples of optimal decisions may be available, and the optimization problem itself must be inferred. This creates a challenging bilevel learning problem because model parameters affect the solutions used to compute the training loss.

The authors propose a gradient-based framework that jointly learns all parameters with flexible cost, constraint, and loss parameterizations. They address issues specific to linear programs, including empty feasible regions and multiple optimal decisions. A batched PyTorch implementation of a homogeneous interior-point algorithm supports implicit differentiation or backpropagation.

Experiments successfully learn synthetic linear programs and minimum-cost multicommodity-flow instances outside the direct scope of previous methods. The abstract does not claim unique identification of the original program from every dataset. Its contribution is a flexible computational framework for learning optimization models, supported by these demonstrations.
summary.tldr: A differentiable optimization framework learns linear-program costs and constraints from observed optimal decisions.

title: Learning Linear Programs from Optimal Decisions

abstract: Although the optimization objectives for learning neural networks are highly non-convex, gradient-based methods have been wildly successful at learning neural networks in practice. This juxtaposition has led to a number of recent studies on provable guarantees for neural networks trained by gradient descent. Unfortunately, the techniques in these works are often highly specific to the particular setup in each problem, making it difficult to generalize across different settings. To address this drawback in the literature, we propose a unified non-convex optimization framework for the analysis of neural network training. We introduce the notions of proxy convexity and proxy Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequalities, which are satisfied if the original objective function induces a proxy objective function that is implicitly minimized when using gradient methods. We show that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on objectives satisfying proxy convexity or the proxy PL inequality leads to efficient guarantees for proxy objective functions. We further show that many existing guarantees for neural networks trained by gradient descent can be unified through proxy convexity and proxy PL inequalities.

paragraphs: Neural-network training objectives are highly nonconvex, yet gradient methods often work well in practice. Many theoretical explanations address particular architectures or learning setups using specialized arguments. This paper proposes a common optimization framework intended to organize those guarantees and make their shared structure easier to identify.

The framework introduces proxy convexity and proxy Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequalities. These conditions connect the original training objective to a proxy objective that gradient methods implicitly minimize. The useful guarantee is therefore expressed through that proxy, allowing the analysis to capture progress without requiring the original neural-network objective itself to be convex.

The authors prove efficient guarantees for stochastic gradient descent when an objective satisfies either proposed condition. They also show that many existing results for gradient-trained neural networks fit within this framework. The contribution is a unifying analytical language, together with optimization results for objectives meeting its requirements. Its scope remains conditional: the paper does not claim every neural network satisfies these properties, but shows that they account for a range of previously established guarantees.
summary.tldr: Proxy convexity and proxy PL inequalities unify many gradient-based neural-network guarantees through implicitly minimized proxy objectives.

title: Proxy Convexity: A Unified Framework for the Analysis of Neural Networks Trained by Gradient Descent

abstract: We address Stackelberg models of combinatorial congestion games (CCGs); we aim to optimize the parameters of CCGs so that the selfish behavior of non-atomic players attains desirable equilibria. This model is essential for designing such social infrastructures as traffic and communication networks. Nevertheless, computational approaches to the model have not been thoroughly studied due to two difficulties: (I) bilevel-programming structures and (II) the combinatorial nature of CCGs. We tackle them by carefully combining (I) the idea of \textit{differentiable} optimization and (II) data structures called \textit{zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams} (ZDDs), which can compactly represent sets of combinatorial strategies. Our algorithm numerically approximates the equilibria of CCGs, which we can differentiate with respect to parameters of CCGs by automatic differentiation. With the resulting derivatives, we can apply gradient-based methods to Stackelberg models of CCGs. Our method is tailored to induce Nesterov's acceleration and can fully utilize the empirical compactness of ZDDs. These technical advantages enable us to deal with CCGs with a vast number of combinatorial strategies. Experiments on real-world network design instances demonstrate the practicality of our method.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose parameters of congestion games so that selfish behavior leads to desirable equilibria. They are difficult because the designer's optimization depends on players' equilibrium behavior, while the players themselves may choose among enormous collections of combinatorial strategies.

The proposed method combines differentiable optimization with zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams, which can represent strategy sets compactly. It numerically approximates an equilibrium and uses automatic differentiation to measure how that approximation changes with game parameters. These derivatives allow gradient-based optimization of the designer's choices within the Stackelberg formulation.

The algorithm is designed to incorporate Nesterov acceleration and exploit the compactness that decision diagrams exhibit empirically. Together, these properties let it handle games with vast strategy collections without treating every strategy as an isolated item. Experiments on real network-design instances demonstrate practical applicability, supporting the combination of compact representations and differentiable equilibrium computation.
summary.tldr: Compact decision diagrams and differentiable equilibrium approximations enable gradient-based design of large combinatorial congestion games.

title: Differentiable Equilibrium Computation with Decision Diagrams for Stackelberg Models of Combinatorial Congestion Games

abstract: In visual-input sim-to-real scenarios, to overcome the reality gap between images rendered in simulators and those from the real world, domain adaptation, i.e., learning an aligned representation space between simulators and the real world, then training and deploying policies in the aligned representation, is a promising direction. Previous methods focus on same-modal domain adaptation. However, those methods require building and running simulators that render high-quality images, which can be difficult and costly. In this paper, we consider a more cost-efficient setting of visual-input sim-to-real where only low-dimensional states are simulated. We first point out that the objective of learning mapping functions in previous methods that align the representation spaces is ill-posed, prone to yield an incorrect mapping. When the mapping crosses modalities, previous methods are easier to fail. Our algorithm, Cross-mOdal Domain Adaptation with Sequential structure (CODAS), mitigates the ill-posedness by utilizing the sequential nature of the data sampling process in RL tasks. Experiments on MuJoCo and Hand Manipulation Suite tasks show that the agents deployed with our method achieve similar performance as it has in the source domain, while those deployed with previous methods designed for same-modal domain adaptation suffer a larger performance gap.

paragraphs: Transferring a visual reinforcement learning policy from simulation to reality often requires aligning simulated and real images. That can make simulation expensive because it must produce high-quality visual output. This paper considers a cheaper setup: simulate only compact states, while the deployed agent receives images from the target environment.

The challenge is then alignment across different kinds of observations. The authors argue that earlier representation-matching objectives are ill-posed: they can produce an incorrect correspondence even when representations appear aligned. They find that crossing modalities makes this failure more likely. CODAS addresses the ambiguity by using the sequential structure of experience collected during reinforcement learning.

That temporal structure supplies information beyond matching observations individually, helping constrain the learned correspondence. Experiments on MuJoCo and Hand Manipulation Suite tasks show deployed agents performing similarly to their source-domain performance. Earlier methods designed for alignment within the same modality exhibit larger performance gaps. These results support the proposed route to transfer without requiring a simulator that renders high-quality images.
summary.tldr: CODAS uses sequential experience to align simulated compact states with visual observations, reducing the need for costly image-rendering simulators.

title: Cross-modal Domain Adaptation for Cost-Efficient Visual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The spectacular success of deep generative models calls for quantitative tools to measure their statistical performance. Divergence frontiers have recently been proposed as an evaluation framework for generative models, due to their ability to measure the quality-diversity trade-off inherent to deep generative modeling. We establish non-asymptotic bounds on the sample complexity of divergence frontiers. We also introduce frontier integrals which provide summary statistics of divergence frontiers. We show how smoothed estimators such as Good-Turing or Krichevsky-Trofimov can overcome the missing mass problem and lead to faster rates of convergence. We illustrate the theoretical results with numerical examples from natural language processing and computer vision.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves both the quality of its outputs and the diversity of what it produces. Divergence frontiers provide a framework for representing that trade-off. This paper studies how reliably those frontiers can be estimated from samples, making the evaluation procedure itself an object of statistical analysis.

The authors establish non-asymptotic sample-complexity bounds. These concern finite amounts of data, rather than only describing what happens as the sample size grows without limit. They also introduce frontier integrals, summary statistics that condense information from a frontier. This connects a trade-off representation with quantities that can be used to summarize model performance.

A central estimation issue is missing mass: probability associated with outcomes that do not appear in the observed sample. The paper shows how smoothing methods, including Good–Turing and Krichevsky–Trofimov estimators, can address this problem and achieve faster convergence. Numerical examples from language and vision illustrate the theory. The contribution helps explain both the data requirements of frontier-based evaluation and how estimator choice affects its reliability.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes finite-sample guarantees and improved estimators for evaluating generative models through quality–diversity frontiers.

title: Divergence Frontiers for Generative Models: Sample Complexity, Quantization Effects, and Frontier Integrals

abstract: Learning neural radiance fields of a scene has recently allowed realistic novel view synthesis of the scene, but they are limited to synthesize images under the original fixed lighting condition. Therefore, they are not flexible for the eagerly desired tasks like relighting, scene editing and scene composition. To tackle this problem, several recent methods propose to disentangle reflectance and illumination from the radiance field. These methods can cope with solid objects with opaque surfaces but participating media are neglected. Also, they take into account only direct illumination or at most one-bounce indirect illumination, thus suffer from energy loss due to ignoring the high-order indirect illumination. We propose to learn neural representations for participating media with a complete simulation of global illumination. We estimate direct illumination via ray tracing and compute indirect illumination with spherical harmonics. Our approach avoids computing the lengthy indirect bounces and does not suffer from energy loss. Our experiments on multiple scenes show that our approach achieves superior visual quality and numerical performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, and it can generalize to deal with solid objects with opaque surfaces as well.

paragraphs: This paper extends neural scene representations toward relighting participating media, where light interacts throughout a medium rather than only at opaque surfaces. The authors identify two shortcomings in the approaches they discuss: neglect of participating media and omission of higher-order indirect illumination. Ignoring those indirect contributions can lead to energy loss in rendered results.

Their method learns a neural representation with a complete simulation of global illumination. It estimates direct lighting through ray tracing and handles indirect lighting with spherical harmonics. The contribution is therefore both a broader treatment of scene materials and a different way to compute lighting, supporting relightable representations that include illumination effects omitted by the methods motivating the work.
summary.tldr: A neural rendering method combines ray tracing and spherical harmonics to relight participating media while accounting for higher-order indirect illumination.

title: Neural Relightable Participating Media Rendering

abstract: We detail a novel class of implicit neural models. Leveraging time-parallel methods for differential equations, Multiple Shooting Layers (MSLs) seek solutions of initial value problems via parallelizable root-finding algorithms. MSLs broadly serve as drop-in replacements for neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs) with improved efficiency in number of function evaluations (NFEs) and wall-clock inference time. We develop the algorithmic framework of MSLs, analyzing the different choices of solution methods from a theoretical and computational perspective. MSLs are showcased in long horizon optimal control of ODEs and PDEs and as latent models for sequence generation. Finally, we investigate the speedups obtained through application of MSL inference in neural controlled differential equations (Neural CDEs) for time series classification of medical data.

This paper introduces Multiple Shooting Layers, an implicit neural model that approaches this computation through methods designed to work across time in parallel. The goal is to make differential-equation-based inference more efficient while retaining its role within trainable neural architectures.

The layers solve initial value problems using parallelizable root-finding algorithms. This makes the numerical solution method a central part of the model design. The authors develop a framework for these layers and examine alternative solution methods from both theoretical and computational perspectives, connecting algorithmic choices to the work required for inference.

Multiple Shooting Layers are presented as broadly usable replacements for Neural ODEs, with improvements in function evaluations and elapsed inference time. Demonstrations cover long-horizon control involving ordinary and partial differential equations, plus latent models for sequence generation. The paper also investigates inference speedups in Neural CDEs used to classify medical time series, extending the approach across several kinds of dynamical learning tasks.
summary.tldr: Multiple Shooting Layers use parallelizable differential-equation solvers to improve the inference efficiency of neural dynamical models.

title: Differentiable Multiple Shooting Layers

abstract: Neural network based deep learning techniques have shown great success for numerous applications. While it is expected to understand their intrinsic decision-making processes, these deep neural networks often work in a black-box way. To this end, in this paper, we aim to discern the decision-making processes of neural networks through a hierarchical voting strategy by developing an explainable deep learning model, namely Voting Transformation-based Explainable Neural Network (VOTEN). Specifically, instead of relying on massive feature combinations, VOTEN creatively models expressive single-valued voting functions between explicitly modeled latent concepts to achieve high fitting ability. Along this line, we first theoretically analyze the major components of VOTEN and prove the relationship and advantages of VOTEN compared with Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the basic structure of deep neural networks. Moreover, we design efficient algorithms to improve the model usability by explicitly showing the decision processes of VOTEN. Finally, extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets clearly validate the performances and explainability of VOTEN.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the difficulty of understanding how a deep neural network reaches a decision. It introduces VOTEN, an explainable network built around hierarchical voting between explicitly represented latent concepts. The aim is to make the decision process visible through the model's own structure while retaining the ability to fit complex data.

VOTEN uses expressive single-valued voting functions to connect these concepts. This makes the functions between concepts central to both prediction and explanation, rather than relying on large combinations of features. The authors theoretically analyze its main components and establish relationships and advantages relative to a multilayer perceptron, the basic architecture underlying many neural networks.

The paper also develops efficient algorithms that explicitly display VOTEN's decision process, making the architecture more usable as an explanatory model. Experiments across multiple real-world datasets support its predictive performance and explainability. The contribution combines an architecture designed for interpretable decisions, a theoretical comparison with a familiar network structure, and empirical evidence about its behavior.
summary.tldr: VOTEN models decisions as hierarchical votes between latent concepts, combining predictive fitting with explicit decision-process explanations.

title: Discerning Decision-Making Process of Deep Neural Networks with Hierarchical Voting Transformation

abstract: We address the unsolved algorithm design problem of choosing a justified regularization parameter in unsupervised domain adaptation. This problem is intriguing as no labels are available in the target domain. Our approach starts with the observation that the widely-used method of minimizing the source error, penalized by a distance measure between source and target feature representations, shares characteristics with regularized ill-posed inverse problems. Regularization parameters in inverse problems are optimally chosen by the fundamental principle of balancing approximation and sampling errors. We use this principle to balance learning errors and domain distance in a target error bound. As a result, we obtain a theoretically justified rule for the choice of the regularization parameter. In contrast to the state of the art, our approach allows source and target distributions with disjoint supports. An empirical comparative study on benchmark datasets underpins the performance of our approach.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation must transfer a model to a target domain without target labels. A common objective combines source-domain prediction error with a penalty measuring the distance between source and target feature representations. Choosing the penalty's weight is difficult because target labels are unavailable to directly assess that choice.

This paper connects the parameter-selection problem to regularized ill-posed inverse problems. In that setting, a balancing principle chooses regularization by trading off approximation and sampling errors. The authors adapt the principle to balance learning errors and domain distance within a target-error bound, obtaining a theoretically justified rule for choosing the regularization parameter.

The approach permits source and target distributions with disjoint supports, so its applicability does not require those distributions to overlap in that sense. A comparative study on benchmark datasets supports the method's performance. The contribution is a principled way to set an influential adaptation parameter under the actual information constraint of the task: the target domain supplies no labels.
summary.tldr: A balancing principle yields a theoretically justified regularization choice for unsupervised domain adaptation, including distributions with disjoint supports.

title: The balancing principle for parameter choice in distance-regularized domain adaptation

abstract: Many widely used datasets for graph machine learning tasks have generally been homophilous, where nodes with similar labels connect to each other. Recently, new Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been developed that move beyond the homophily regime; however, their evaluation has often been conducted on small graphs with limited application domains. We collect and introduce diverse non-homophilous datasets from a variety of application areas that have up to 384x more nodes and 1398x more edges than prior datasets. We further show that existing scalable graph learning and graph minibatching techniques lead to performance degradation on these non-homophilous datasets, thus highlighting the need for further work on scalable non-homophilous methods. To address these concerns, we introduce LINKX --- a strong simple method that admits straightforward minibatch training and inference. Extensive experimental results with representative simple methods and GNNs across our proposed datasets show that LINKX achieves state-of-the-art performance for learning on non-homophilous graphs. Our codes and data are available at https://github.com/CUAI/Non-Homophily-Large-Scale.

paragraphs: Many graph-learning benchmarks connect nodes that tend to share labels, a property called homophily. Methods designed for graphs without that tendency had often been tested on small datasets from a narrow range of applications. This paper introduces more varied non-homophilous datasets, with up to 384 times as many nodes and 1,398 times as many edges as prior datasets.

The larger benchmarks expose a practical issue: existing scalable graph-learning and minibatching techniques suffer performance degradation on these data. Scaling a method to more nodes is therefore not the only concern. The method must also work when connections do not reliably link nodes with similar labels.

To address this combination, the authors introduce LINKX, a simple method that supports straightforward minibatch training and inference. Extensive comparisons with representative simple methods and graph neural networks show state-of-the-art performance across the proposed datasets. The paper contributes both a broader evaluation setting and evidence that a relatively simple method can perform strongly on large non-homophilous graphs.
summary.tldr: New large non-homophilous graph benchmarks expose scaling weaknesses, while LINKX achieves strong performance with straightforward minibatch computation.

title: Large Scale Learning on Non-Homophilous Graphs: New Benchmarks and Strong Simple Methods

abstract: We study the fundamental problem of ReLU regression, where the goal is to fit Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) to data. This supervised learning task is efficiently solvable in the realizable setting, but is known to be computationally hard with adversarial label noise. In this work, we focus on ReLU regression in the Massart noise model, a natural and well-studied semi-random noise model. In this model, the label of every point is generated according to a function in the class, but an adversary is allowed to change this value arbitrarily with some probability, which is {\em at most} $\eta < 1/2$. We develop an efficient algorithm that achieves exact parameter recovery in this model under mild anti-concentration assumptions on the underlying distribution. Such assumptions are necessary for exact recovery to be information-theoretically possible. We demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms naive applications of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ regression on both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: ReLU regression fits a rectified linear unit to labeled data. The task can be solved efficiently when the labels exactly follow the model, but arbitrary adversarial label noise makes it computationally hard. This paper examines an intermediate setting, Massart noise, in which corruption is adversarial but its probability is bounded.

Specifically, each point initially receives the label prescribed by a function in the target class. An adversary may replace that label with any value, but the replacement probability is at most η, with η below one half. The authors develop an efficient algorithm that exactly recovers the parameters under mild anti-concentration assumptions on the input distribution.

Those distributional assumptions matter: the abstract states that such assumptions are necessary for exact recovery to be possible from the available information. The theorem therefore combines a constrained corruption model with conditions on the data distribution. Experiments on synthetic and real data show substantial improvements over naive applications of L1 and L2 regression, complementing the conditional exact-recovery guarantee.
summary.tldr: An efficient ReLU regression algorithm exactly recovers parameters under Massart noise and mild anti-concentration assumptions.

title: ReLU Regression with Massart Noise

abstract: Identifying an effective model of a dynamical system from sensory data and using it for future state prediction and control is challenging. Recent data-driven algorithms based on Koopman theory are a promising approach to this problem, but they typically never update the model once it has been identified from a relatively small set of observation, thus making long-term prediction and control difficult for realistic systems, in robotics or fluid mechanics for example. This paper introduces a novel method for learning an embedding of the state space with linear dynamics from sensory data. Unlike previous approaches, the dynamics model can be updated online and thus easily applied to systems with non-linear dynamics in the original configuration space. The proposed approach is evaluated empirically on several classical dynamical systems and sensory modalities, with good performance on long-term prediction and control.

paragraphs: Predicting and controlling a dynamical system from sensory observations requires a useful model of how its state changes. The paper points to a weakness in existing data-driven Koopman approaches: they typically identify a model from a relatively small observation set and then leave it fixed. That can make long-term prediction and control difficult for realistic systems.

The proposed method learns an embedding of the state space in which dynamics are linear. This allows systems with nonlinear dynamics in their original configuration space to be modeled through a different representation. A central feature is that the dynamics model can be updated online, allowing learning to continue as sensory observations arrive.

The authors evaluate the method on several classical dynamical systems and sensory modalities, reporting good long-term prediction and control performance. The contribution combines a linear-dynamics representation with ongoing model updates. This addresses the stated difficulty of relying indefinitely on a model identified from a limited initial set of observations, while retaining the useful structure of linear dynamics in the learned space.
summary.tldr: The method learns a linear-dynamics embedding from sensory input and updates its dynamics model online for prediction and control.

title: Online Learning and Control of Complex Dynamical Systems from Sensory Input

abstract: We present the Habitat-Matterport 3D (HM3D) dataset. HM3D is a large-scale dataset of 1,000 building-scale 3D reconstructions from a diverse set of real-world locations. Each scene in the dataset consists of a textured 3D mesh reconstruction of interiors such as multi-ﬂoor residences, stores, and other private indoor spaces.HM3D surpasses existing datasets available for academic research in terms of physical scale, completeness of the reconstruction, and visual ﬁdelity. HM3D contains 112.5k m^2 of navigable space, which is 1.4 - 3.7× larger than other building-scale datasets (MP3D, Gibson). When compared to existing photorealistic 3D datasets (Replica, MP3D, Gibson, ScanNet), rendered images from HM3D have 20 - 85% higher visual ﬁdelity w.r.t. counterpart images captured with real cameras, and HM3D meshes have 34 - 91% fewer artifacts due to incomplete surface reconstruction.The increased scale, ﬁdelity, and diversity of HM3D directly impacts the performance of embodied AI agents trained using it. In fact, we ﬁnd that HM3D is ‘pareto optimal’ in the following sense – agents trained to perform PointGoal navigation on HM3D achieve the highest performance regardless of whether they are evaluated on HM3D, Gibson, or MP3D. No similar claim can be made about training on other datasets. HM3D-trained PointNav agents achieve 100% performance on Gibson-test dataset, suggesting that it might be time to retire that episode dataset. The HM3D dataset, analysis code, and pre-trained models are publicly released: https://aihabitat.org/datasets/hm3d/.

paragraphs: HM3D supplies 1,000 building-scale reconstructions of real indoor environments, including residences and stores. Each environment is a textured three-dimensional mesh. Its 112,500 square meters of navigable space provide a large collection of settings for training agents that learn to move through virtual representations of physical places.

The paper reports advantages over the comparison datasets in scale, visual fidelity, and reconstruction completeness. Navigable area is 1.4–3.7 times larger than MP3D and Gibson. Across the stated photorealistic dataset comparisons, rendered images have 20–85% higher fidelity relative to real camera images, and meshes have 34–91% fewer artifacts associated with incomplete surface reconstruction.

summary.tldr: HM3D offers 1,000 detailed indoor reconstructions and yields the strongest reported PointGoal navigation results across three evaluation datasets.

title: Habitat-Matterport 3D Dataset (HM3D): 1000 Large-scale 3D Environments for Embodied AI

abstract: By forcing N out of M consecutive weights to be non-zero, the recent N:M fine-grained network sparsity has received increasing attention with its two attractive advantages over traditional irregular network sparsity methods: 1) Promising performance at a high sparsity. 2) Significant speedups when performed on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Current implementation on N:M sparsity requires a tedious pre-training phase or computationally heavy from-scratch training. To circumvent these problems, this paper presents an efficient solution for achieving N:M fine-grained sparsity from scratch. Specifically, we first make a re-formulation to convert the N:M fine-grained sparsity into a combinatorial problem, in which, the object falls into choosing the best weight combination among $C_M^N$ candidates. Then, we equip each combination with a learnable importance score, which can be jointly optimized along with its associated weights. Through rigorous proof, we demonstrate that the magnitude of the optimized score well reflects the importance of its corresponding weights combination to the training loss. Therefore, by gradually removing combinations with smaller scores till the best one is left, N:M fine-grained sparsity can be efficiently optimized during the normal training phase without any extra expenditure. Comprehensive experimental results have demonstrated that our proposed method for learning best combination, dubbed as LBC, consistently increases the efficacy of the off-the-shelf N:M methods across varying networks and datasets. Our project is released at https://github.com/zyxxmu/LBC.

paragraphs: N:M sparsity constrains each group of M consecutive network weights to contain N nonzero weights. This structure can combine strong predictive performance with acceleration on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, but existing training approaches can require pretraining or expensive training from scratch. This paper proposes learning the sparse structure during ordinary training.

The method, called Learning Best Combination, treats each group as a choice among all possible combinations of N retained weights. Every candidate combination receives a learnable importance score that is optimized jointly with its weights. The authors prove that the magnitude of an optimized score reflects the corresponding combination's importance to the training loss.

Training progressively removes combinations with smaller scores until one remains. This connects the final sparsity pattern to learned combination-level importance and avoids a separate pretraining phase. Across the networks and datasets examined, the method consistently improves the efficacy of existing N:M approaches. Its main contribution is making structured sparsity a selection process embedded in training, with theoretical support for the scores used to make those selections.
summary.tldr: LBC learns scores for candidate weight combinations and progressively selects an N:M sparse pattern during training from scratch.

title: Learning Best Combination for Efficient N:M Sparsity

abstract: A fundamental ability of an intelligent web-based agent is seeking out and acquiring new information. Internet search engines reliably find the correct vicinity but the top results may be a few links away from the desired target. A complementary approach is navigation via hyperlinks, employing a policy that comprehends local content and selects a link that moves it closer to the target. In this paper, we show that behavioral cloning of randomly sampled trajectories is sufficient to learn an effective link selection policy. We demonstrate the approach on a graph version of Wikipedia with 38M nodes and 387M edges. The model is able to efficiently navigate between nodes 5 and 20 steps apart 96% and 92% of the time, respectively. We then use the resulting embeddings and policy in downstream fact verification and question answering tasks where, in combination with basic TF-IDF search and ranking methods, they are competitive results to the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Finding information online can require several hyperlink steps after a search engine reaches the right neighborhood. This paper studies a navigation policy that reads local content and chooses links that move toward a target. Its central question is whether useful navigation can be learned from randomly sampled trajectories.

The authors show that behavioral cloning of those trajectories is sufficient to learn an effective link-selection policy in their setting. They evaluate the approach on a Wikipedia graph containing 38 million nodes and 387 million edges. The model successfully navigates between nodes five steps apart 96% of the time and between nodes twenty steps apart 92% of the time.

The learned embeddings and navigation policy are also used for fact verification and question answering. Combined with basic TF-IDF search and ranking, they achieve results competitive with state-of-the-art methods. These findings connect hyperlink navigation to downstream information tasks: a policy trained from random walks can help acquire relevant information after an initial search, as well as navigate the graph itself.
summary.tldr: Behavioral cloning of random walks learns effective Wikipedia navigation and supports competitive fact verification and question answering when combined with basic search.

title: Learning to Navigate Wikipedia by Taking Random Walks

abstract: Score-based generative models (SGMs) are a powerful class of generative models that exhibit remarkable empirical performance.Score-based generative modelling (SGM) consists of a ``noising'' stage, whereby a diffusion is used to gradually add Gaussian noise to data, and a generative model, which entails a ``denoising'' process defined by approximating the time-reversal of the diffusion. Existing SGMs assume that data is supported on a Euclidean space, i.e. a manifold with flat geometry. In many domains such as robotics, geoscience or protein modelling, data is often naturally described by distributions living on Riemannian manifolds and current SGM techniques are not appropriate. We introduce here \emph{Riemannian Score-based Generative Models} (RSGMs), a class of generative models extending SGMs to Riemannian manifolds. We demonstrate our approach on a variety of compact manifolds, and in particular with earth and climate science spherical data.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn to generate data by approximately reversing a process that gradually adds noise. Standard versions assume that data lives in a flat Euclidean space. This paper addresses settings where the natural space of the data has curved geometry, as can occur in robotics, geoscience, and protein modeling.

The authors introduce Riemannian Score-based Generative Models, extending the score-based approach to Riemannian manifolds. The central change is to formulate the generative process for the geometry on which the distribution lives. This matters because the space containing the data is part of the modeling problem, and existing flat-space techniques are not appropriate for the manifold settings considered.

The approach is demonstrated on several compact manifolds, including spherical data from earth and climate science. These examples establish the method's application to curved data domains. The contribution is therefore an extension of the noising-and-denoising framework that makes score-based generation applicable to distributions whose natural geometry is more structured than ordinary flat coordinates.
summary.tldr: Riemannian score-based models extend diffusion-style generation to curved spaces, with demonstrations including spherical earth and climate data.

title: Riemannian Score-Based Generative Modelling

abstract: Improving the performance of deep networks in data-limited regimes has warranted much attention. In this work, we empirically show that “winning tickets” (small sub-networks) obtained via magnitude pruning based on the lottery ticket hypothesis, apart from being sparse are also effective recognizers in data-limited regimes. Based on extensive experiments, we find that in low data regimes (datasets of 50-100 examples per class), sparse winning tickets substantially outperform the original dense networks. This approach, when combined with augmentations or fine-tuning from a self-supervised backbone network, shows further improvements in performance by as much as 16% (absolute) on low-sample datasets and long-tailed classification. Further, sparse winning tickets are more robust to synthetic noise and distribution shifts compared to their dense counterparts. Our analysis of winning tickets on small datasets indicates that, though sparse, the networks retain density in the initial layers and their representations are more generalizable. Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/DataEfficientLTH.

paragraphs: This paper examines small subnetworks called winning tickets as image recognizers when training data are scarce. The subnetworks are obtained through magnitude pruning under the lottery ticket hypothesis. The main empirical finding is that sparsity can accompany improved recognition: with 50–100 examples per class, these subnetworks substantially outperform their original dense networks.

The authors also combine winning tickets with data augmentation and with fine-tuning from a self-supervised backbone. These combinations produce further improvements, reaching as much as 16 percentage points on low-sample datasets and long-tailed classification. The results show that the benefits observed for sparse subnetworks can work alongside these additional approaches to learning from limited data.

Further experiments find greater robustness to synthetic noise and distribution shifts than in the dense counterparts. Analysis shows that the sparse networks retain relatively dense initial layers and learn more generalizable representations. Together, these observations support using winning tickets as data-efficient recognizers in the studied settings. The paper's evidence concerns their empirical recognition and robustness benefits as well as their reduced number of weights.
summary.tldr: Magnitude-pruned winning tickets outperform dense image networks in studied low-data settings and show improved robustness to noise and distribution shifts.

title: Sparse Winning Tickets are Data-Efficient Image Recognizers

abstract: Light-weight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are specially designed for applications on mobile devices with faster inference speed. The convolutional operation can only capture local information in a window region, which prevents performance from being further improved. Introducing self-attention into convolution can capture global information well, but it will largely encumber the actual speed. In this paper, we propose a hardware-friendly attention mechanism (dubbed DFC attention) and then present a new GhostNetV2 architecture for mobile applications. The proposed DFC attention is constructed based on fully-connected layers, which can not only execute fast on common hardware but also capture the dependence between long-range pixels. We further revisit the expressiveness bottleneck in previous GhostNet and propose to enhance expanded features produced by cheap operations with DFC attention, so that a GhostNetV2 block can aggregate local and long-range information simultaneously. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of GhostNetV2 over existing architectures. For example, it achieves 75.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 167M FLOPs, significantly suppressing GhostNetV1 (74.5%) with a similar computational cost. The source code will be available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Efficient-AI-Backbones/tree/master/ghostnetv2_pytorch and https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/ghostnetv2.

The convolutional operation can only capture local information in a window region, which prevents performance from being further improved. In this paper, we propose a hardware-friendly attention mechanism (dubbed DFC attention) and then present a new GhostNetV2 architecture for mobile applications. The proposed DFC attention is constructed based on fully-connected layers, which can not only execute fast on common hardware but also capture the dependence between long-range pixels. We further revisit the expressiveness bottleneck in previous GhostNet and propose to enhance expanded features produced by cheap operations with DFC attention, so that a GhostNetV2 block can aggregate local and long-range information simultaneously. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of GhostNetV2 over existing architectures. For example, it achieves 75.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 167M FLOPs, significantly suppressing GhostNetV1 (74.5%) with a similar computational cost. The source code will be available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Efficient-AI-Backbones/tree/master/ghostnetv2_pytorch and https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/ghostnetv2.

paragraphs: Lightweight convolutional networks aim to make prediction fast enough for mobile applications. Their local convolution windows, however, limit how directly they capture relationships between distant image regions. Adding self-attention can supply global information, but its practical speed cost creates a problem for architectures designed around efficient inference.

GhostNetV2 introduces DFC attention, a mechanism built from fully connected layers that captures dependencies between distant pixels while executing efficiently on common hardware. The authors apply it to features expanded through GhostNet's inexpensive operations. A resulting block combines local information with longer-range relationships, addressing an expressiveness bottleneck in the earlier architecture.

Experiments report improvements over existing architectures. One concrete result is 75.3% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 167 million floating-point operations, compared with GhostNetV1's 74.5% at similar computational cost. This comparison supports the value of enriching cheaply generated features with broader context. The architecture's contribution is therefore both where it adds attention and how it implements that attention for mobile-oriented computation.
summary.tldr: GhostNetV2 enriches inexpensive convolutional features with hardware-friendly long-range attention, improving ImageNet accuracy at similar computational cost.

title: GhostNetV2: Enhance Cheap Operation with Long-Range Attention

abstract: Protecting the privacy of user data is crucial for text generation models, which can leak sensitive information during generation. Differentially private (DP) learning methods provide guarantees against identifying the existence of a training sample from model outputs. PATE is a recent DP learning algorithm that achieves high utility with strong privacy protection on training samples. However, text generation models output tokens sequentially in a large output space; the classic PATE algorithm is not customized for this setting. Furthermore, PATE works well to protect sample-level privacy, but is not designed to protect phrases in samples. In this paper, we propose SeqPATE, an extension of PATE to text generation that protects the privacy of individual training samples and sensitive phrases in training data. To adapt PATE to text generation, we generate pseudo-contexts and reduce the sequence generation problem to a next-word prediction problem. To handle the large output space, we propose a candidate filtering strategy to dynamically reduce the output space, and refine the teacher aggregation of PATE to avoid low agreement due to voting for a large number of candidates. To further reduce privacy losses, we use knowledge distillation to reduce the number of teacher queries. The experiments verify the effectiveness of SeqPATE in protecting both training samples and sensitive phrases.

Experiments support its effectiveness in protecting both training samples and sensitive phrases. The paper's contribution is a coordinated adaptation of context generation, candidate selection, aggregation, and distillation so that private teacher-based learning can serve sequential text models.
summary.tldr: SeqPATE adapts private teacher aggregation and distillation to text generation, protecting training samples and sensitive phrases.

title: SeqPATE: Differentially Private Text Generation via Knowledge Distillation

abstract: The collaborative inference systems are designed to speed up the prediction processes in edge-cloud scenarios, where the local devices and the cloud system work together to run a complex deep-learning model. However, those edge-cloud collaborative inference systems are vulnerable to emerging reconstruction attacks, where malicious cloud service providers are able to recover the edge-side users’ private data. To defend against such attacks, several defense countermeasures have been recently introduced. Unfortunately, little is known about the robustness of those defense countermeasures. In this paper, we take the first step towards measuring the robustness of those state-of-the-art defenses with respect to reconstruction attacks. Specifically, we show that the latent privacy features are still retained in the obfuscated representations. Motivated by such an observation, we design a technology called Sensitive Feature Distillation (SFD) to restore sensitive information from the protected feature representations. Our experiments show that SFD can break through defense mechanisms in model partitioning scenarios, demonstrating the inadequacy of existing defense mechanisms as a privacy-preserving technique against reconstruction attacks. We hope our findings inspire further work in improving the robustness of defense mechanisms against reconstruction attacks for collaborative inference systems.

This arrangement can expose private inputs because a malicious cloud provider may reconstruct them from the representations it receives. Existing defenses attempt to protect those representations, but their resistance to reconstruction needs to be tested.

The paper studies the robustness of such defenses and observes that sensitive information can remain in representations even after they have been obfuscated. Motivated by this finding, the authors develop Sensitive Feature Distillation, or SFD, to recover sensitive information from protected features. The method serves as a way to probe what the defenses actually conceal.
