These results demonstrate inadequacies in the tested mechanisms as protection against reconstruction attacks. The practical implication is that altering or obscuring a representation can leave recoverable private information inside it. By exposing this residual information, the work provides evidence for improving how collaborative-inference defenses are designed and assessed.
summary.tldr: Sensitive Feature Distillation recovers private information from protected intermediate representations, exposing weaknesses in evaluated collaborative-inference defenses.

title: Measuring Data Reconstruction Defenses in Collaborative Inference Systems

abstract: Equilibrium propagation (EP) is an alternative to backpropagation (BP) that allows the training of deep neural networks with local learning rules. It thus provides a compelling framework for training neuromorphic systems and understanding learning in neurobiology. However, EP requires infinitesimal teaching signals, thereby limiting its applicability to noisy physical systems. Moreover, the algorithm requires separate temporal phases and has not been applied to large-scale problems. Here we address these issues by extending EP to holomorphic networks. We show analytically that this extension naturally leads to exact gradients for finite-amplitude teaching signals. Importantly, the gradient can be computed as the first Fourier coefficient from finite neuronal activity oscillations in continuous time without requiring separate phases. Further, we demonstrate in numerical simulations that our approach permits robust estimation of gradients in the presence of noise and that deeper models benefit from the finite teaching signals. Finally, we establish the first benchmark for EP on the ImageNet $32 \times 32$ dataset and show that it matches the performance of an equivalent network trained with BP. Our work provides analytical insights that enable scaling EP to large-scale problems and establishes a formal framework for how oscillations could support learning in biological and neuromorphic systems.

paragraphs: Equilibrium propagation offers a way to train neural networks using local learning rules, making it relevant to neuromorphic systems and models of biological learning. However, its requirement for infinitesimal teaching signals is problematic in noisy physical systems. Separate temporal phases and limited application at scale present additional obstacles.

The paper extends equilibrium propagation to holomorphic networks. Within this framework, the authors analytically derive exact gradients using teaching signals with finite amplitude. The gradient can be obtained from the first Fourier coefficient of continuous neuronal activity oscillations. This provides a way to extract the learning signal from oscillatory activity without requiring separate phases.

Numerical simulations show robust gradient estimation in the presence of noise and benefits from finite teaching signals in deeper models. The authors also establish an equilibrium-propagation benchmark on ImageNet at 32-by-32 resolution, matching an equivalent network trained with backpropagation. The work combines an analytical gradient result with computational evidence, offering a formal account of how oscillations could support learning in biological or neuromorphic systems.
summary.tldr: Holomorphic equilibrium propagation derives exact gradients from finite oscillations and supports learning without separate temporal phases.

title: Holomorphic Equilibrium Propagation Computes Exact Gradients Through Finite Size Oscillations

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has witnessed significant progress with the development of value function factorization methods. It allows optimizing a joint action-value function through the maximization of factorized per-agent utilities. In this paper, we show that in partially observable MARL problems, an agent's ordering over its own actions could impose concurrent constraints (across different states) on the representable function class, causing significant estimation errors during training. We tackle this limitation and propose PAC, a new framework leveraging Assistive information generated from Counterfactual Predictions of optimal joint action selection, which enable explicit assistance to value function factorization through a novel counterfactual loss. A variational inference-based information encoding method is developed to collect and encode the counterfactual predictions from an estimated baseline. To enable decentralized execution, we also derive factorized per-agent policies inspired by a maximum-entropy MARL framework. We evaluate the proposed PAC on multi-agent predator-prey and a set of StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. Empirical results demonstrate improved results of PAC over state-of-the-art value-based and policy-based multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms on all benchmarks.

paragraphs: Value factorization helps multiple agents learn together by relating a joint action-value function to utilities for individual agents. This paper identifies a representational problem under partial observability: an agent's ordering of its actions can impose simultaneous constraints across different states. Those constraints can restrict the functions the system can represent and cause substantial estimation errors during training.

PAC adds assistance derived from counterfactual predictions of optimal joint action selection. A new counterfactual loss uses this information to guide value factorization. The framework also uses variational inference to collect and encode the predictions from an estimated baseline, making the additional information part of the learning procedure.

For decentralized execution, the authors derive separate per-agent policies inspired by maximum-entropy multi-agent reinforcement learning. They evaluate PAC on multi-agent predator-prey and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art value-based and policy-based methods on every evaluated benchmark. The results support counterfactual assistance as a way to address the identified training constraints while retaining decentralized policies.
summary.tldr: PAC uses counterfactual joint-action predictions to assist value factorization and improve learning under partial observability.

title: PAC: Assisted Value Factorization with Counterfactual Predictions in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning an optimal Individualized Treatment Rule (ITR) is a very important problem in precision medicine. This paper is concerned with the challenge when the number of treatment arms is large, and some groups of treatments in the large treatment space may work similarly for the patients. Motivated by the recent development of supervised clustering, we propose a novel adaptive fusion based method to cluster the treatments with similar treatment effects together and estimate the optimal ITR simultaneously through a single convex optimization. The problem is formulated as balancing \textit{loss}$+$\textit{penalty} terms with a tuning parameter, which allows the entire solution path of the treatment clustering process to be clearly visualized hierarchically. For computation, we propose an efficient algorithm based on accelerated proximal gradient and further conduct a novel group-lasso based algorithm for variable selection to boost the performance. Moreover, we demonstrate the theoretical guarantee of recovering the underlying true clustering structure of the treatments for our method. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method via both simulations and a real data application on cancer treatment, which may assist the decision making process for doctors.

paragraphs: An individualized treatment rule selects a treatment using a patient's characteristics. Learning such a rule becomes challenging when many treatments are available, especially when some treatments may have similar effects. This paper proposes learning which treatments belong together while simultaneously estimating the treatment rule, allowing the grouping to inform the decision problem.

The method uses adaptive fusion in a single convex optimization problem. A loss term measures fit, while a penalty encourages similar treatments to merge into groups. Varying the tuning parameter produces a hierarchy that makes the treatment-clustering path visible. An accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm handles computation, and a group-lasso procedure selects variables to further improve performance.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for recovering the underlying treatment groups. Simulations and a cancer-treatment data application show superior performance in the reported evaluations. The practical contribution is a joint approach to simplifying a large treatment space and learning personalized choices, with a hierarchical representation that may help doctors understand the resulting treatment organization.
summary.tldr: Adaptive fusion jointly groups treatments with similar effects and learns individualized treatment rules through convex optimization.

title: Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments: A Supervised Clustering Approach Using Adaptive Fusion

abstract: Diagnosing and mitigating changes in model fairness under distribution shift is an important component of the safe deployment of machine learning in healthcare settings. Importantly, the success of any mitigation strategy strongly depends on the \textit{structure} of the shift. Despite this, there has been little discussion of how to empirically assess the structure of a distribution shift that one is encountering in practice. In this work, we adopt a causal framing to motivate conditional independence tests as a key tool for characterizing distribution shifts. Using our approach in two medical applications, we show that this knowledge can help diagnose failures of fairness transfer, including cases where real-world shifts are more complex than is often assumed in the literature. Based on these results, we discuss potential remedies at each step of the machine learning pipeline.

paragraphs: A medical model’s fairness can change when the data distribution changes between settings. Choosing an effective response depends on the structure of that change: different relationships in the data may have shifted. This paper addresses how to investigate that structure empirically, making the diagnosis of distribution shift part of assessing whether fairness transfers.

The authors use a causal framing to motivate conditional independence tests. These tests examine whether variables remain independent once other variables are taken into account. Within the proposed approach, such evidence helps characterize the shift being encountered and interpret why fairness properties established in one setting may fail to carry over to another.

Applications in two medical settings show that this information can help diagnose failures of fairness transfer. They also reveal shifts more complicated than assumptions commonly used in the literature. Based on these findings, the authors discuss potential remedies across the machine-learning pipeline. The contribution is a diagnostic approach that connects empirical evidence about the shift to the choice of possible mitigation strategies.
summary.tldr: Causally motivated conditional independence tests help diagnose why model fairness fails to transfer across medical distribution shifts.

title: Diagnosing failures of fairness transfer across distribution shift in real-world medical settings

abstract: Federated learning is a learning paradigm to enable collaborative learning across different parties without revealing raw data. Notably, vertical federated learning (VFL), where parties share the same set of samples but only hold partial features, has a wide range of real-world applications. However, most existing studies in VFL disregard the "record linkage'' process. They design algorithms either assuming the data from different parties can be exactly linked or simply linking each record with its most similar neighboring record. These approaches may fail to capture the key features from other less similar records. Moreover, such improper linkage cannot be corrected by training since existing approaches provide no feedback on linkage during training. In this paper, we design a novel coupled training paradigm, FedSim, that integrates one-to-many linkage into the training process. Besides enabling VFL in many real-world applications with fuzzy identifiers, FedSim also achieves better performance in traditional VFL tasks. Moreover, we theoretically analyze the additional privacy risk incurred by sharing similarities. Our experiments on eight datasets with various similarity metrics show that FedSim outperforms other state-of-the-art baselines. The codes of FedSim are available at https://github.com/Xtra-Computing/FedSim.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning lets organizations collaborate when they hold different features about the same samples, without revealing their raw data. A practical obstacle is deciding which records correspond across organizations. Existing approaches often assume exact matches or select only the most similar record, potentially overlooking useful information in other plausible matches.

FedSim connects this record-linking process to model training. Its one-to-many linkage allows a record to be associated with multiple candidates, bringing record similarity into the learning procedure. This addresses a weakness of treating linkage as a fixed preliminary step: the training process otherwise has no way to provide feedback on those associations.

Experiments on eight datasets using different similarity measures show FedSim outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The authors report benefits both for fuzzy identifiers and for traditional vertical federated learning tasks. They also theoretically analyze the additional privacy risk from sharing similarities, treating that information exchange as part of the method’s implications.
summary.tldr: FedSim integrates one-to-many record matching into vertical federated learning to improve predictions when record identities are uncertain.

title: A Coupled Design of Exploiting Record Similarity for Practical Vertical Federated Learning

abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics enabled the study of cellular heterogeneity in response to perturbations at the resolution of individual cells. However, scaling high-throughput screens (HTSs) to measure cellular responses for many drugs remains a challenge due to technical limitations and, more importantly, the cost of such multiplexed experiments. Thus, transferring information from routinely performed bulk RNA HTS is required to enrich single-cell data meaningfully.We introduce chemCPA, a new encoder-decoder architecture to study the perturbational effects of unseen drugs. We combine the model with an architecture surgery for transfer learning and demonstrate how training on existing bulk RNA HTS datasets can improve generalisation performance. Better generalisation reduces the need for extensive and costly screens at single-cell resolution. We envision that our proposed method will facilitate more efficient experiment designs through its ability to generate in-silico hypotheses, ultimately accelerating drug discovery.

paragraphs: Single-cell measurements reveal how individual cells respond differently to a drug, but measuring these responses for many drugs is technically difficult and expensive. Bulk RNA screening data are more routinely available. The paper investigates how information from those existing screens can improve predictions at the level of individual cells.

The authors introduce chemCPA, an encoder-decoder architecture designed to study responses to drugs that were not seen during training. They combine it with an architectural modification for transfer learning, allowing training on existing bulk RNA screening datasets to inform the single-cell prediction task. The reported finding is that this transfer improves generalization.

Better prediction of unseen drug effects can reduce the need for extensive single-cell screening. The authors envision using the model to generate computational hypotheses and guide more efficient experiments, with the longer-term aim of accelerating drug discovery. That prospective application is distinct from the demonstrated finding: the abstract establishes improved generalization through bulk-data transfer, while presenting improved experimental design as an intended use.
summary.tldr: chemCPA transfers information from bulk RNA screens to improve generalization when predicting single-cell responses to unseen drugs.

title: Predicting Cellular Responses to Novel Drug Perturbations at a Single-Cell Resolution

abstract: Graph neural networks have been extensively studied for learning with inter-connected data. Despite this, recent evidence has revealed GNNs' deficiencies related to over-squashing, heterophily, handling long-range dependencies, edge incompleteness and particularly, the absence of graphs altogether. While a plausible solution is to learn new adaptive topology for message passing, issues concerning quadratic complexity hinder simultaneous guarantees for scalability and precision in large networks. In this paper, we introduce a novel all-pair message passing scheme for efficiently propagating node signals between arbitrary nodes, as an important building block for a new class of Transformer networks for node classification on large graphs, dubbed as NodeFormer. Specifically, the efficient computation is enabled by a kernerlized Gumbel-Softmax operator that reduces the algorithmic complexity to linearity w.r.t. node numbers for learning latent graph structures from large, potentially fully-connected graphs in a differentiable manner. We also provide accompanying theory as justification for our design. Extensive experiments demonstrate the promising efficacy of the method in various tasks including node classification on graphs (with up to 2M nodes) and graph-enhanced applications (e.g., image classification) where input graphs are missing. The codes are available at https://github.com/qitianwu/NodeFormer.

paragraphs: Graph learning can struggle when supplied connections are incomplete, poorly suited to the task, or absent entirely. Learning new connections offers a possible remedy, but considering every pair of nodes normally creates a quadratic computational burden. NodeFormer addresses this tension between flexible communication and scalability when classifying nodes in large datasets.

The method introduces an all-pair message-passing scheme that allows signals to travel between arbitrary nodes. A kernelized Gumbel-Softmax operator enables differentiable learning of latent graph structure with complexity linear in the number of nodes. This makes potentially fully connected relationships available to the model without the usual quadratic scaling. The paper also supplies theory supporting this design.

Experiments report promising performance on node-classification tasks with graphs containing up to two million nodes. They also cover applications such as image classification where an input graph is missing. Together, these results support learning useful connectivity rather than relying entirely on a supplied graph, while making that approach computationally practical at the tested scales.
summary.tldr: NodeFormer learns latent graph connections through all-pair message passing whose computational complexity scales linearly with node count.

title: NodeFormer: A Scalable Graph Structure Learning Transformer for Node Classification

abstract: Existing open-vocabulary object detectors typically enlarge their vocabulary sizes by leveraging different forms of weak supervision. This helps generalize to novel objects at inference. Two popular forms of weak-supervision used in open-vocabulary detection (OVD) include pretrained CLIP model and image-level supervision. We note that both these modes of supervision are not optimally aligned for the detection task: CLIP is trained with image-text pairs and lacks precise localization of objects while the image-level supervision has been used with heuristics that do not accurately specify local object regions. In this work, we propose to address this problem by performing object-centric alignment of the language embeddings from the CLIP model. Furthermore, we visually ground the objects with only image-level supervision using a pseudo-labeling process that provides high-quality object proposals and helps expand the vocabulary during training. We establish a bridge between the above two object-alignment strategies via a novel weight transfer function that aggregates their complimentary strengths. In essence, the proposed model seeks to minimize the gap between object and image-centric representations in the OVD setting. On the COCO benchmark, our proposed approach achieves 36.6 AP50 on novel classes, an absolute 8.2 gain over the previous best performance. For LVIS, we surpass the state-of-the-art ViLD model by 5.0 mask AP for rare categories and 3.4 overall. Code: https://github.com/hanoonaR/object-centric-ovd.

This paper identifies a mismatch in two common sources of weak supervision. The proposed method addresses both sides of that mismatch. It aligns CLIP language embeddings with objects and uses a pseudo-labeling process to obtain high-quality object proposals from image-level supervision. These proposals also help expand the vocabulary during training. A learned weight transfer function connects the two alignment strategies so their complementary strengths can be combined.

On COCO, the approach reaches 36.6 AP50 for novel classes, an absolute improvement of 8.2 over the previous best result reported in the abstract. On LVIS, it exceeds ViLD by 5.0 mask AP for rare categories and 3.4 overall. These findings support the value of making weak supervision more object-specific when transferring broad vocabulary knowledge into localization.
summary.tldr: Object-centric alignment connects CLIP and image-level supervision to improve open-vocabulary detection, including novel and rare categories.

title: Bridging the Gap between Object and Image-level Representations for Open-Vocabulary Detection

abstract: Inspired by the problem of improving classification accuracy on rare or hard subsets of a population, there has been recent interest in models of learning where the goal is to generalize to a collection of distributions, each representing a ``group''. We consider a variant of this problem from the perspective of active learning, where the learner is endowed with the power to decide which examples are labeled from each distribution in the collection, and the goal is to minimize the number of label queries while maintaining PAC-learning guarantees. Our main challenge is that standard active learning techniques such as disagreement-based active learning do not directly apply to the multi-group learning objective. We modify existing algorithms to provide a consistent active learning algorithm for an agnostic formulation of multi-group learning, which given a collection of $G$ distributions and a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ with VC-dimension $d$, outputs an $\epsilon$-optimal hypothesis using $\tilde{O}\left( (\nu^2/\epsilon^2) G d \theta_{\mathcal{G}}^2 \log^2(1/\epsilon) + G\log(1/\epsilon)/\epsilon^2 \right)$ label queries, where $\theta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the worst-case disagreement coefficient over the collection. Roughly speaking, this guarantee improves upon the label complexity of standard multi-group learning in regimes where disagreement-based active learning algorithms may be expected to succeed, and the number of groups is not too large. We also consider the special case where each distribution in the collection is individually realizable with respect to $\mathcal{H}$, and demonstrate $\tilde{O}\left( G d \theta_{\mathcal{G}} \log(1/\epsilon) \right)$ label queries are sufficient for learning in this case. We further give an approximation result for the full agnostic case inspired by the group realizable strategy.

paragraphs: Learning across multiple population groups requires attention to rare or difficult groups, rather than relying only on overall classification performance. This paper studies how to do so while requesting fewer labels. The learner can choose which examples to label from each group’s distribution, but must still satisfy formal guarantees about learning accuracy.

Standard active learning methods do not directly handle this objective. The authors modify existing algorithms for an agnostic setting, which allows imperfect prediction within the chosen hypothesis class. Their label bound depends on the number of groups, the class’s VC dimension, the desired accuracy, and the worst disagreement coefficient across groups. This coefficient enters the guarantee through the difficulty of disagreement-based learning.

The bound improves on standard multi-group learning in favorable active learning regimes when the group count is not too large. The authors also establish a stronger sufficient label bound when each group is individually realizable within the hypothesis class. That special-case strategy further motivates an approximation result for the fully agnostic setting.
summary.tldr: Modified active learning algorithms provide conditional label savings when learning a classifier across multiple population groups.

title: Agnostic Multi-Group Active Learning

abstract: Source-free domain adaptive semantic segmentation aims to adapt a pre-trained source model to the unlabeled target domain without accessing the private source data. Previous methods usually fine-tune the entire network, which suffers from expensive parameter tuning. To avoid this problem, we propose to utilize visual prompt tuning for parameter-efficient adaptation. However, the existing visual prompt tuning methods are unsuitable for source-free domain adaptive semantic segmentation due to the following two reasons: (1) Commonly used visual prompts like input tokens or pixel-level perturbations cannot reliably learn informative knowledge beneficial for semantic segmentation. (2) Visual prompts require sufficient labeled data to fill the gap between the pre-trained model and downstream tasks. To alleviate these problems, we propose a universal unsupervised visual prompt tuning (Uni-UVPT) framework, which is applicable to various transformer-based backbones. Specifically, we first divide the source pre-trained backbone with frozen parameters into multiple stages, and propose a lightweight prompt adapter for progressively encoding informative knowledge into prompts and enhancing the generalization of target features between adjacent backbone stages. Cooperatively, a novel adaptive pseudo-label correction strategy with a multiscale consistency loss is designed to alleviate the negative effect of target samples with noisy pseudo labels and raise the capacity of visual prompts to spatial perturbations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Uni-UVPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on GTA5 $\to$ Cityscapes and SYNTHIA $\to$ Cityscapes tasks and can serve as a universal and parameter-efficient framework for large-model unsupervised knowledge transfer. Code will be available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/uni-uvpt and https://github.com/huawei-noah/noah-research/tree/master/uni-uvpt.

summary.tldr: Uni-UVPT adapts frozen transformer segmentation models using staged prompts, pseudo-label correction, and multiscale consistency.

title: When Visual Prompt Tuning Meets Source-Free Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Learning relies on coordinated synaptic changes in recurrently connected populations of neurons. Therefore, understanding the collective evolution of synaptic connectivity over learning is a key challenge in neuroscience and machine learning. In particular, recent work has shown that the weight matrices of task-trained RNNs are typically low rank, but how this low rank structure unfolds over learning is unknown. To address this, we investigate the rank of the 3-tensor formed by the weight matrices throughout learning. By fitting RNNs of varying rank to large-scale neural recordings during a motor learning task, we find that the inferred weights are low-tensor-rank and therefore evolve over a fixed low-dimensional subspace throughout the entire course of learning. We next validate the observation of low-tensor-rank learning on an RNN trained to solve the same task. Finally, we present a set of mathematical results bounding the matrix and tensor ranks of gradient descent learning dynamics which show that low-tensor-rank weights emerge naturally in RNNs trained to solve low-dimensional tasks. Taken together, our findings provide insight on the evolution of population connectivity over learning in both biological and artificial neural networks, and enable reverse engineering of learning-induced changes in recurrent dynamics from large-scale neural recordings.

paragraphs: Understanding learning in recurrent neural populations requires tracking how connections change together over time. Previous work found that trained recurrent networks often have low-rank weight matrices, but that describes individual stages of learning. This paper examines the tensor formed by collecting weight matrices throughout the learning process.

The authors fit recurrent networks of different ranks to large-scale neural recordings from a motor-learning task. They find that the inferred connectivity has low tensor rank, meaning its evolution remains within a fixed low-dimensional subspace across learning. They then validate this observation in an artificial recurrent network trained to perform the same task.

These results show how low-tensor-rank weights can arise naturally in recurrent networks trained on low-dimensional tasks. Together, the empirical and theoretical findings describe a compact structure in how connectivity evolves, extending the focus beyond the rank of a final trained network. The approach also enables reconstruction of learning-related changes in recurrent dynamics from neural recordings.
summary.tldr: Neural-recording fits, trained recurrent networks, and mathematical analysis reveal low-dimensional structure in connectivity changes across learning.

title: Low Tensor Rank Learning of Neural Dynamics

abstract: We develop a series of differential privacy (DP) algorithms from a family of random projection (RP) and sign random projection (SignRP) methods. We first show how to improve the previous DP-RP approach using the ``optimal Gaussian mechanism''. Then, we propose a series of DP-SignRP algorithms that leverage the robustness of the ``sign flipping probability'' of random projections. That is, given $x = \sum_{i=1}^p u_i w_{i}$ where $u$ is a $p$-dimensional data vector and $w$ is a symmetric random vector, $sign(x)$ only has a fairly small probability to be flipped if there is a small modification on data $u$, depending on the specific distribution of $w$. This robustness leads to our novel design of ``smooth flipping probability'' for SignRP-type algorithms with better utility than using the standard randomized response mechanism. Retrieval and classification experiments demonstrate that, among the presented DP-RP algorithms, \textbf{DP-SignOPORP} (where OPORP is an improvement over the celebrated count-sketch algorithms), performs the best in general.In the industrial practice, DP methods were not very popular for machine learning or search, largely because the performance typically would drop substantially if DP is applied. Since our proposed new DP algorithms have significantly improved the performance, it is anticipated that our work will motivate a wide adoption of DP in practice. Finally, we stress that, since our methods are applied to the original data (i.e., feature vectors), the privacy of downstream tasks is naturally protected.

paragraphs: Random projections can compress feature vectors, but adding differential privacy often reduces downstream usefulness. This paper develops private random-projection and sign-random-projection methods that exploit how rarely a small input change flips the sign of a random projection.

The authors improve a previous random-projection approach using the optimal Gaussian mechanism and introduce smooth flipping probability for sign-based algorithms. This design aims to provide better utility than standard randomized response by using the robustness of the underlying projection.

Retrieval and classification experiments find DP-SignOPORP generally best among the presented alternatives. Because privacy is applied to the original feature representation, downstream processing inherits the corresponding protection. The abstract does not specify privacy-budget values or numerical gains. Its suggestion of wider industrial adoption is a prospective implication, while the demonstrated result is improved utility in the evaluated private-representation methods.
summary.tldr: Smooth sign-flipping probabilities improve the utility of private random-projection representations.

title: Smooth Flipping Probability for Differential Private Sign Random Projection Methods

abstract: In this work, we decouple the iterative bi-level offline RL (value estimation and policy extraction) from the offline training phase, forming a non-iterative bi-level paradigm and avoiding the iterative error propagation over two levels. Specifically, this non-iterative paradigm allows us to conduct inner-level optimization (value estimation) in training, while performing outer-level optimization (policy extraction) in testing. Naturally, such a paradigm raises three core questions that are not fully answered by prior non-iterative offline RL counterparts like reward-conditioned policy: (q1) What information should we transfer from the inner-level to the outer-level? (q2) What should we pay attention to when exploiting the transferred information for safe/confident outer-level optimization? (q3) What are the benefits of concurrently conducting outer-level optimization during testing? Motivated by model-based optimization (MBO), we propose DROP (design from policies), which fully answers the above questions. Specifically, in the inner-level, DROP decomposes offline data into multiple subsets, and learns an MBO score model (a1). To keep safe exploitation to the score model in the outer-level, we explicitly learn a behavior embedding and introduce a conservative regularization (a2). During testing, we show that DROP permits deployment adaptation, enabling an adaptive inference across states (a3). Empirically, we evaluate DROP on various tasks, showing that DROP gains comparable or better performance compared to prior methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often alternates between estimating values and extracting a policy from those estimates. Errors can propagate as the two stages repeatedly influence each other. DROP separates these tasks in time: value estimation happens during training, while policy extraction happens during testing, creating a non-iterative relationship between the two levels.

This separation requires deciding what information to pass forward and how to use it conservatively. Drawing on model-based optimization, DROP splits the offline data into subsets and learns a score model. It also learns a representation of behavior and introduces conservative regularization to guide how the score model is exploited when selecting a policy.

Performing policy optimization during testing allows deployment adaptation, with inference adapting across states. This gives the separation a practical purpose beyond avoiding repeated error propagation: policy extraction can respond at deployment time. Experiments across various tasks show performance comparable to or better than prior methods. The results support this alternative organization of offline policy optimization, combining learned scores with constraints on their use.
summary.tldr: DROP separates offline value learning from conservative policy optimization at test time, enabling adaptation during deployment.

title: Design from Policies: Conservative Test-Time Adaptation for Offline Policy Optimization

abstract: The capability of generalizing to out-of-distribution data is crucial for the deployment of machine learning models in the real world. Existing domain generalization (DG) mainly embarks on offline and discrete scenarios, where multiple source domains are simultaneously accessible and the distribution shift among domains is abrupt and violent. Nevertheless, such setting may not be universally applicable to all real-world applications, as there are cases where the data distribution gradually changes over time due to various factors, e.g., the process of aging. Additionally, as the domain constantly evolves, new domains will continually emerge. Re-training and updating models with both new and previous domains using existing DG methods can be resource-intensive and inefficient. Therefore, in this paper, we present a problem formulation for Continual Domain Generalization over Temporal Drift (CDGTD). CDGTD addresses the challenge of gradually shifting data distributions over time, where domains arrive sequentially and models can only access the data of the current domain. The goal is to generalize to unseen domains that are not too far into the future. To this end, we propose an Evolving Standardization (EvoS) method, which characterizes the evolving pattern of feature distribution and mitigates the distribution shift by standardizing features with generated statistics of corresponding domain. Specifically, inspired by the powerful ability of transformers to model sequence relations, we design a multi-scale attention module (MSAM) to learn the evolving pattern under sliding time windows of different lengths. MSAM can generate statistics of current domain based on the statistics of previous domains and the learned evolving pattern. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets including images and texts validate the efficacy of our EvoS.

This differs from offline domain generalization, where several source domains are available together.

It generates domain-specific statistics and uses them to standardize features, reducing the effect of distribution shift. The module predicts current-domain statistics from earlier statistics and the learned evolution pattern. This uses historical distribution summaries while respecting the setting's restriction on access to previous domain data. Experiments on real-world image and text datasets support the method's effectiveness. Its objective is specifically generalization under gradual temporal drift to domains that are not too far ahead, making temporal structure central to both the problem and the solution.
summary.tldr: EvoS learns how feature statistics evolve over time to improve generalization to nearby future domains.

title: Evolving Standardization for Continual Domain Generalization over Temporal Drift

abstract: We present a new representation learning framework, Intensity Profile Projection, for continuous-time dynamic network data. Given triples $(i,j,t)$, each representing a time-stamped ($t$) interaction between two entities ($i,j$), our procedure returns a continuous-time trajectory for each node, representing its behaviour over time. The framework consists of three stages: estimating pairwise intensity functions, e.g. via kernel smoothing; learning a projection which minimises a notion of intensity reconstruction error; and constructing evolving node representations via the learned projection. The trajectories satisfy two properties, known as structural and temporal coherence, which we see as fundamental for reliable inference. Moreoever, we develop estimation theory providing tight control on the error of any estimated trajectory, indicating that the representations could even be used in quite noise-sensitive follow-on analyses. The theory also elucidates the role of smoothing as a bias-variance trade-off, and shows how we can reduce the level of smoothing as the signal-to-noise ratio increases on account of the algorithm `borrowing strength' across the network.

paragraphs: A dynamic network can be recorded as interactions between pairs of entities, each with a timestamp. Intensity Profile Projection turns these events into a continuous trajectory for every node. The trajectory represents how that node's behavior changes over time, providing an evolving representation directly from timestamped interactions.

The framework has three stages. It first estimates how pairwise interaction intensities vary over time, for example through kernel smoothing. It then learns a projection that minimizes an intensity reconstruction error. Finally, it applies that projection to construct the node trajectories. The resulting representations satisfy the structural and temporal coherence properties that the authors identify as important for reliable inference.

The paper also develops estimation theory that tightly controls trajectory error. This suggests the representations could support downstream analyses sensitive to noise. The theory explains smoothing as a balance between bias and variance, and shows that less smoothing is possible as the signal-to-noise ratio increases. Sharing information across the network helps the method estimate individual trajectories more effectively.
summary.tldr: Intensity Profile Projection converts timestamped network interactions into coherent continuous node trajectories with theoretical error control.

title: Intensity Profile Projection: A Framework for Continuous-Time Representation Learning for Dynamic Networks

abstract: Closed-form differential equations, including partial differential equations and higher-order ordinary differential equations, are one of the most important tools used by scientists to model and better understand natural phenomena. Discovering these equations directly from data is challenging because it requires modeling relationships between various derivatives that are not observed in the data (equation-data mismatch) and it involves searching across a huge space of possible equations. Current approaches make strong assumptions about the form of the equation and thus fail to discover many well-known phenomena. Moreover, many of them resolve the equation-data mismatch by estimating the derivatives, which makes them inadequate for noisy and infrequent observations. To this end, we propose D-CIPHER, which is robust to measurement artifacts and can uncover a new and very general class of differential equations. We further design a novel optimization procedure, CoLLie, to help D-CIPHER search through this class efficiently. Finally, we demonstrate empirically that it can discover many well-known equations that are beyond the capabilities of current methods.

paragraphs: Differential equations express relationships involving derivatives, yet measurements usually record the underlying quantities rather than those derivatives. Discovering equations from data therefore involves an equation-data mismatch as well as an enormous search over possible mathematical expressions. The paper addresses both obstacles for partial differential equations and higher-order ordinary differential equations.

Existing approaches often restrict the form of the equation strongly enough to exclude familiar phenomena. Many also estimate derivatives directly from observations, which makes noisy or infrequent measurements particularly troublesome. D-CIPHER is designed to discover a broad new class of equations while remaining robust to measurement artifacts. The authors pair it with a new optimization procedure, CoLLie, to search this class efficiently.

The empirical results show that D-CIPHER can recover many well-known equations beyond the capabilities of the existing methods considered. This matters because equation discovery should recover scientifically useful relationships without requiring overly restrictive guesses about their form. The paper's contribution combines broader expressiveness, robustness to imperfect observations, and an optimization procedure intended to make that broader search manageable.
summary.tldr: D-CIPHER combines a broad differential-equation search space with efficient optimization and robustness to measurement artifacts.

title: D-CIPHER: Discovery of Closed-form Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Breaking down a problem into intermediate steps has demonstrated impressive performance in Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, the growth of the reasoning chain introduces uncertainty and error accumulation, making it challenging to elicit accurate final results. To tackle this challenge of uncertainty in multi-step reasoning, we introduce a stepwise self-evaluation mechanism to guide and calibrate the reasoning process of LLMs. We propose a decoding algorithm integrating the self-evaluation guidance via stochastic beam search. The self-evaluation guidance serves as a better-calibrated automatic criterion, facilitating an efficient search in the reasoning space and resulting in superior prediction quality. Stochastic beam search balances exploitation and exploration of the search space with temperature-controlled randomness. Our approach surpasses the corresponding Codex-backboned baselines in few-shot accuracy by $6.34$%, $9.56$%, and $5.46$% on the GSM8K, AQuA, and StrategyQA benchmarks, respectively. Experiment results with Llama-2 on arithmetic reasoning demonstrate the efficiency of our method in outperforming the baseline methods with comparable computational budgets. Further analysis in multi-step reasoning finds our self-evaluation guidance pinpoints logic failures and leads to higher consistency and robustness. Our code is publicly available at [https://guideddecoding.github.io/](https://guideddecoding.github.io/).

This paper introduces a mechanism that evaluates reasoning step by step. Those evaluations guide which developing reasoning paths the model explores as it searches for an answer.

The decoding algorithm combines self-evaluation with stochastic beam search. Self-evaluation supplies an automatic criterion for judging intermediate reasoning, while temperature-controlled randomness balances following promising paths with exploring alternatives. The approach makes assessment part of the search process, so the model can use intermediate judgments when choosing how to continue a chain.

For Codex-based systems, the authors report few-shot accuracy improvements of 6.34%, 9.56%, and 5.46% over the corresponding baselines on GSM8K, AQuA, and StrategyQA. Llama-2 arithmetic experiments also show improvements over baselines at comparable computational budgets. Further analysis finds that the guidance identifies logical failures and improves consistency and robustness. These results support stepwise evaluation as a useful search signal in the tested multi-step reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: Stepwise self-evaluation guides stochastic beam search toward more accurate and consistent language-model reasoning in the reported experiments.

title: Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning

abstract: We present AircraftVerse, a publicly available aerial vehicle design dataset. Aircraft design encompasses different physics domains and, hence, multiple modalities of representation. The evaluation of these designs requires the use of scientific analytical and simulation models ranging from computer-aided design tools for structural and manufacturing analysis, computational fluid dynamics tools for drag and lift computation, battery models for energy estimation, and simulation models for flight control and dynamics. AircraftVerse contains $27{,}714$ diverse air vehicle designs - the largest corpus of designs with this level of complexity. Each design comprises the following artifacts: a symbolic design tree describing topology, propulsion subsystem, battery subsystem, and other design details; a STandard for the Exchange of Product (STEP) model data; a 3D CAD design using a stereolithography (STL) file format; a 3D point cloud for the shape of the design; and evaluation results from high fidelity state-of-the-art physics models that characterize performance metrics such as maximum flight distance and hover-time. We also present baseline surrogate models that use different modalities of design representation to predict design performance metrics, which we provide as part of our dataset release. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of this dataset on the use of learning in aircraft design, and more generally, in the emerging field of deep learning for scientific design. AircraftVerse is accompanied by a datasheet as suggested in the recent literature, and it is released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (CC BY-SA) license. The dataset with baseline models are hosted at http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6525446, code at https://github.com/SRI-CSL/AircraftVerse, and the dataset description at https://uavdesignverse.onrender.com/.

title: AircraftVerse: A Large-Scale Multimodal Dataset of Aerial Vehicle Designs

abstract: We present a method that reconstructs and animates a 3D head avatar from a single-view portrait image. Existing methods either involve time-consuming optimization for a specific person with multiple images, or they struggle to synthesize intricate appearance details beyond the facial region. To address these limitations, we propose a framework that not only generalizes to unseen identities based on a single-view image without requiring person-specific optimization, but also captures characteristic details within and beyond the face area (e.g. hairstyle, accessories, etc.). At the core of our method are three branches that produce three tri-planes representing the coarse 3D geometry, detailed appearance of a source image, as well as the expression of a target image. By applying volumetric rendering to the combination of the three tri-planes followed by a super-resolution module, our method yields a high fidelity image of the desired identity, expression and pose. Once trained, our model enables efficient 3D head avatar reconstruction and animation via a single forward pass through a network. Experiments show that the proposed approach generalizes well to unseen validation datasets, surpassing SOTA baseline methods by a large margin on head avatar reconstruction and animation.

title: Generalizable One-shot 3D Neural Head Avatar

abstract: Reproducing kernel Hilbert $C^*$-module (RKHM) is a generalization of reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) by means of $C^*$-algebra, and the Perron-Frobenius operator is a linear operator related to the composition of functions. Combining these two concepts, we present deep RKHM, a deep learning framework for kernel methods. We derive a new Rademacher generalization bound in this setting and provide a theoretical interpretation of benign overfitting by means of Perron-Frobenius operators. By virtue of $C^*$-algebra, the dependency of the bound on output dimension is milder than existing bounds. We show that $C^*$-algebra is a suitable tool for deep learning with kernels, enabling us to take advantage of the product structure of operators and to provide a clear connection with convolutional neural networks. Our theoretical analysis provides a new lens through which one can design and analyze deep kernel methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical framework for building deep learning models with kernels. Its starting point is the reproducing kernel Hilbert C*-module, or RKHM, which extends the familiar reproducing kernel Hilbert space using C*-algebra. The authors combine this structure with the Perron-Frobenius operator, a linear operator connected to composing functions, to describe a framework called deep RKHM.

The central contribution is theoretical: the authors derive a new Rademacher generalization bound and use Perron-Frobenius operators to interpret benign overfitting. The bound describes generalization within this framework, and its dependence on output dimension is milder than that of existing bounds. This gives a more favorable theoretical treatment of output dimensionality, rather than establishing an unconditional guarantee of better predictive performance.

The algebraic formulation also exposes the product structure of operators and provides a connection to convolutional neural networks. Together, these results offer tools for reasoning about how layered kernel models are constructed and how they generalize. The paper’s stated value is a new perspective for designing and analyzing deep kernel methods, grounded in a shared operator-based mathematical language.
summary.tldr: Deep RKHM combines generalized kernel spaces and composition operators to analyze deep kernel models, including generalization and benign overfitting.

title: Deep learning with kernels through RKHM and the Perron-Frobenius operator

abstract: Recent advances in fine-grained representation learning leverage local-to-global (emergent) relationships for achieving state-of-the-art results. The relational representations relied upon by such methods, however, are abstract. We aim to deconstruct this abstraction by expressing them as interpretable graphs over image views. We begin by theoretically showing that abstract relational representations are nothing but a way of recovering transitive relationships among local views. Based on this, we design Transitivity Recovering Decompositions (TRD), a graph-space search algorithm that identifies interpretable equivalents of abstract emergent relationships at both instance and class levels, and with no post-hoc computations. We additionally show that TRD is provably robust to noisy views, with empirical evidence also supporting this finding. The latter allows TRD to perform at par or even better than the state-of-the-art, while being fully interpretable. Implementation is available at https://github.com/abhrac/trd.

paragraphs: Fine-grained representation learning can benefit from relationships that emerge between local image views and the image as a whole. Those relational representations can be difficult to interpret. This paper aims to express them as understandable graphs over image views, making the relationships used by the model more explicit.

The authors first show theoretically that the abstract relational representations recover transitive relationships among local views. They use this result to design Transitivity Recovering Decompositions, or TRD, a search algorithm operating in graph space. TRD identifies interpretable equivalents of the emergent relationships at both the individual-instance and class levels, without requiring separate post-hoc computations.

The paper also proves robustness to noisy views and provides empirical evidence supporting that result. In the reported evaluations, TRD matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance while remaining fully interpretable. The significance is that the graph representation serves as part of the relationship-learning approach itself, and its robustness helps preserve predictive performance when some views are noisy. The work links an explanatory decomposition with both theoretical and empirical support.
summary.tldr: TRD expresses fine-grained image relationships as interpretable graphs and provides theoretical and empirical robustness to noisy views.

title: Transitivity Recovering Decompositions: Interpretable and Robust Fine-Grained Relationships

abstract: Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) is a nonparametric particle-based deterministic sampling algorithm. Despite its wide usage, understanding the theoretical properties of SVGD has remained a challenging problem. For sampling from a Gaussian target, the SVGD dynamics with a bilinear kernel will remain Gaussian as long as the initializer is Gaussian. Inspired by this fact, we undertake a detailed theoretical study of the Gaussian-SVGD, i.e., SVGD projected to the family of Gaussian distributions via the bilinear kernel, or equivalently Gaussian variational inference (GVI) with SVGD. We present a complete picture by considering both the mean-field PDE and discrete particle systems. When the target is strongly log-concave, the mean-field Gaussian-SVGD dynamics is proven to converge linearly to the Gaussian distribution closest to the target in KL divergence. In the finite-particle setting, there is both uniform in time convergence to the mean-field limit and linear convergence in time to the equilibrium if the target is Gaussian. In the general case, we propose a density-based and a particle-based implementation of the Gaussian-SVGD, and show that several recent algorithms for GVI, proposed from different perspectives, emerge as special cases of our unified framework. Interestingly, one of the new particle-based instance from this framework empirically outperforms existing approaches. Our results make concrete contributions towards obtaining a deeper understanding of both SVGD and GVI.

paragraphs: Stein Variational Gradient Descent represents distributions through deterministically moving particles, but its theoretical behavior can be difficult to characterize. The paper studies a Gaussian version built using a bilinear kernel. A motivating property is that, for a Gaussian target and Gaussian initialization, the resulting distribution dynamics remain Gaussian.

The analysis covers both a continuous mean-field description and systems with finitely many particles. For a strongly log-concave target, the mean-field dynamics converge linearly to the Gaussian distribution closest to the target in KL divergence. summary.tldr: Gaussian-SVGD receives conditional convergence guarantees and a unified framework that connects several Gaussian variational-inference methods.

title: Towards Understanding the Dynamics of Gaussian-Stein Variational Gradient Descent

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a generalization of the standard Stackelberg Games (SGs) framework: _Calibrated Stackelberg Games_. In CSGs, a principal repeatedly interacts with an agent who (contrary to standard SGs) does not have direct access to the principal's action but instead best responds to _calibrated forecasts_ about it. CSG is a powerful modeling tool that goes beyond assuming that agents use ad hoc and highly specified algorithms for interacting in strategic settings to infer the principal's actions and thus more robustly addresses real-life applications that SGs were originally intended to capture. Along with CSGs, we also introduce a stronger notion of calibration, termed _adaptive calibration_, that provides fine-grained any-time calibration guarantees against adversarial sequences. We give a general approach for obtaining adaptive calibration algorithms and specialize them for finite CSGs. In our main technical result, we show that in CSGs, the principal can achieve utility that converges to the optimum Stackelberg value of the game both in _finite_ and _continuous_ settings and that no higher utility is achievable. Two prominent and immediate applications of our results are the settings of learning in Stackelberg Security Games and strategic classification, both against _calibrated_ agents.

paragraphs: Standard Stackelberg games model a principal choosing an action and an agent responding to it. This paper changes the information available to the agent: the agent cannot directly observe the principal's action and instead responds optimally to calibrated forecasts about it. The principal and agent interact repeatedly, allowing the framework to address decisions based on predictions.

The resulting Calibrated Stackelberg Games avoid requiring one highly specified algorithm for how the agent infers the principal's behavior. The authors also introduce adaptive calibration, a stronger forecasting requirement that gives fine-grained guarantees at arbitrary times against adversarial sequences. They provide a general method for constructing algorithms with this property and specialize it to finite games.

The main result establishes that the principal's utility can converge to the optimal standard Stackelberg value in both finite and continuous settings, and that a higher value is not achievable in this framework. Thus, replacing direct observation with calibrated forecasts preserves the stated optimal utility benchmark. The paper identifies security games and strategic classification against calibrated agents as immediate applications.
summary.tldr: A generalized Stackelberg framework shows that a principal can attain the optimal Stackelberg value against agents responding to calibrated forecasts.

title: Calibrated Stackelberg Games: Learning Optimal Commitments Against Calibrated Agents

abstract: With the emergence of various molecular tasks and massive datasets, how to perform efficient training has become an urgent yet under-explored issue in the area. Data pruning (DP), as an oft-stated approach to saving training burdens, filters out less influential samples to form a coreset for training. However, the increasing reliance on pretrained models for molecular tasks renders traditional in-domain DP methods incompatible. Therefore, we propose a **Mol**ecular data **P**runing framework for **e**nhanced **G**eneralization (**MolPeg**), which focuses on the source-free data pruning scenario, where data pruning is applied with pretrained models. By maintaining two models with different updating paces during training, we introduce a novel scoring function to measure the informativeness of samples based on the loss discrepancy. As a plug-and-play framework, MolPeg realizes the perception of both source and target domain and consistently outperforms existing DP methods across four downstream tasks. Remarkably, it can surpass the performance obtained from full-dataset training, even when pruning up to 60-70% of the data on HIV and PCBA dataset. Our work suggests that the discovery of effective data-pruning metrics could provide a viable path to both enhanced efficiency and superior generalization in transfer learning.

paragraphs: Data pruning reduces training work by selecting a smaller set of informative examples. This paper asks how to make that selection useful for molecular tasks built on pretrained models. Traditional pruning methods designed around training within one domain do not fit this transfer setting well. MolPeg instead addresses source-free pruning, where selection must work with a pretrained model without the original source data.

MolPeg maintains two models that update at different speeds during training. It scores examples using the difference between the models' losses, treating that discrepancy as a measure of informativeness. This gives the pruning process a way to account for both source and target domains within a framework that can be added to an existing training setup.

Across four downstream tasks, MolPeg consistently outperforms the compared pruning methods. On HIV and PCBA, it can even exceed full-dataset training performance while removing up to 60–70% of examples. These results suggest that selecting data carefully can improve transfer generalization as well as reduce training demands.
summary.tldr: MolPeg uses loss differences between differently paced models to prune molecular training data, sometimes improving performance even after removing most examples.

title: Beyond Efficiency: Molecular Data Pruning for Enhanced Generalization

abstract: Recent researches have proven that pre-training on large-scale person images extracted from internet videos is an effective way in learning better representations for person re-identification. However, these researches are mostly confined to pre-training at the instance-level or single-video tracklet-level. They ignore the identity-invariance in images of the same person across different videos, which is a key focus in person re-identification. To address this issue, we propose a Cross-video Identity-cOrrelating pre-traiNing (CION) framework. Defining a noise concept that comprehensively considers both intra-identity consistency and inter-identity discrimination, CION seeks the identity correlation from cross-video images by modeling it as a progressive multi-level denoising problem. Furthermore, an identity-guided self-distillation loss is proposed to implement better large-scale pre-training by mining the identity-invariance within person images. We conduct extensive experiments to verify the superiority of our CION in terms of efficiency and performance. CION achieves significantly leading performance with even fewer training samples. For example, compared with the previous state-of-the-art ISR, CION with the same ResNet50-IBN achieves higher mAP of 93.3% and 74.3% on Market1501 and MSMT17, while only utilizing 8% training samples. Finally, with CION demonstrating superior model-agnostic ability, we contribute a model zoo named ReIDZoo to meet diverse research and application needs in this field. It contains a series of CION pre-trained models with spanning structures and parameters, totaling 32 models with 10 different structures, including GhostNet, ConvNext, RepViT, FastViT and so on. The code and models will be open-sourced.

Its noise definition accounts for both consistency among images of one identity and discrimination between different identities. summary.tldr: CION learns cross-video identity consistency to improve person re-identification pre-training with fewer training samples.

title: Cross-video Identity Correlating for Person Re-identification Pre-training

abstract: We study online control for continuous-time linear systems with finite sampling rates, where the objective is to design an online procedure that learns under non-stochastic noise and performs comparably to a fixed optimal linear controller. We present a novel two-level online algorithm, by integrating a higher-level learning strategy and a lower-level feedback control strategy. This method offers a practical and robust solution for online control, which achieves sublinear regret. Our work provides the first nonasymptotic results for controlling continuous-time linear systems with finite number of interactions with the system. Moreover, we examine how to train an agent in domain randomization environments from a non-stochastic control perspective. By applying our method to the SAC (Soft Actor-Critic) algorithm, we achieved improved results in multiple reinforcement learning tasks within domain randomization environments. Our work provides new insights into non-asymptotic analyses of controlling continuous-time systems. Furthermore, our work brings practical intuition into controller learning under non-stochastic environments.

paragraphs: A continuously evolving system can still be observed and controlled only at discrete sampling times. This paper studies online learning in that setting for linear systems subject to non-stochastic disturbances. The objective is to learn a controller whose performance is comparable to that of a fixed optimal linear controller despite the disturbances.

The proposed algorithm separates the task into two levels: a higher-level learning strategy and a lower-level feedback control strategy. It achieves sublinear regret, so its accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the comparison horizon. The authors also provide nonasymptotic results for continuous-time control with finitely many system interactions, making the finite-interaction setting central to the theory.

The paper then examines domain randomization through the same non-stochastic control perspective. Applying its method to Soft Actor-Critic improves results on multiple reinforcement learning tasks in domain-randomized environments. This connects the formal control analysis to empirical agent training, offering both guarantees for the studied linear systems and practical evidence in the reported reinforcement learning settings.
summary.tldr: A two-level learning and feedback algorithm achieves sublinear regret for sampled continuous-time linear control under non-stochastic disturbances.

title: Online Control with Adversarial Disturbance for Continuous-time Linear Systems

abstract: Speech language models have significantly advanced in generating realistic speech, with neural codec language models standing out. However, the integration of preference optimization to align speech outputs to human preferences is often neglected. This paper addresses this gap by first analyzing the distribution gap in codec language models, highlighting how it leads to discrepancies between the training and inference phases, which negatively affects performance. Then we explore leveraging preference optimization to bridge the distribution gap. We introduce SpeechAlign, an iterative self-improvement strategy that aligns speech language models to human preferences. SpeechAlign involves constructing a preference codec dataset contrasting golden codec tokens against synthetic tokens, followed by preference optimization to improve the codec language model. This cycle of improvement is carried out iteratively to steadily convert weak models to strong ones. Through both subjective and objective evaluations, we show that SpeechAlign can bridge the distribution gap and facilitating continuous self-improvement of the speech language model. Moreover, SpeechAlign exhibits robust generalization capabilities and works for smaller models. Demos are available at https://0nutation.github.io/SpeechAlign.github.io/.

However, the integration of preference optimization to align speech outputs to human preferences is often neglected. This paper addresses this gap by first analyzing the distribution gap in codec language models, highlighting how it leads to discrepancies between the training and inference phases, which negatively affects performance. Then we explore leveraging preference optimization to bridge the distribution gap. We introduce SpeechAlign, an iterative self-improvement strategy that aligns speech language models to human preferences. SpeechAlign involves constructing a preference codec dataset contrasting golden codec tokens against synthetic tokens, followed by preference optimization to improve the codec language model. This cycle of improvement is carried out iteratively to steadily convert weak models to strong ones. Through both subjective and objective evaluations, we show that SpeechAlign can bridge the distribution gap and facilitating continuous self-improvement of the speech language model. Moreover, SpeechAlign exhibits robust generalization capabilities and works for smaller models. Demos are available at https://0nutation.github.io/SpeechAlign.github.io/.

paragraphs: SpeechAlign studies how preference optimization can improve speech generated by neural codec language models. The paper first analyzes a distribution gap between training and inference and connects that mismatch to degraded performance. Its central proposal is to use an iterative preference-based learning process to reduce the gap and better align speech output with human preferences.

Each iteration constructs a preference dataset contrasting golden codec tokens with synthetic tokens. The model then undergoes preference optimization using these contrasts. Repeating dataset construction and optimization creates a self-improvement cycle, with the goal of progressively strengthening the speech model through successive rounds of training.

Both subjective and objective evaluations support the claim that SpeechAlign can bridge the distribution gap and enable continued improvement. The authors also report strong generalization and effectiveness for smaller models. Together, these findings suggest that preference optimization can serve as a repeated improvement mechanism for speech generation, connecting the training procedure more closely to the kinds of outputs the model produces during use.
summary.tldr: SpeechAlign iteratively optimizes preferences over reference and synthetic codec tokens to improve speech generation and reduce training–inference mismatch.

title: SpeechAlign: Aligning Speech Generation to Human Preferences

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models (PTMs) provide remarkable zero-shot classification capability covering a wide variety of object classes. However, practical applications do not always require the classification of all kinds of objects, and leaving the model capable of recognizing unnecessary classes not only degrades overall accuracy but also leads to operational disadvantages. To mitigate this issue, we explore the selective forgetting problem for PTMs, where the task is to make the model unable to recognize only the specified classes, while maintaining accuracy for the rest. All the existing methods assume ''white-box'' settings, where model information such as architectures, parameters, and gradients is available for training. However, PTMs are often ''black-box,'' where information on such models is unavailable for commercial reasons or social responsibilities. In this paper, we address a novel problem of selective forgetting for black-box models, named Black-Box Forgetting, and propose an approach to the problem. Given that information on the model is unavailable, we optimize the input prompt to decrease the accuracy of specified classes through derivative-free optimization. To avoid difficult high-dimensional optimization while ensuring high forgetting performance, we propose Latent Context Sharing, which introduces common low-dimensional latent components among multiple tokens for the prompt. Experiments on four standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method with reasonable baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/yusukekwn/Black-Box-Forgetting.

paragraphs: A pretrained classifier may recognize many categories that an application does not need. This paper studies selective forgetting: reducing recognition of designated categories while preserving accuracy on the others. Its particular challenge is a black-box setting, where the model's architecture, parameters, and gradients are unavailable, preventing the kinds of internal modifications assumed by previous approaches.

The proposed method works through the input prompt. It uses derivative-free optimization to search for prompts that lower accuracy on the classes selected for forgetting. Searching over many prompt tokens would create a difficult high-dimensional optimization problem. Latent Context Sharing reduces that burden by giving multiple tokens common components in a lower-dimensional latent representation.

Experiments on four standard datasets show better performance than the baselines considered by the authors. The contribution is a method for changing selective recognition behavior through prompts under restricted model access. The stated objective concerns classification accuracy on selected and retained categories; the mechanism described in the abstract operates at the input interface rather than modifying the pretrained model's parameters.
summary.tldr: Shared low-dimensional prompt components enable selective forgetting in classifiers whose internal parameters and gradients are inaccessible.

title: Black-Box Forgetting

abstract: In the realizable online setting, a learner is tasked with making predictions for a stream of instances, where the correct answer is revealed after each prediction. A learning rule is online consistent if its mistake rate eventually vanishes. The nearest neighbor rule is fundamental prediction strategy, but it is only known to be consistent under strong statistical or geometric assumptions: the instances come i.i.d. or the label classes are well-separated. We prove online consistency for all measurable functions in doubling metric spaces under the mild assumption that instances are generated by a process that is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to an underlying finite, upper doubling measure.

paragraphs: In online prediction, a learner answers each arriving instance before seeing its correct label. A rule is consistent when its fraction of mistakes eventually tends to zero. This paper studies that property for nearest-neighbor prediction in the realizable setting, where the answers follow an underlying target function. The question is when this simple rule can keep improving along a stream of instances.

Earlier consistency results required strong conditions, such as independent, identically distributed instances or well-separated label classes. The authors prove consistency for every measurable target function in doubling metric spaces under a different assumption on the instance-generating process. That process must be uniformly absolutely continuous relative to a finite, upper doubling measure.

The result broadens the theoretical conditions under which nearest-neighbor prediction is known to work online. Its guarantee concerns the long-run mistake rate, so it does not require mistakes to cease after a finite time. The geometric and process assumptions remain part of the theorem: within those conditions, consistency holds across all measurable target functions.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor prediction has vanishing online mistake rates under specified geometric and process assumptions beyond earlier consistency settings.

title: Online Consistency of the Nearest Neighbor Rule

abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.
