paragraphs: This paper studies how transformers learn to use patterns within their current input through a controlled sequence-modeling task. Each example comes from a Markov chain sampled from a prior distribution over chains. The setup lets the authors examine whether a model learns the transition statistics present in each context.

Training proceeds through several phases. Predictions are initially uniform, then begin using individual-token frequencies, or unigram statistics. A rapid transition later produces the correct solution based on adjacent-token, or bigram, statistics. The resulting statistical induction heads compute accurate next-token probabilities from those context-dependent bigram counts.

Empirical and theoretical analyses connect successful learning to interactions between transformer layers. The authors also find evidence that the easier unigram solution may delay the emergence of the better bigram solution. They vary the prior over Markov chains and consider extensions to longer token patterns. The study provides a concrete setting in which an intermediate strategy can be useful yet potentially slow the development of a more appropriate in-context computation.
summary.tldr: A controlled Markov-chain task reveals transformers progressing from token-frequency heuristics to accurate context-dependent transition modeling.

title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains

abstract: Adam is one of the most popular optimization algorithms in deep learning. However, it is known that Adam does not converge in theory unless choosing a hyperparameter, i.e., $\beta_2$, in a problem-dependent manner. There have been many attempts to fix the non-convergence (e.g., AMSGrad), but they require an impractical assumption that the gradient noise is uniformly bounded. In this paper, we propose a new adaptive gradient method named ADOPT, which achieves the optimal convergence rate of $\mathcal{O} ( 1 / \sqrt{T} )$ with any choice of $\beta_2$ without depending on the bounded noise assumption. ADOPT addresses the non-convergence issue of Adam by removing the current gradient from the second moment estimate and changing the order of the momentum update and the normalization by the second moment estimate. We also conduct intensive numerical experiments, and verify that our ADOPT achieves superior results compared to Adam and its variants across a wide range of tasks, including image classification, generative modeling, natural language processing, and deep reinforcement learning. The implementation is available at https://github.com/iShohei220/adopt.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used to train neural networks, but its theoretical convergence depends on choosing its second-moment hyperparameter, beta_2, in a way that suits the problem. Earlier attempts to repair this issue can require a uniform bound on gradient noise. This paper introduces ADOPT to remove these particular obstacles to a convergence guarantee.

ADOPT makes two changes to the update calculation. It excludes the current gradient from the second-moment estimate used for normalization, and it changes the order of normalization and the momentum update. These modifications alter how gradient information enters the adaptive update. The authors prove an optimal convergence rate of O(1/√T), for any choice of beta_2, without requiring uniformly bounded gradient noise.

The paper also tests ADOPT on image classification, generative modeling, natural language processing, and deep reinforcement learning. It reports better results than Adam and its variants across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a stronger convergence result with empirical evidence that the modified update can be useful in varied deep learning settings.
summary.tldr: ADOPT modifies Adam’s update to obtain an optimal convergence rate for any beta_2 without assuming uniformly bounded gradient noise.

title: ADOPT: Modified Adam Can Converge with Any $\beta_2$ with the Optimal Rate

abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to clean rooms has long been a pursued dream within humanoid research communities. However, many tasks require multi-humanoid collaboration, such as carrying large and heavy furniture together. Given the scarcity of motion capture data on multi-humanoid collaboration and the efficiency challenges associated with multi-agent learning, these tasks cannot be straightforwardly addressed using training paradigms designed for single-agent scenarios. In this paper, we introduce **Coo**perative **H**uman-**O**bject **I**nteraction (**CooHOI**), a framework designed to tackle the challenge of multi-humanoid object transportation problem through a two-phase learning paradigm: individual skill learning and subsequent policy transfer. First, a single humanoid character learns to interact with objects through imitation learning from human motion priors. Then, the humanoid learns to collaborate with others by considering the shared dynamics of the manipulated object using centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) multi-agent RL algorithms. When one agent interacts with the object, resulting in specific object dynamics changes, the other agents learn to respond appropriately, thereby achieving implicit communication and coordination between teammates. Unlike previous approaches that relied on tracking-based methods for multi-humanoid HOI, CooHOI is inherently efficient, does not depend on motion capture data of multi-humanoid interactions, and can be seamlessly extended to include more participants and a wide range of object types.

paragraphs: CooHOI addresses cooperative object transportation by multiple humanoid characters, such as jointly moving large furniture. The paper identifies two difficulties: motion-capture examples of group cooperation are scarce, and learning with multiple agents creates efficiency challenges. Its approach separates acquiring individual interaction skills from learning how to coordinate those skills with teammates.

In the first phase, one humanoid learns to interact with objects through imitation learning using human motion priors. The second phase transfers that capability into a cooperative setting using multi-agent reinforcement learning with centralized training and decentralized execution. Coordination centers on the dynamics of the shared object: when one participant changes its motion, the others learn how to respond.

The manipulated object therefore provides a route for implicit communication between teammates. The authors describe the framework as efficient, independent of motion-capture data specifically showing multi-humanoid interactions, and extendable to more participants and varied object types. Its central contribution is a training strategy that builds cooperation around shared physical effects while reusing skills first learned by an individual character.
summary.tldr: CooHOI transfers individual humanoid interaction skills into cooperation by teaching agents to respond to changes in a shared object's dynamics.

title: CooHOI: Learning Cooperative Human-Object Interaction with Manipulated Object Dynamics

abstract: Multiple clustering aims to discover various latent structures of data from different aspects. Deep multiple clustering methods have achieved remarkable performance by exploiting complex patterns and relationships in data. However, existing works struggle to flexibly adapt to diverse user-specific needs in data grouping, which may require manual understanding of each clustering. To address these limitations, we introduce Multi-Sub, a novel end-to-end multiple clustering approach that incorporates a multi-modal subspace proxy learning framework in this work. Utilizing the synergistic capabilities of CLIP and GPT-4, Multi-Sub aligns textual prompts expressing user preferences with their corresponding visual representations. This is achieved by automatically generating proxy words from large language models that act as subspace bases, thus allowing for the customized representation of data in terms specific to the user’s interests. Our method consistently outperforms existing baselines across a broad set of datasets in visual multiple clustering tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Alexander-Yao/Multi-Sub.

paragraphs: The same visual dataset can contain several meaningful ways to group its contents. Multiple clustering tries to uncover these different structures, but a collection of automatically discovered groupings may still require users to interpret which one fits their needs. Multi-Sub makes the user's requested perspective part of the clustering process.

The method combines CLIP and GPT-4 to connect text describing user preferences with visual representations. A language model automatically generates proxy words that serve as bases for a representation subspace. These words provide a way to express the data through concepts related to the user's interests, guiding how the visual information is represented for grouping.

This mechanism forms an end-to-end framework for customized multiple clustering. Across the visual clustering datasets studied, Multi-Sub consistently outperforms the existing baselines. The reported contribution is therefore both a method for communicating desired grouping criteria and evidence that incorporating those criteria through multimodal representations can improve clustering performance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Multi-Sub uses language-generated proxy words and vision-language representations to cluster images according to user preferences.

title: Customized Multiple Clustering via Multi-Modal Subspace Proxy Learning

abstract: In high-stakes sectors such as network security, IoT security, accurately distinguishing between normal and anomalous data is critical due to the significant implications for operational success and safety in decision-making. The complexity is exacerbated by the presence of unlabeled data and the opaque nature of black-box anomaly detection models, which obscure the rationale behind their predictions. In this paper, we present a novel method to interpret the decision-making processes of these models, which are essential for detecting malicious activities without labeled attack data. We put forward the Segmentation Clustering Decision Tree (SCD-Tree), designed to dissect and understand the structure of normal data distributions. The SCD-Tree integrates predictions from the anomaly detection model into its splitting criteria, enhancing the clustering process with the model's insights into anomalies. To further refine these segments, the Gaussian Boundary Delineation (GBD) algorithm is employed to define boundaries within each segmented distribution, effectively delineating normal from anomalous data points. At this point, this approach addresses the curse of dimensionality by segmenting high-dimensional data and ensures resilience to data drift and perturbations through flexible boundary fitting. We transform the intricate operations of anomaly detection into an interpretable rule's format, constructing a comprehensive set of rules for understanding. Our method's evaluation on diverse datasets and models demonstrates superior explanation accuracy, fidelity, and robustness over existing method, proving its efficacy in environments where interpretability is paramount.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector can flag unusual activity without labeled examples of attacks, yet leave users unable to understand its decisions. This paper develops a way to express those decisions as interpretable rules. Its focus is on understanding the structure of normal data and the boundaries separating normal observations from anomalies.

The method first uses a Segmentation Clustering Decision Tree to divide the data into regions. Predictions from the original anomaly detector help determine the tree's splits, so the segmentation reflects information from the model being explained. A Gaussian Boundary Delineation algorithm then fits boundaries within the resulting regions, providing a more detailed distinction between normal and anomalous points.

Together, segmentation and flexible boundary fitting are intended to address high dimensionality and maintain resilience to data drift and perturbations. The resulting boundaries are translated into a collection of understandable rules. Across the datasets and models evaluated, the authors report better explanation accuracy, agreement with the original detector, and robustness than existing methods. These findings concern how faithfully and reliably the rules explain the detector's behavior.
summary.tldr: A model-guided decision tree and locally fitted boundaries turn black-box anomaly detection decisions into interpretable rules.

title: Dissect Black Box: Interpreting for Rule-Based Explanations in Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for knowledge-seeking purposes yet suffer from hallucinations. The knowledge boundary of an LLM limits its factual understanding, beyond which it may begin to hallucinate. Investigating the perception of LLMs' knowledge boundary is crucial for detecting hallucinations and LLMs' reliable generation. Current studies perceive LLMs' knowledge boundary on questions with concrete answers (close-ended questions) while paying limited attention to semi-open-ended questions that correspond to many potential answers. Some researchers achieve it by judging whether the question is answerable or not. However, this paradigm is not so suitable for semi-open-ended questions, which are usually ``partially answerable questions'' containing both answerable answers and ambiguous (unanswerable) answers. Ambiguous answers are essential for knowledge-seeking, but it may go beyond the knowledge boundary of LLMs. In this paper, we perceive the LLMs' knowledge boundary with semi-open-ended questions by discovering more ambiguous answers. First, we apply an LLM-based approach to construct semi-open-ended questions and obtain answers from a target LLM. Unfortunately, the output probabilities of mainstream black-box LLMs are inaccessible to sample more low-probability ambiguous answers. Therefore, we apply an open-sourced auxiliary model to explore ambiguous answers for the target LLM. We calculate the nearest semantic representation for existing answers to estimate their probabilities, with which we reduce the generation probability of high-probability existing answers to achieve a more effective generation. Finally, we compare the results from the RAG-based evaluation and LLM self-evaluation to categorize four types of ambiguous answers that are beyond the knowledge boundary of the target LLM. Following our method, we construct a dataset to perceive the knowledge boundary for GPT-4. We find that GPT-4 performs poorly on semi-open-ended questions and is often unaware of its knowledge boundary. Besides, our auxiliary model, LLaMA-2-13B, is effective in discovering many ambiguous answers, including correct answers neglected by GPT-4 and delusive wrong answers GPT-4 struggles to identify.

paragraphs: Questions with many possible answers can expose a language model's knowledge boundary differently from questions with one concrete answer. A model may know some valid responses while producing uncertain or incorrect others. This paper therefore probes individual ambiguous answers to semi-open-ended questions instead of treating each whole question as simply answerable or unanswerable.

The method constructs questions with a language model and gathers responses from a target model. Because black-box output probabilities are unavailable, an open-source auxiliary model helps explore less obvious answers. Semantic representations support probability estimates for existing answers, and their generation probabilities are reduced to encourage broader exploration. Retrieval-augmented evaluation and the target's self-evaluation then support four categories of ambiguous answers.

Using this process, the authors build a dataset probing GPT-4. They find poor performance on semi-open-ended questions and frequent failure to recognize its own knowledge boundary. The auxiliary LLaMA-2-13B model discovers both correct answers GPT-4 overlooked and misleading wrong answers it struggles to reject, revealing weaknesses that question-level answerability checks can miss.
summary.tldr: Exploring ambiguous answers to semi-open-ended questions reveals gaps in GPT-4's knowledge and awareness of those gaps.

title: Perception of Knowledge Boundary for Large Language Models through Semi-open-ended Question Answering

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced the field of drug discovery, enhancing the speed and efficiency of molecular identification. However, training these GNNs demands vast amounts of molecular data, which has spurred the emergence of collaborative model-sharing initiatives. These initiatives facilitate the sharing of molecular pre-trained models among organizations without exposing proprietary training data. Despite the benefits, these molecular pre-trained models may still pose privacy risks. For example, malicious adversaries could perform data extraction attack to recover private training data, thereby threatening commercial secrets and collaborative trust. This work, for the first time, explores the risks of extracting private training molecular data from molecular pre-trained models. This task is nontrivial as the molecular pre-trained models are non-generative and exhibit a diversity of model architectures, which differs significantly from language and image models. To address these issues, we introduce a molecule generation approach and propose a novel, model-independent scoring function for selecting promising molecules. To efficiently reduce the search space of potential molecules, we further introduce a Molecule Extraction Policy Network for molecule extraction. Our experiments demonstrate that even with only query access to molecular pre-trained models, there is a considerable risk of extracting training data, challenging the assumption that model sharing alone provides adequate protection against data extraction attacks. Our codes are publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/renH2/Molextract}.

paragraphs: Organizations can share pretrained molecular models without directly releasing the proprietary molecules used for training. This paper investigates whether those models can nevertheless expose training data through extraction attacks. The question matters for collaborative drug-discovery efforts that depend on sharing useful models while preserving commercial confidentiality.

Extraction is challenging because the molecular models are non-generative and vary in architecture. The authors introduce a molecule-generation approach alongside a model-independent scoring function for identifying promising candidate molecules. They also develop a Molecule Extraction Policy Network to reduce the search space efficiently. These components make candidate generation and selection central to the extraction process.

Experiments demonstrate a considerable risk of recovering training molecules even when an attacker has only query access to the pretrained model. The result challenges the assumption that withholding the training dataset while sharing the model provides adequate protection by itself. Its scope is an empirical demonstration of extraction risk through model access, with direct implications for the trust underlying molecular model-sharing initiatives.
summary.tldr: A molecule-generation and selection approach demonstrates that query access to pretrained molecular models can expose private training molecules.

title: Extracting Training Data from Molecular Pre-trained Models

abstract: Leveraging human preferences for steering the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) has demonstrated notable success in recent years. Nonetheless, data selection and labeling are still a bottleneck for these systems, particularly at large scale. Hence, selecting the most informative points for acquiring human feedback may considerably reduce the cost of preference labeling and unleash the further development of LLMs. Bayesian Active Learning provides a principled framework for addressing this challenge and has demonstrated remarkable success in diverse settings. However, previous attempts to employ it for Preference Modeling did not meet such expectations. In this work, we identify that naive epistemic uncertainty estimation leads to the acquisition of redundant samples. We address this by proposing the Bayesian Active Learner for Preference Modeling (BAL-PM), a novel stochastic acquisition policy that not only targets points of high epistemic uncertainty according to the preference model but also seeks to maximize the entropy of the acquired prompt distribution in the feature space spanned by the employed LLM. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that BAL-PM requires 33\% to 68\% fewer preference labels in two popular human preference datasets and exceeds previous stochastic Bayesian acquisition policies.

Active learning tries to reduce that cost by selecting examples that will teach a preference model the most. This paper investigates why earlier Bayesian approaches to that selection problem did not deliver the expected benefits.

The authors identify redundancy as a problem with naive estimates of epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty associated with what the model has not yet learned. Selecting highly uncertain examples can repeatedly acquire similar information. Their method, BAL-PM, combines attention to uncertain examples with an objective that increases the entropy of the selected prompt distribution in the language model's feature space, encouraging a more varied selection.

BAL-PM implements this combination through a stochastic acquisition policy. On two human-preference datasets, the authors report needing 33% to 68% fewer preference labels and outperforming earlier stochastic Bayesian acquisition policies. The findings support using both uncertainty and prompt diversity when selecting feedback, rather than assuming that uncertainty alone identifies the most useful collection of examples.
summary.tldr: BAL-PM combines model uncertainty with prompt diversity to reduce preference-label requirements by 33% to 68% in two evaluated datasets.

title: Deep Bayesian Active Learning for Preference Modeling in Large Language Models

abstract: Reducing parameter redundancies in neural network architectures is crucial for achieving feasible computational and memory requirements during train and inference of large networks. Given its easy implementation and flexibility, one promising approach is layer factorization, which reshapes weight tensors into a matrix format and parameterizes it as the product of two rank-r matrices. However, this family of approaches often requires an initial full-model warm-up phase, prior knowledge of a feasible rank, and it is sensitive to parameter initialization.In this work, we introduce a novel approach to train the factors of a Tucker decomposition of the weight tensors. Our training proposal proves to be optimal in locally approximating the original unfactorized dynamics and stable for the initialization. Furthermore, the rank of each mode is dynamically updated during training.We provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm, showing convergence, approximation and local descent guarantees. The method's performance is further illustrated through a variety of experiments, showing remarkable training compression rates and comparable or even better performance than the full baseline and alternative layer factorization strategies.

paragraphs: Factorizing neural-network layers can reduce the parameters needed for training and inference. A common approach reshapes a weight tensor into a matrix and represents it using two low-rank factors. The paper identifies drawbacks of this family of methods: they often need a full-model warm-up, advance knowledge of a suitable rank, and careful initialization.

The proposed method trains factors in a Tucker decomposition of the weight tensors. Its updates are designed to optimally approximate the original unfactorized training dynamics locally, while remaining stable with respect to initialization. It also updates the rank of each tensor mode during training, allowing the factorization's size to adapt as learning proceeds.

The authors provide convergence, approximation, and local descent guarantees. Experiments show substantial training compression with performance comparable to, or sometimes better than, the full baseline and alternative factorization methods. The local approximation claim explains the training design, while the experiments show that reducing the parameter representation can preserve predictive performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Geometry-aware Tucker-factor training adapts ranks during learning and achieves substantial compression with theoretical guarantees and competitive experimental performance.

title: Geometry-aware training of factorized layers in tensor Tucker format

abstract: The current paradigm of evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) through static benchmarks comes with significant limitations, such as vulnerability to data contamination and a lack of adaptability to the evolving capabilities of LLMs. Therefore, evaluation methods that can adapt and generate evaluation data with controlled complexity are urgently needed. In this work, we introduce Dynamic Evaluation of LLMs via Adaptive Reasoning Graph Evolvement (DARG) to dynamically extend current benchmarks with controlled complexity and diversity. Specifically, we first extract the reasoning graphs of data points in current benchmarks and then perturb the reasoning graphs to generate novel testing data. Such newly generated test samples can have different levels of complexity while maintaining linguistic diversity similar to the original benchmarks. We further use a code-augmented LLM to ensure the label correctness of newly generated data. We apply our DARG framework to diverse reasoning tasks in four domains with 15 state-of-the-art LLMs. Experimental results show that almost all LLMs experience a performance decrease with increased complexity and certain LLMs exhibit significant drops. Additionally, we find that LLMs exhibit more biases when being evaluated via the data generated by DARG with higher complexity levels. These observations provide useful insights into how to dynamically and adaptively evaluate LLMs.

paragraphs: Static language-model benchmarks face two problems: their examples may become contaminated by training data, and their difficulty does not adapt as models improve. DARG addresses these concerns by extending existing benchmarks with newly generated questions whose reasoning complexity can be controlled.

The framework first extracts a reasoning graph from each benchmark example, then changes that graph to create new test data. These alterations produce different complexity levels while maintaining linguistic diversity similar to the original benchmark. A language model augmented with code is used to ensure that the generated examples receive correct labels. This couples changes to the reasoning structure with a mechanism for checking the resulting answers.

The authors evaluate 15 language models on reasoning tasks across four domains. Almost all perform worse as complexity increases, with some showing substantial declines. The harder generated examples also reveal more model biases. These observations show how varying difficulty can expose behavior that a single fixed benchmark score may obscure and support adaptive evaluation as a useful complement to existing tests.
summary.tldr: DARG modifies benchmark reasoning graphs to create tests of controlled difficulty, revealing performance declines and increased biases as complexity rises.

title: DARG: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models via Adaptive Reasoning Graph

abstract: Complex visual reasoning and question answering (VQA) is a challenging task that requires compositional multi-step processing and higher-level reasoning capabilities beyond the immediate recognition and localization of objects and events. Here, we introduce a fully neural Iterative and Parallel Reasoning Mechanism (IPRM) that combines two distinct forms of computation -- iterative and parallel -- to better address complex VQA scenarios. Specifically, IPRM's "iterative" computation facilitates compositional step-by-step reasoning for scenarios wherein individual operations need to be computed, stored, and recalled dynamically (e.g. when computing the query “determine the color of pen to the left of the child in red t-shirt sitting at the white table”). Meanwhile, its "parallel'' computation allows for the simultaneous exploration of different reasoning paths and benefits more robust and efficient execution of operations that are mutually independent (e.g. when counting individual colors for the query: "determine the maximum occurring color amongst all t-shirts'"). We design IPRM as a lightweight and fully-differentiable neural module that can be conveniently applied to both transformer and non-transformer vision-language backbones. It notably outperforms prior task-specific methods and transformer-based attention modules across various image and video VQA benchmarks testing distinct complex reasoning capabilities such as compositional spatiotemporal reasoning (AGQA), situational reasoning (STAR), multi-hop reasoning generalization (CLEVR-Humans) and causal event linking (CLEVRER-Humans). Further, IPRM's internal computations can be visualized across reasoning steps, aiding interpretability and diagnosis of its errors.

paragraphs: Complex visual questions can require several connected operations, along with independent operations that can proceed simultaneously. The Iterative and Parallel Reasoning Mechanism, or IPRM, combines these two forms of computation in a neural module. It targets reasoning that goes beyond immediately recognizing objects or locating events in an image or video.

Its iterative component supports step-by-step computation in which intermediate results must be stored and recalled. Its parallel component explores multiple reasoning paths together, helping execute independent operations robustly and efficiently. The module is lightweight and fully differentiable, allowing it to be applied to both transformer and non-transformer vision-language architectures.

Experiments report improvements over prior task-specific methods and transformer attention modules on image and video question-answering benchmarks. These cover spatial and temporal composition, situational reasoning, multi-hop generalization, and causal event linking. The internal computations can also be visualized across reasoning steps, giving researchers a way to inspect how an answer develops and diagnose errors in that process.
summary.tldr: IPRM combines sequential and parallel neural reasoning to improve complex visual question answering while making reasoning steps inspectable.

title: Learning to Reason Iteratively and Parallelly for Complex Visual Reasoning Scenarios

abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection (OV-3Det) aims to generalize beyond the limited number of base categories labeled during the training phase. The biggest bottleneck is the scarcity of annotated 3D data, whereas 2D image datasets are abundant and richly annotated. Consequently, it is intuitive to leverage the wealth of annotations in 2D images to alleviate the inherent data scarcity in OV-3Det. In this paper, we push the task setup to its limits by exploring the potential of using solely 2D images to learn OV-3Det. The major challenges for this setup is the modality gap between training images and testing point clouds, which prevents effective integration of 2D knowledge into OV-3Det. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework ImOV3D to leverage pseudo multimodal representation containing both images and point clouds (PC) to close the modality gap. The key of ImOV3D lies in flexible modality conversion where 2D images can be lifted into 3D using monocular depth estimation and can also be derived from 3D scenes through rendering. This allows unifying both training images and testing point clouds into a common image-PC representation, encompassing a wealth of 2D semantic information and also incorporating the depth and structural characteristics of 3D spatial data. We carefully conduct such conversion to minimize the domain gap between training and test cases. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, SUNRGBD and ScanNet, show that ImOV3D significantly outperforms existing methods, even in the absence of ground truth 3D training data. With the inclusion of a minimal amount of real 3D data for fine-tuning, the performance also significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art. Codes and pre-trained models are released on the https://github.com/yangtiming/ImOV3D.

paragraphs: ImOV3D studies whether a detector can learn from only two-dimensional images and then identify objects in three-dimensional point clouds, including categories beyond those labeled during training. This setup addresses the shortage of annotated 3D data by drawing on the richer supply of annotated images. The central obstacle is that training images and test-time point clouds present information in different forms.

The framework creates a shared representation containing both an image and a point cloud. It estimates depth from a single image to construct 3D information, and renders 3D scenes to obtain images. These conversions bring training and testing into a common format that combines visual semantics with depth and spatial structure. The conversions are designed to reduce the mismatch between the two settings.

Experiments on SUNRGBD and ScanNet report significant improvements over existing methods without ground-truth 3D training data. Adding a small amount of real 3D data for fine-tuning also significantly exceeds the previous state of the art. The findings support the usefulness of this shared representation for transferring image-based knowledge into 3D detection.
summary.tldr: ImOV3D learns open-vocabulary 3D detection from 2D images by converting images and point clouds into a shared multimodal representation.

title: ImOV3D: Learning Open Vocabulary Point Clouds 3D Object Detection from Only 2D Images

abstract: Clustering-based nearest neighbor search algorithms partition points into shards to form an index, and search only a subset of shards to process a query. Even though search efficacy is heavily influenced by the algorithm that identifies the shards to probe, it has received little attention in the literature. We study routing in clustering-based maximum inner product search, which includes cosine similarity search. We unpack existing routers and notice the surprising role of optimism. We then take a page from the sequential decision making literature and formalize that insight following the principle of ``optimism in the face of uncertainty.'' In particular, we present a framework that incorporates the moments of the distribution of inner products within each shard to estimate the maximum inner product. We then develop a practical instance of our algorithm that uses only the first two moments to reach the same accuracy as state-of-the-art routers by probing up to $50\%$ fewer points on benchmark datasets without compromising efficiency. Our algorithm is also space-efficient: we design a sketch of the second moment whose size is independent of the number of points and requires $\mathcal{O}(1)$ vectors per shard.

paragraphs: Clustering-based search partitions stored points into shards and examines only selected shards for each query. This paper focuses on the router that chooses those shards for maximum inner product search, including cosine similarity search. A good router must identify where the strongest matches are likely to be without inspecting everything.

The authors formalize an optimistic routing principle inspired by sequential decision making. Their framework uses moments of the inner-product distribution within each shard to estimate its maximum inner product. A practical version needs only the first two moments, incorporating information about variation as well as the average when assessing a shard’s potential.

On benchmark datasets, the method reaches the accuracy of state-of-the-art routers while probing up to 50% fewer points without sacrificing efficiency. It also stores a compact sketch of the second moment whose size does not grow with the number of points and requires only a constant number of vectors per shard. The contribution makes shard selection more informative while keeping its storage requirements controlled.
summary.tldr: An optimistic shard router uses compact distribution statistics to match leading search accuracy while probing up to 50% fewer points.

title: Optimistic Query Routing in Clustering-based Approximate Maximum Inner Product Search

abstract: We address the challenge of point cloud registration using color information, where traditional methods relying solely on geometric features often struggle in low-overlap and incomplete scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose GeGS-PCR, a novel two-stage method that combines geometric, color, and Gaussian information for robust registration. Our approach incorporates a dedicated color encoder that enhances color features by extracting multi-level geometric and color data from the original point cloud. We introduce the Geometric-3DGS module, which encodes the local neighborhood information of colored superpoints to ensure a globally invariant geometric-color context. Leveraging LORA optimization, we maintain high performance while preserving the expressiveness of 3DGS. Additionally, fast differentiable rendering is utilized to refine the registration process, leading to improved convergence. To further enhance performance, we propose a joint photometric loss that exploits both geometric and color features. This enables strong performance in challenging conditions with extremely low point cloud overlap. We validate our method by colorizing the Kitti dataset as ColorKitti and testing on both Color3DMatch and Color3DLoMatch datasets. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with Registration Recall at 99.9%, Relative Rotation Error as low as 0.013, and Relative Translation Error as low as 0.024, improving precision by at least a factor of 2.

GeGS-PCR combines geometric structure, color, and Gaussian information in a two-stage approach intended to make those difficult alignments more robust.

A dedicated color encoder extracts information at multiple levels, while a Geometric-3DGS module represents neighborhoods around colored superpoints to provide an invariant geometric-color context. The method also uses LORA optimization and fast differentiable rendering to refine registration. A joint photometric loss brings geometric and color information into the optimization, supporting alignment when shared point coverage is extremely limited.

summary.tldr: GeGS-PCR combines color, geometry, and Gaussian representations to improve point cloud alignment under low overlap and incomplete observations.

title: GeGS-PCR: Fast and Robust Color 3D Point Cloud Registration with Two-Stage Geometric-3DGS Fusion

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to incrementally train a model to a sequence of tasks while maintaining performance on previously seen ones. Despite effectiveness in mitigating forgetting, data storage and replay may be infeasible due to privacy or security constraints, and are impractical or unavailable for arbitrary pre-trained models. Data-free or examplar-free CL aims to continually update models with new tasks without storing previous data. In addition to regularizing updates, we employ model inversion to synthesize data from the trained model, anchoring learned knowledge through replay without retaining old data. However, model inversion in predictive models faces two key challenges. First, generating inputs (e.g., images) solely from highly compressed output labels (e.g., classes) often causes drift between synthetic and real data. Replaying on such synthetic data can contaminate and erode knowledge learned from real data, further degrading inversion quality over time. Second, performing inversion is usually computationally expensive, as each iteration requires backpropagation through the entire model and many steps are needed for convergence. These problems are more severe with large pre-trained models such as Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models. To improve model inversion efficiency, we propose Per-layer Model Inversion (PMI) approach inspired by the faster convergence of single-layer optimization. The inputs optimized from PMI provide strong initialization for full-model inversion, significantly reducing the number of iterations required for convergence. To address feature distribution shift, we model class-wise feature distribution using a Gaussian distribution and preserve distributional information with a contrastive model. Sampling features for inversion ensures alignment between synthetic and real feature distributions. Combining PMI and feature modeling, we demonstrate the feasibility of incrementally training models on new classes by generating data from pseudo image features mapped through semantic-aware feature projection. Our method shows strong effectiveness and compatibility across multiple CL settings.

abstract: Squared families of probability distributions have been studied and applied in numerous machine learning contexts. Typically, they appear as likelihoods, where their advantageous computational, geometric and statistical properties are exploited for fast estimation algorithms, representational properties and statistical guarantees. Here, we investigate the use of squared families as prior beliefs in Bayesian inference. We find that they can form helpful conjugate families, often allowing for closed-form and tractable Bayesian inference and marginal likelihoods. We apply such conjugate families to Bayesian regression in feature space using end-to-end learnable neural network features. Such a setting allows for a rich multi-modal alternative to Gaussian processes with neural network features, often called deep kernel learning. We demonstrate our method on few shot learning, outperforming existing neural methods based on Gaussian processes and normalising flows.

These families have more commonly served as likelihoods, describing how observations arise. The authors investigate their role on the other side of the Bayesian update, asking whether they can support useful and computationally manageable prior distributions.

They find that squared families can form conjugate families, often making inference and marginal likelihood calculations tractable or available in closed form. The application is Bayesian regression over features learned by a neural network, with feature learning performed end to end. This produces a rich, multimodal alternative to Gaussian processes using neural features, a setting commonly called deep kernel learning.

The method is demonstrated on few-shot learning, where the authors report outperforming existing neural approaches based on Gaussian processes and normalizing flows. The significance is the combination of richer distributions with manageable Bayesian calculations. The abstract qualifies that computational advantage as occurring often, so the result supports useful conjugate constructions without implying every squared-family prior yields closed-form inference.
summary.tldr: Squared probability families can provide tractable conjugate priors and a multimodal Bayesian regression alternative that performs well in few-shot learning.

title: Squared families are useful conjugate priors

abstract: Widely adopted evaluation metrics for sparse-view CT reconstruction, such as Structural Similarity Index Measure and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio, prioritize pixel-wise fidelity but often fail to capture the completeness of critical anatomical structures, particularly small or thin regions that are easily missed. To address this limitation, we propose a suite of novel anatomy-aware evaluation metrics designed to assess structural completeness across anatomical structures, including large organs, small organs, intestines, and vessels. Building on these metrics, we introduce CARE, a Completeness-Aware Reconstruction Enhancement framework that incorporates structural penalties during training to encourage anatomical preservation of significant structures. CARE is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into analytical, implicit, and generative methods. When applied to these methods, CARE substantially improves structural completeness in CT reconstructions, achieving up to **32%** improvement for large organs, **22%** for small organs, **40%** for intestines, and **36%** for vessels.
originalAbstract: Widely adopted evaluation metrics for sparse-view CT reconstruction, such as Structural Similarity Index Measure and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio, prioritize pixel-wise fidelity but often fail to capture the completeness of critical anatomical structures, particularly small or thin regions that are easily missed. To address this limitation, we propose a suite of novel anatomy-aware evaluation metrics designed to assess structural completeness across anatomical structures, including large organs, small organs, intestines, and vessels. Building on these metrics, we introduce CARE, a Completeness-Aware Reconstruction Enhancement framework that incorporates structural penalties during training to encourage anatomical preservation of significant structures. CARE is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into analytical, implicit, and generative methods. When applied to these methods, CARE substantially improves structural completeness in CT reconstructions, achieving up to **32%** improvement for large organs, **22%** for small organs, **40%** for intestines, and **36%** for vessels.

paragraphs: A reconstructed CT image can score well on common image similarity measures while still missing important anatomy. The paper focuses on sparse-view reconstruction, where small or thin structures are especially vulnerable. Measures such as SSIM and PSNR emphasize image fidelity but can fail to reflect whether anatomical structures have been preserved completely.

The authors introduce anatomy-aware metrics that assess completeness across large organs, small organs, intestines, and vessels. They then use this perspective to build CARE, a reconstruction enhancement framework. CARE adds structural penalties during training so that preserving significant anatomy becomes part of the learning objective, connecting the proposed evaluation criteria to an actionable improvement method.

CARE can be integrated into analytical, implicit, and generative reconstruction approaches. Across the methods studied, reported completeness improvements reach up to 32% for large organs, 22% for small organs, 40% for intestines, and 36% for vessels. These are category-specific maxima, showing that explicitly evaluating and encouraging anatomical preservation can improve aspects of reconstruction that conventional metrics overlook.
summary.tldr: Anatomy-aware metrics and CARE training penalties improve the structural completeness of CT reconstructions beyond what conventional image metrics capture.

title: Are Pixel-Wise Metrics Reliable for Computerized Tomography Reconstruction?

abstract: Geometric molecule generative models have found expanding applications across various scientific domains, but their generation inefficiency has become a critical bottleneck. Through a systematic investigation of the generative trajectory, we discover a unique challenge for molecule geometric graph generation: generative models require determining the permutation order of atoms in the molecule before refining its atomic feature values. Based on this insight, we decompose the generation process into permutation phase and adjustment phase, and propose a geometric-informed prior and consistency parameter objective to accelerate each phase. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance with approximately 10 sampling steps, 7.5 × faster than previous state-of-the-art models and approximately 100 × faster than diffusion-based models, offering a significant step towards scalable molecular generation.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule’s three-dimensional structure can require many successive updates, making generation speed a practical bottleneck. This paper investigates the sequence of intermediate states produced during generation to understand where that work goes. Its central finding is that geometric graph generators must establish an ordering of the molecule’s atoms before refining their atomic feature values.

The authors use this diagnosis to divide generation into a permutation phase and an adjustment phase. This distinction gives the acceleration method two specific targets: resolving atom ordering and refining the resulting representation. They introduce a geometry-informed prior and a consistency parameter objective to accelerate these phases, connecting the design of the method to the observed structure of the generation process.

Experiments report competitive performance with approximately ten sampling steps. The method is about 7.5 times faster than previous state-of-the-art models and about 100 times faster than diffusion-based models in the reported comparisons. The contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of the generation trajectory and an acceleration approach built around that diagnosis.
summary.tldr: Diagnosing molecule generation as atom ordering followed by feature refinement enables competitive generation in approximately ten sampling steps.

title: Accelerating 3D Molecule Generative Models with Trajectory Diagnosis

abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models have facilitated progress in sketch generation. However, existing specialized methods primarily focus on generic synthesis and lack mechanisms for precise control over sketch styles. In this work, we propose a training-free framework based on diffusion models that enables explicit style guidance via textual prompts and referenced style sketches. Unlike previous style transfer methods that overwrite key and value matrices in self-attention, we incorporate the reference features as auxiliary information with linear smoothing and leverage a style-content guidance mechanism. This design effectively reduces content leakage from reference sketches and enhances synthesis quality, especially in cases with low structural similarity between reference and target sketches. Furthermore, we extend our framework to support controllable multi-style generation by integrating features from multiple reference sketches, coordinated via a joint AdaIN module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves high-quality sketch generation with accurate style alignment and improved flexibility in style control. The official implementation of M3S is available at https://github.com/CMACH508/M3S.

paragraphs: Generating a sketch from text becomes more useful when users can control its drawing style as well as its subject. This paper presents M3S, a training-free diffusion framework guided by text prompts and reference sketches. It targets a common style-transfer problem: copying unwanted subject matter from the reference along with its visual style.

The method supplies reference features as auxiliary information, using linear smoothing and a style-content guidance mechanism. It avoids overwriting the key and value matrices in self-attention, as previous methods do. The authors report that this design reduces reference-content leakage and improves synthesis, especially when the reference and desired sketch have little structural similarity.

M3S also combines features from multiple reference sketches through a joint AdaIN module, enabling controllable generation with more than one style source. Experiments report high-quality outputs, accurate style alignment, and more flexible control. The contribution is therefore both a way to preserve the intended content during style guidance and a mechanism for coordinating several style references within one generation process.
summary.tldr: M3S generates sketches with controllable reference-based styles while reducing unwanted transfer of reference content.

title: Text to Sketch Generation with Multi-Styles

abstract: In-context learning, the ability of large language models to perform tasks using only examples provided in the prompt, has recently been adapted for time series forecasting. This paradigm enables zero-shot prediction, where past values serve as context for forecasting future values, making powerful forecasting tools accessible to non-experts and increasing the performance when training data are scarce. Most existing zero-shot forecasting approaches rely on transformer architectures, which, despite their success in language, often fall short of expectations in time series forecasting, where recurrent models like LSTMs frequently have the edge. Conversely, while LSTMs are well-suited for time series modeling due to their state-tracking capabilities, they lack strong in-context learning abilities. We introduce *TiRex* that closes this gap by leveraging xLSTM, an enhanced LSTM with competitive in-context learning skills. Unlike transformers, state-space models, or parallelizable RNNs such as RWKV, TiRex retains state tracking, a critical property for long-horizon forecasting. To further facilitate its state-tracking ability, we propose a training-time masking strategy called CPM. TiRex sets a new state of the art in zero-shot time series forecasting on the Hugging Face benchmarks *GiftEval* and *Chronos-ZS*, outperforming significantly larger models including *TabPFN-TS* (Prior Labs), *Chronos Bolt* (Amazon), *TimesFM* (Google), and *Moirai* (Salesforce) across both short- and long-term forecasts.

TiRex outperforms substantially larger models, including TabPFN-TS, Chronos Bolt, TimesFM, and Moirai, across short- and long-term forecasting. The findings support recurrent state tracking combined with stronger in-context learning as an effective architecture choice for the evaluated forecasting benchmarks.
summary.tldr: TiRex combines xLSTM state tracking with enhanced in-context learning to achieve leading zero-shot forecasting results across short and long horizons.

title: TiRex: Zero-Shot Forecasting Across Long and Short Horizons with Enhanced In-Context Learning

abstract: When agents trade in a Duality-based Cost Function prediction market, they collectively implement the learning algorithm Follow-The-Regularized-Leader [Abernethy et al., 2013]. We ask whether other learning algorithms could be used to inspire the design of prediction markets. By decomposing and modifying the Duality-based Cost Function Market Maker's (DCFMM) pricing mechanism, we propose a new prediction market, called the Smooth Quadratic Prediction Market, the incentivizes agents to collectively implement general steepest gradient descent. Relative to the DCFMM, the Smooth Quadratic Prediction Market has a better worst-case monetary loss for AD securities while preserving axiom guarantees such as the existence of instantaneous price, information incorporation, expressiveness, no arbitrage, and a form of incentive compatibility. To motivate the application of the Smooth Quadratic Prediction Market, we independently examine agents' trading behavior under two realistic constraints: bounded budgets and buy-only securities. Finally, we provide an introductory analysis of an approach to facilitate adaptive liquidity using the Smooth Quadratic Prediction Market. Our results suggest future designs where the price update rule is separate from the fee structure, yet guarantees are preserved.

paragraphs: Prediction markets combine traders' information through changing prices. The design comes from decomposing and modifying the existing market maker's pricing mechanism. More broadly, the results suggest that future markets could separate price-update rules from fee structures while retaining useful guarantees.
summary.tldr: Smooth Quadratic Prediction Markets connect trading to gradient descent while improving a worst-case loss guarantee and preserving key market properties.

title: Smooth Quadratic Prediction Markets

abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have made significant advancements in arithmetic reasoning. However, the internal mechanism of how LLMs solve arithmetic problems remains unclear. In this paper, we propose explaining arithmetic reasoning in LLMs using game-theoretic interactions. Specifically, we disentangle the output score of the LLM into numerous interactions between the input words. We quantify different types of interactions encoded by LLMs during forward propagation to explore the internal mechanism of LLMs for solving arithmetic problems. We find that (1) the internal mechanism of LLMs for solving simple one-operator arithmetic problems is their capability to encode operand-operator interactions and high-order interactions from input samples. Additionally, we find that LLMs with weak one-operator arithmetic capabilities focus more on background interactions. (2) The internal mechanism of LLMs for solving relatively complex two-operator arithmetic problems is their capability to encode operator interactions and operand interactions from input samples. (3) We explain the task-specific nature of the LoRA method from the perspective of interactions.

paragraphs: This paper studies arithmetic reasoning by examining how combinations of input words contribute to a language model's output score. It uses game-theoretic interactions to separate that score into contributions involving different groups of words. Measuring these interactions during forward propagation provides a way to investigate which relationships the model encodes while solving arithmetic problems.

For problems with one operator, the authors identify operand-operator interactions and higher-order interactions as central to the observed mechanism. Models with weaker performance on these problems place more emphasis on background interactions. This connects arithmetic ability to whether the model's encoded relationships involve the relevant numerical and operational information.

For problems with two operators, the analysis instead highlights interactions among operators and among operands. The paper also uses this perspective to explain the task-specific nature of LoRA adaptation. Together, the findings provide an interaction-based account of differences across arithmetic tasks and model capabilities, linking output behavior to measurable relationships among elements of the input.
summary.tldr: Game-theoretic decomposition connects LLM arithmetic performance to the operand, operator, and background interactions encoded from input text.

title: Interpreting Arithmetic Reasoning in Large Language Models using Game-Theoretic Interactions

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive results on complex reasoning tasks, but their high inference cost remains a major barrier to real-world deployment. A promising solution is to use cascaded inference, where small, cheap models handle easy queries, and only the hardest examples are escalated to more powerful models. However, existing cascade methods typically rely on supervised training with labeled data, offer no theoretical generalization guarantees, and provide limited control over test-time computational cost. We introduce **C3PO** (*Cost Controlled Cascaded Prediction Optimization*), a self-supervised framework for optimizing LLM cascades under probabilistic cost constraints. By focusing on minimizing regret with respect to the most powerful model (MPM), C3PO avoids the need for labeled data by constructing a cascade using only unlabeled model outputs. It leverages conformal prediction to bound the probability that inference cost exceeds a user-specified budget. We provide theoretical guarantees on both cost control and generalization error, and show that our optimization procedure is effective even with small calibration sets. Empirically, C3PO achieves state-of-the-art performance across a diverse set of reasoning benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH-500, BigBench-Hard and AIME, outperforming strong LLM cascading baselines in both accuracy and cost-efficiency. Our results demonstrate that principled, label-free cascade optimization can enable scalable LLM deployment.

paragraphs: Language-model cascades reduce reasoning costs by sending easier queries to inexpensive models and escalating harder ones to stronger models. Choosing when to escalate is difficult: a cascade should preserve answer quality while keeping spending under control. C3PO addresses this routing problem without requiring labeled examples of correct answers.

The framework optimizes regret relative to the most powerful model, using unlabeled model outputs to construct the cascade. It combines this objective with conformal prediction to bound the probability that inference cost exceeds a user-selected budget. This is probabilistic cost control, so the guarantee concerns how often the budget may be exceeded rather than imposing a hard ceiling on every query.

Across GSM8K, MATH-500, BigBench-Hard, and AIME, C3PO outperforms strong cascade baselines in accuracy and cost-efficiency. The findings support using a powerful model as a reference for label-free cascade optimization while giving users a principled way to manage computational risk.
summary.tldr: C3PO learns language-model cascades without labeled answers while bounding the probability of exceeding a chosen inference budget.

title: C3PO: Optimized Large Language Model Cascades with Probabilistic Cost Constraints for Reasoning

abstract: In this paper, we propose an optimally structured gradient coding scheme to mitigate the straggler problem in distributed learning. Conventional gradient coding methods often assume homogeneous straggler models or rely on excessive data replication, limiting performance in real-world heterogeneous systems. To address these limitations, we formulate an optimization problem minimizing residual error while ensuring unbiased gradient estimation by explicitly considering individual straggler probabilities. We derive closed-form solutions for optimal encoding and decoding coefficients via Lagrangian duality and convex optimization, and propose data allocation strategies that reduce both redundancy and computational load. We also analyze convergence behavior for $\lambda$-strongly convex and $\mu$-smooth loss functions. Numerical results show that our approach significantly reduces the impact of stragglers and accelerates convergence compared to existing methods.

To address these limitations, we formulate an optimization problem minimizing residual error while ensuring unbiased gradient estimation by explicitly considering individual straggler probabilities. We derive closed-form solutions for optimal encoding and decoding coefficients via Lagrangian duality and convex optimization, and propose data allocation strategies that reduce both redundancy and computational load. paragraphs: Distributed learning can be slowed by workers that return their computations late. Gradient coding addresses this straggler problem by organizing computations so that useful gradient information remains available when some workers fail to respond promptly. This paper focuses on heterogeneous systems, where different workers have different probabilities of becoming stragglers.

The authors formulate an optimization problem that accounts for each worker’s straggler probability. It minimizes residual estimation error while requiring the gradient estimate to remain unbiased, meaning that its average does not systematically depart from the target gradient. Using Lagrangian duality and convex optimization, they derive closed-form encoding and decoding coefficients. They also develop data-allocation strategies intended to reduce redundant work and computational load.

The convergence analysis applies to loss functions that are strongly convex and smooth. Numerical evaluations show reduced disruption from stragglers and faster convergence than existing methods in the tested settings. The central contribution is to make coding and allocation reflect unequal worker reliability, instead of relying on a uniform straggler model or excessive replication of training data.
summary.tldr: A gradient-coding scheme accounts for unequal worker straggler probabilities to reduce estimation error and accelerate distributed learning.

title: Approximate Gradient Coding for Distributed Learning with Heterogeneous Stragglers

abstract: Existing large language models (LLMs) face challenges of following complex instructions, especially when multiple constraints are present and organized in paralleling, chaining, and branching structures. One intuitive solution, namely chain-of-thought (CoT), is expected to universally improve capabilities of LLMs. However, we find that the vanilla CoT exerts a negative impact on performance due to its superficial reasoning pattern of simply paraphrasing the instructions. It fails to peel back the compositions of constraints for identifying their relationship across hierarchies of types and dimensions. To this end, we propose RAIF, a systematic method to boost LLMs in dealing with complex instructions via incentivizing reasoning for test-time compute scaling. First, we stem from the decomposition of complex instructions under existing taxonomies and propose a reproducible data acquisition method. Second, we exploit reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rule-centric reward signals to cultivate reasoning specifically for instruction following. We address the shallow, non-essential nature of reasoning under complex instructions via sample-wise contrast for superior CoT enforcement. We also exploit behavior cloning of experts to facilitate steady distribution shift from fast-thinking LLMs to skillful reasoners. Extensive evaluations on seven comprehensive benchmarks confirm the validity of the proposed method, where a 1.5B LLM achieves 11.74% gains with performance comparable to a 8B LLM. Evaluation on OOD constraints also confirms the generalizability of our RAIF.

paragraphs: Complex instructions can contain requirements that operate in parallel, depend on earlier steps, or branch into different cases. The authors find that ordinary chain-of-thought prompting can hurt performance on such instructions when the generated reasoning merely restates them. Useful reasoning needs to uncover how the constraints fit together across their different types and levels.

RAIF develops that ability through a systematic training approach. It starts with reproducible data acquisition based on decomposing complex instructions, then uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards centered on rules. Sample-wise contrast encourages stronger reasoning traces, while behavior cloning from experts helps move the model toward more capable reasoning behavior in a steady way.

Evaluations on seven benchmarks support the method's effectiveness. The authors report gains of 11.74% for a 1.5-billion-parameter model, with performance comparable to an 8-billion-parameter model, and additional evidence of generalization to out-of-distribution constraints. The findings suggest that training the content of reasoning specifically for instruction following can make additional test-time computation more useful.
summary.tldr: RAIF trains models to reason about relationships among instruction constraints, improving complex instruction following and generalization to unfamiliar constraints.

title: Incentivizing Reasoning for Advanced Instruction-Following of Large Language Models

abstract: Visual In-Context Learning (VICL) has emerged as a prominent approach for adapting visual foundation models to novel tasks, by effectively exploiting contextual information embedded in in-context examples, which can be formulated as a global ranking problem of potential candidates. Current VICL methods, such as Partial2Global and VPR, are grounded in the similarity-priority assumption that images more visually similar to a query image serve as better in-context examples. This foundational assumption, while intuitive, lacks sufficient justification for its efficacy in selecting optimal in-context examples. Furthermore, Partial2Global constructs its global ranking from a series of randomly sampled pairwise preference predictions. Such a reliance on random sampling can lead to incomplete coverage and redundant samplings of comparisons, thus further adversely impacting the final global ranking. To address these issues, this paper introduces an enhanced variant of Partial2Global designed for reliable and holistic selection of in-context examples in VICL. Our proposed method, dubbed RH-Partial2Global, leverages a jackknife conformal prediction-guided strategy to construct reliable alternative sets and a covering design-based sampling approach to ensure comprehensive and uniform coverage of pairwise preferences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RH-Partial2Global achieves excellent performance and outperforms Partial2Global across diverse visual tasks.

paragraphs: Visual in-context learning adapts a model to a task through examples included in its context. Choosing these examples can be treated as ranking a pool of candidates. This paper questions the common assumption that greater visual similarity to a query reliably identifies better examples, noting that this assumption lacks sufficient justification.

The authors also examine how Partial2Global builds an overall ranking from sampled pairwise preferences. Random sampling can leave some comparisons poorly covered while repeatedly selecting others. Their enhanced method, RH-Partial2Global, uses jackknife conformal prediction to construct reliable alternative sets and a covering-design sampling strategy to obtain comprehensive, uniform coverage of pairwise preferences.

The approach therefore addresses both the reliability of the candidate alternatives and the structure of the comparisons used to rank them. Experiments across diverse visual tasks show that RH-Partial2Global outperforms Partial2Global. The findings support more systematic prompt selection, where the quality of a global ranking depends on how candidates and comparisons are assembled as well as on the individual preference predictions.
summary.tldr: RH-Partial2Global improves visual in-context example selection using conformal prediction and systematically balanced pairwise comparisons.

title: Towards Reliable and Holistic Visual In-Context Learning Prompt Selection

abstract: We introduce HBLLM, a wavelet-enhanced high-fidelity $1$-bit post-training quantization method for Large Language Models (LLMs). By leveraging Haar wavelet transforms to enhance expressive capacity through frequency decomposition, HBLLM significantly improves quantization fidelity while maintaining minimal overhead. This approach features two innovative structure-aware grouping strategies: (1) frequency-aware multi-parameter intra-row grouping and (2) $\ell_2$-norm-based saliency-driven column selection. For non-salient weights, a shared mean is employed across quantization groups within each frequency band to optimize storage efficiency. Experiments conducted on the OPT and LLaMA models demonstrate that HBLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance in $1$-bit quantization, attaining a perplexity of $6.71$ on LLaMA$2$-$13$B with an average weight storage of only $1.08$ bits. Code available at: https://github.com/Yeyke/HBLLM.

paragraphs: HBLLM compresses the weights of an already trained language model toward one-bit storage while aiming to retain model quality. At such low precision, the way weights are represented and grouped becomes central to preserving information. The method uses a Haar wavelet transform to separate frequency components and improve the expressive capacity of the quantized representation.

Its grouping strategy accounts for structure in two ways. Within rows, it uses frequency-aware groups with multiple parameters. Across columns, it uses L2 norms to select salient weights. For weights treated as non-salient, groups within each frequency band share a mean, reducing the storage required for supporting information.

Experiments on OPT and LLaMA models report state-of-the-art one-bit quantization performance. One stated result is a perplexity of 6.71 for LLaMA2-13B with average weight storage of 1.08 bits. That average captures the method's storage beyond the one-bit label. The results support combining frequency decomposition and selective parameter allocation to improve fidelity while keeping overhead small.
summary.tldr: HBLLM combines wavelet decomposition and structure-aware grouping to preserve language-model quality at approximately one bit per weight.

title: HBLLM: Wavelet-Enhanced High-Fidelity 1-Bit Quantization for LLMs

abstract: Graph Edit Distance (GED) is a fundamental graph similarity metric widely used in various applications. However, computing GED is an NP-hard problem. Recent state-of-the-art hybrid GED solver has shown promising performance by formulating GED as a bipartite graph matching problem, then leveraging a generative diffusion model to predict node matching between two graphs, from which both the GED and its corresponding edit path can be extracted using a traditional algorithm. However, such methods typically rely heavily on ground-truth supervision, where the ground-truth node matchings are often costly to obtain in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose GEDRanker, a novel unsupervised GAN-based framework for GED computation. Specifically, GEDRanker consists of a matching-based GED solver and introduces an interpretable preference-aware discriminator. By leveraging preference signals over different node matchings derived from edit path lengths, the discriminator can guide the matching-based solver toward generating high-quality node matching without the need for ground-truth supervision. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our GEDRanker enables the matching-based GED solver to achieve near-optimal solution quality without any ground-truth supervision.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance measures graph similarity through the edits needed to transform one graph into another, but computing it is NP-hard. Matching-based solvers approach the task by predicting correspondences between nodes and extracting an edit path from those correspondences. Training such predictors with correct node matchings can be difficult because those supervision targets are costly to obtain.

GEDRanker replaces ground-truth matching supervision with preferences between candidate matchings. Its GAN-based framework contains a matching solver and an interpretable preference-aware discriminator. Edit-path lengths provide the preference signals: candidate matchings can be compared through the edit paths they produce. The discriminator uses those comparisons to guide the solver toward better node correspondences.

Experiments on benchmark datasets show that this training approach enables near-optimal solution quality without ground-truth supervision. That finding concerns the evaluated solutions rather than a guarantee of exact graph edit distance for every graph pair. The contribution demonstrates how relative quality signals available from candidate outputs can train a matching-based solver when obtaining the correct matching itself is expensive.
summary.tldr: GEDRanker trains graph-edit matching solvers without ground-truth matchings by learning preferences derived from candidate edit-path lengths.

title: Towards Unsupervised Training of Matching-based Graph Edit Distance Solver via Preference-aware GAN

abstract: Grounding large language models (LLMs) in domain-specific tasks like post-hoc dash-cam driving video analysis is challenging due to their general-purpose training and lack of structured inductive biases. As vision is often the sole modality available for such analysis (i.e., no LiDAR, GPS, etc.), existing video-based vision-language models (V-VLMs) struggle with spatial reasoning, causal inference, and explainability of events in the input video. To this end, we introduce iFinder, a structured semantic grounding framework that decouples perception from reasoning by translating dash-cam videos into a hierarchical, interpretable data structure for LLMs. iFinder operates as a modular, training-free pipeline that employs pretrained vision models to extract critical cues—object pose, lane positions, and object trajectories—which are hierarchically organized into frame- and video-level structures. Combined with a three-block prompting strategy, it enables step-wise, grounded reasoning for the LLM to refine a peer V-VLM's outputs and provide accurate reasoning. Evaluations on four public dash-cam video benchmarks show that iFinder's proposed grounding with domain-specific cues—especially object orientation and global context—significantly outperforms end-to-end V-VLMs on four zero-shot driving benchmarks, with up to 39% gains in accident reasoning accuracy. By grounding LLMs with driving domain-specific representations, iFinder offers a zero-shot, interpretable, and reliable alternative to end-to-end V-VLMs for post-hoc driving video understanding.
