paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce useful representations while still overlooking meaningful distinctions. With supervision, representations of subclasses may collapse together within a broader class. Without supervision, the model may favor easy features unrelated to the class and suppress harder features that matter. This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for understanding both behaviors.

The analysis identifies the tendency of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent to favor simpler solutions as a key factor. This simplicity bias can determine which features are learned and which distinctions disappear. The framework therefore connects representation failures at test time with the behavior of the optimization procedure used during training.

The authors present larger embedding dimensions and higher-quality data augmentations as theoretically motivated responses to feature suppression. They also explain theoretically why combining supervised and unsupervised contrastive learning can produce better representations, including with commonly used stochastic gradient methods. The contribution links feature selection, optimization bias, and several remedies within a shared explanation of contrastive representation quality.
summary.tldr: A unified theory links contrastive feature suppression and subclass collapse to optimization's simplicity bias and motivates ways to improve representations.

title: Which Features are Learnt by Contrastive Learning? On the Role of Simplicity Bias in Class Collapse and Feature Suppression

abstract: The phenomenon of $\textit{bias amplification}$ occurs when models amplify training set biases at test time. Existing metrics measure bias amplification with respect to single annotated attributes (e.g., $\texttt{computer}$). However, large-scale datasets typically consist of instances with multiple attribute annotations (e.g., $\{\texttt{computer}, \texttt{keyboard}\}$). We demonstrate models can learn to exploit correlations with respect to multiple attributes, which are not accounted for by current metrics. Moreover, we show that current metrics can give the erroneous impression that little to no bias amplification has occurred as they aggregate positive and negative bias scores. Further, these metrics lack an ideal value, making them difficult to interpret. To address these shortcomings, we propose a new metric: $\textit{Multi-Attribute Bias Amplification}$. We validate our metric’s utility through a bias amplification analysis on the COCO, imSitu, and CelebA datasets. Finally, we benchmark bias mitigation methods using our proposed metric, suggesting possible avenues for future bias mitigation efforts.

We validate our metric’s utility through a bias amplification analysis on the COCO, imSitu, and CelebA datasets. Finally, we benchmark bias mitigation methods using our proposed metric, suggesting possible avenues for future bias mitigation efforts.

paragraphs: Bias amplification occurs when a model’s test-time behavior strengthens biases already present in its training data. Existing measures typically examine individual annotated attributes. This paper argues that such measurements can miss biases involving combinations of attributes, even though many datasets label each example with several attributes at once.

The authors demonstrate that models can exploit correlations involving multiple attributes. They also identify a separate measurement problem: positive and negative bias scores can cancel when aggregated, making amplification appear small or absent. Existing metrics additionally lack a clear ideal value, which makes their results harder to interpret. These issues motivate the proposed Multi-Attribute Bias Amplification metric.

The paper evaluates the metric through analyses of COCO, imSitu, and CelebA, and uses it to benchmark bias mitigation methods. Its contribution is a way to examine amplification that single-attribute summaries can overlook. The findings also suggest directions for improving mitigation efforts by evaluating them against a broader account of the correlations models learn.
summary.tldr: A multi-attribute metric reveals bias amplification that individual-attribute measurements and canceling aggregate scores can hide.

title: Men Also Do Laundry: Multi-Attribute Bias Amplification

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial noise. Denoising model-based defense is a major protection strategy. However, denoising models may fail and induce negative effects in fully white-box scenarios. In this work, we start from the latent inherent properties of adversarial samples to break the limitations. Unlike solely learning a mapping from adversarial samples to natural samples, we aim to achieve denoising by destroying the spatial characteristics of adversarial noise and preserving the robust features of natural information. Motivated by this, we propose a defense based on information discard and robust representation restoration. Our method utilize complementary masks to disrupt adversarial noise and guided denoising models to restore robust-predictive representations from masked samples. Experimental results show that our method has competitive performance against white-box attacks and effectively reverses the negative effect of denoising models.

paragraphs: Adversarial noise can cause a neural network to make incorrect predictions, and denoising models are one way to defend against it. However, the paper notes that denoisers can fail or even have negative effects when an attacker has full knowledge of the defense. It therefore changes how denoising is approached.

The method first discards information using complementary masks. The purpose is to disrupt the spatial structure of adversarial noise while retaining robust information about the underlying sample. Guided denoising models then reconstruct representations useful for reliable prediction from the masked inputs. The two stages combine deliberate disruption with selective restoration.

This design focuses on preserving robust predictive features rather than only learning a direct transformation from an attacked sample into a natural-looking sample. Experiments report competitive performance against white-box attacks and show that the approach reverses the negative effects of denoising models in the tested settings. The contribution is an empirically supported defense strategy in which removing some information can help a restoration model recover the information that matters for prediction.
summary.tldr: Complementary masking followed by guided representation restoration provides competitive defense against the white-box attacks evaluated in the paper.

title: Eliminating Adversarial Noise via Information Discard and Robust Representation Restoration

abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) is an effective approach for addressing the substantial training resource requirements posed by the ever-increasing size of the Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Characterized by its dynamic "train-prune-grow” schedule during training, DST implicitly develops a bi-level structure for training the weights while discovering a subnetwork topology. However, such a structure is consistently overlooked by the current DST algorithms for further optimization opportunities, and these algorithms, on the other hand, solely optimize the weights while determining masks heuristically. In this paper, we extensively study DST algorithms and argue that the training scheme of DST naturally forms a bi-level problem in which the updating of weight and mask is interdependent. Based on this observation, we introduce a novel efficient training framework called BiDST, which for the first time, introduces bi-level optimization methodology into dynamic sparse training domain. Unlike traditional partial-heuristic DST schemes, which suffer from sub-optimal search efficiency for masks and miss the opportunity to fully explore the topological space of neural networks, BiDST excels at discovering excellent sparse patterns by optimizing mask and weight simultaneously, resulting in maximum 2.62% higher accuracy, 2.1$\times$ faster execution speed, and 25$\times$ reduced overhead. Code available at https://github.com/jjsrf/BiDST-ICML2024.

paragraphs: Dynamic sparse training reduces neural network training demands by repeatedly training connections, pruning some, and growing others. This process must choose both the numerical weights and the pattern of connections that remain active. The paper argues that these are interdependent optimization decisions, even though existing methods typically optimize weights while choosing connection masks through heuristics.

The authors formulate this interaction as a bi-level optimization problem and introduce BiDST to exploit that structure. A mask determines which weights participate in the network, while the trained weights affect which masks are useful. Coordinating their optimization gives the method a more systematic way to search for effective sparse network structures.

The reported results include a maximum accuracy improvement of 2.62%, execution that is 2.1 times faster, and a 25-fold reduction in overhead. These are reported outcomes of the framework, rather than universal gains for every sparse network. The contribution is to make the changing connectivity pattern an explicit optimization target alongside the weights, expanding how dynamic sparse training searches for useful subnetworks.
summary.tldr: BiDST jointly optimizes network weights and sparse connection masks through a bi-level formulation, with reported gains in accuracy, speed, and overhead.

title: Advancing Dynamic Sparse Training by Exploring Optimization Opportunities

abstract: Semantic image synthesis (SIS) is a task to generate realistic images corresponding to semantic maps (labels). However, in real-world applications, SIS often encounters noisy user inputs. To address this, we propose Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Model (SCDM), which is a robust conditional diffusion model that features novel forward and generation processes tailored for SIS with noisy labels. It enhances robustness by stochastically perturbing the semantic label maps through Label Diffusion, which diffuses the labels with discrete diffusion. Through the diffusion of labels, the noisy and clean semantic maps become similar as the timestep increases, eventually becoming identical at $t=T$. This facilitates the generation of an image close to a clean image, enabling robust generation. Furthermore, we propose a class-wise noise schedule to differentially diffuse the labels depending on the class. We demonstrate that the proposed method generates high-quality samples through extensive experiments and analyses on benchmark datasets, including a novel experimental setup simulating human errors during real-world applications. Code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/SCDM.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis generates an image from a map of labels describing its contents. In practical use, those maps can contain mistakes, making robustness to noisy input important. This paper introduces a Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Model, or SCDM, whose forward and generation processes are designed specifically for synthesis with noisy labels.

Its central mechanism is Label Diffusion, which randomly perturbs semantic maps through a discrete diffusion process. As the timestep increases, noisy and clean versions of a map become more similar, eventually becoming identical at the final timestep. This convergence facilitates generating an image close to a clean image despite imperfections in the original labels.

The method also uses a class-wise noise schedule, allowing labels from different classes to undergo diffusion differently. Experiments and analyses on benchmark datasets demonstrate high-quality generated samples, including in a new setup that simulates human input errors. The findings support explicitly modeling uncertainty in the conditioning labels as part of the generation process when semantic maps may be imperfect.
summary.tldr: SCDM diffuses semantic labels alongside its image-generation process to improve robustness to noisy input maps.

title: Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Models for Robust Semantic Image Synthesis

abstract: Hybrid dynamical systems are prevalent in science and engineering to express complex systems with continuous and discrete states. To learn laws of systems, all previous methods for equation discovery in hybrid systems follow a two-stage paradigm, i.e. they first group time series into small cluster fragments and then discover equations in each fragment separately through methods in non-hybrid systems. Although effective, performance is then limited because these methods ignore the commonalities in the shared dynamics of fragments that are driven by the same equations. Besides, the two-stage paradigm breaks the interdependence between categorizing and representing dynamics that jointly form hybrid systems. In this paper, we reformulate the problem and propose an end-to-end learning framework, i.e. Amortized Equation Discovery (AMORE), to jointly categorize modes and discover equations characterizing motion dynamics of each mode by all segments of the mode. Experiments on four hybrid and six non-hybrid systems demonstrate the superior performance of our method against previous methods on equation discovery, segmentation, and forecasting.

Besides, the two-stage paradigm breaks the interdependence between categorizing and representing dynamics that jointly form hybrid systems. paragraphs: Hybrid dynamical systems combine continuous motion with switches between discrete modes. Discovering their governing equations therefore involves two connected questions: which mode is active at each point, and which equation describes that mode? The paper argues that separating these questions can discard information needed to answer both well.

Earlier approaches first divide time series into small groups and then fit equations independently within those fragments. AMORE instead learns mode assignments and equations together in an end-to-end framework. Segments assigned to the same mode collectively inform its equation, allowing repeated appearances of the same dynamics to contribute to one shared description.

This matters because a fragment’s equation can help determine its mode, while its mode determines which other fragments provide relevant evidence. Joint learning preserves that relationship. Across four hybrid systems and six non-hybrid systems, the authors report better equation discovery, segmentation, and forecasting than previous methods. These results support sharing information across segments while jointly identifying the system’s modes.
summary.tldr: AMORE jointly identifies dynamical modes and their equations, pooling evidence across segments to improve discovery, segmentation, and forecasting in experiments.

title: Amortized Equation Discovery in Hybrid Dynamical Systems

abstract: NeurAlly-Decomposed Oracle (NADO) is a powerful approach for controllable generation with large language models. It is designed to avoid catastrophic forgetting while achieving guaranteed convergence to an entropy-maximized closed-form optimal solution with reasonable modeling capacity. Despite the success, several challenges arise when apply NADO to a wide range of scenarios. Vanilla NADO suffers from gradient vanishing for low-probability control signals and is highly reliant on a regularization to satisfy the stochastic version of Bellman equation. In addition, the vanilla implementation of NADO introduces a few additional transformer layers, suffering from a limited capacity especially compared to other finetune-based model adaptation methods like LoRA. In this paper, we propose a improved version of the NADO algorithm, namely DiNADO (norm-Disentangled NeurAlly-Decomposed Oracles), which improves the performance of the NADO algorithm through disentangling the step-wise global norm over the approximated oracle $R$-value for all potential next-tokens, allowing DiNADO to be combined with finetuning methods like LoRA. We discuss in depth how DiNADO achieves better capacity, stability and flexibility with both empirical and theoretical results. Experiments on formality control in machine translation and the lexically constrained generation task CommonGen demonstrates the significance of the improvements.

paragraphs: DiNADO improves a method for steering language generation called NADO. The original approach aims to preserve existing model abilities while converging, with sufficient modeling capacity, to an optimal solution that maximizes entropy. Its practical implementation nevertheless faces several obstacles: weak gradients for low-probability control signals, dependence on regularization, and limited capacity from a small number of added transformer layers.

The proposed change separates the step-wise global normalization from the approximate oracle values assigned to possible next tokens. This reformulation allows DiNADO to work with fine-tuning methods such as LoRA. That compatibility matters because it expands the adaptation options beyond the extra-layer implementation whose capacity the authors identify as restrictive.

The paper presents theoretical and empirical arguments for improvements in capacity, stability, and flexibility. Experiments examine formality control in machine translation and lexically constrained generation on CommonGen, with reported improvements in both settings. The contribution is therefore a reformulation of an existing control approach that makes it more adaptable to different training methods and more effective on the evaluated generation tasks.
summary.tldr: DiNADO reformulates NADO’s normalization to improve controllable generation and enable integration with fine-tuning methods such as LoRA.

title: DiNADO: Norm-Disentangled Neurally-Decomposed Oracles for Controlling Language Models

abstract: Time series data across scientific domains are often collected under distinct states (e.g., tasks), wherein latent processes (e.g., biological factors) create complex inter- and intra-state variability. A key approach to capture this complexity is to uncover fundamental interpretable units within the data, Building Blocks (BBs), which modulate their activity and adjust their structure across observations. Existing methods for identifying BBs in multi-way data often overlook inter- vs. intra-state variability, produce uninterpretable components, or do not align with properties of real-world data, such as missing samples and sessions of different duration. Here, we present a framework for Similarity-driven Building Block Inference using Graphs across States (SiBBlInGS). SiBBlInGS offers a graph-based dictionary learning approach for discovering sparse BBs along with their temporal traces, based on co-activity patterns and inter- vs. intra-state relationships. Moreover, SiBBlInGS captures per-trial temporal variability and controlled cross-state structural BB adaptations, identifies state-specific vs. state-invariant components, and accommodates variability in the number and duration of observed sessions across states. We demonstrate SiBBlInGS’s ability to reveal insights into complex phenomena as well as its robustness to noise and missing samples through several synthetic and real-world examples, including web search and neural data.

paragraphs: Time series collected across different tasks or states can vary for several reasons. Underlying processes may change their activity within a state, while their structure may also differ across states. SiBBlInGS seeks interpretable building blocks that represent these distinctions instead of combining all variability into undifferentiated components.

The method uses graph-based dictionary learning to discover sparse building blocks and their temporal activity traces. It draws on co-activity patterns and relationships both within and between states. The framework allows trial-specific timing changes and controlled structural adaptation across states, helping distinguish components shared across states from those specific to one state.

SiBBlInGS also accommodates states with different numbers of sessions and sessions of unequal duration. Synthetic and real-world examples, including web search and neural data, demonstrate its ability to reveal structure in complex observations and its robustness to noise and missing samples. The contribution combines interpretable decomposition with flexibility for the uneven and variable observations found in multi-state time series.
summary.tldr: SiBBlInGS extracts interpretable time-series building blocks while distinguishing within-state variability from structural changes across states.

title: SiBBlInGS: Similarity-driven Building-Block Inference using Graphs across States

abstract: Diffusion models have recently been increasingly applied to temporal data such as video, fluid mechanics simulations, or climate data. These methods generally treat subsequent frames equally regarding the amount of noise in the diffusion process. This paper explores Rolling Diffusion: a new approach that uses a sliding window denoising process. It ensures that the diffusion process progressively corrupts through time by assigning more noise to frames that appear later in a sequence, reflecting greater uncertainty about the future as the generation process unfolds. Empirically, we show that when the temporal dynamics are complex, Rolling Diffusion is superior to standard diffusion. In particular, this result is demonstrated in a video prediction task using the Kinetics-600 video dataset and in a chaotic fluid dynamics forecasting experiment.

paragraphs: Diffusion models applied to sequences commonly use the same noise level for successive frames. Rolling Diffusion changes that arrangement to reflect the greater uncertainty associated with the more distant future. Instead of treating every frame equally during diffusion, it assigns more noise to frames appearing later in the sequence.

The method uses a sliding window for denoising. Within this temporal setup, corruption increases toward later frames as generation unfolds. The central idea is to make the noise pattern follow time, so the process distinguishes nearer frames from more uncertain future ones. This introduces temporal structure into how diffusion handles a sequence, beyond simply applying a common noise level across its frames.

The authors report empirical advantages over standard diffusion when temporal dynamics are complex. They demonstrate this in video prediction on Kinetics-600 and in forecasting chaotic fluid dynamics. These findings support the proposed treatment of future uncertainty in the tested settings, with the strongest stated conclusion tied to complex dynamics rather than every possible temporal-generation task.
summary.tldr: Rolling Diffusion gives later frames more noise and uses sliding-window denoising, improving prediction in tested settings with complex temporal dynamics.

title: Rolling Diffusion Models

abstract: In this paper, we investigate a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) setting where an arm exits the game if the algorithm continuously neglects it. This setup is motivated by real-world scenarios, such as online advertising and crowdsourcing, where arms only gain benefits after being pulled by the algorithm. We identify the intrinsic hardness of this problem and limitations in existing approaches. We propose FC-SE algorithm with expected regret upper bounds as our solution to this problem. As an extension, we even allow new arms to enter after the game starts and design FC-Entry algorithm with performance guarantees for this setup. Finally, we conduct experiments to validate our theoretical results.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we investigate a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) setting where an arm exits the game if the algorithm continuously neglects it. This setup is motivated by real-world scenarios, such as online advertising and crowdsourcing, where arms only gain benefits after being pulled by the algorithm. We identify the intrinsic hardness of this problem and limitations in existing approaches. We propose FC-SE algorithm with expected regret upper bounds as our solution to this problem. As an extension, we even allow new arms to enter after the game starts and design FC-Entry algorithm with performance guarantees for this setup. Finally, we conduct experiments to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which an available option can leave if the algorithm repeatedly neglects it. The setting is motivated by online advertising and crowdsourcing, where participants benefit only when selected. Choices therefore affect both the reward obtained now and which options remain available for future decisions.

The authors analyze the inherent difficulty of this setting and identify limitations of existing approaches. They propose FC-SE and establish upper bounds on its expected regret, the performance shortfall measured against the comparison used in the analysis. The guarantee addresses decision making when continued access to an option depends on giving it sufficient attention.

They then extend the problem to allow new options to arrive after the process has begun. A second algorithm, FC-Entry, comes with performance guarantees for that changing population. Experiments validate the theoretical findings. Together, the two algorithms address availability as part of the learning problem, accounting for participants who can exit and, in the extension, enter over time.
summary.tldr: FC-SE and FC-Entry provide guarantees for bandit learning when neglected options leave and new options may arrive.

title: On Multi-Armed Bandit with Impatient Arms

abstract: Constrained optimization offers a powerful framework to prescribe desired behaviors in neural network models. Typically, constrained problems are solved via their min-max Lagrangian formulations, which exhibit unstable oscillatory dynamics when optimized using gradient descent-ascent. The adoption of constrained optimization techniques in the machine learning community is currently limited by the lack of reliable, general-purpose update schemes for the Lagrange multipliers. This paper proposes the νPI algorithm and contributes an optimization perspective on Lagrange multiplier updates based on PI controllers, extending the work of Stooke, Achiam and Abbeel (2020). We provide theoretical and empirical insights explaining the inability of momentum methods to address the shortcomings of gradient descent-ascent, and contrast this with the empirical success of our proposed νPI controller. Moreover, we prove that νPI generalizes popular momentum methods for single-objective minimization. Our experiments demonstrate that νPI reliably stabilizes the multiplier dynamics and its hyperparameters enjoy robust and predictable behavior.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization provides a way to specify behaviors that a neural network should satisfy. A common formulation introduces Lagrange multipliers and turns training into a min-max problem. Updating the model and multipliers through gradient descent-ascent can produce unstable oscillations, making reliable multiplier updates an important obstacle to using constraints in practice.

The paper proposes νPI, an update algorithm based on proportional-integral controllers, and analyzes it from an optimization perspective. It provides theoretical and empirical explanations for why momentum methods fail to resolve the shortcomings of gradient descent-ascent. This analysis is paired with empirical evidence that the proposed controller handles multiplier dynamics successfully.

The authors also prove that νPI generalizes popular momentum methods in single-objective minimization, connecting the controller approach to familiar optimization tools. In experiments, νPI reliably stabilizes multiplier updates, and its hyperparameters behave robustly and predictably. These results support a more manageable approach to constrained training, while the stabilization evidence reported here is experimental rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every constrained problem.
summary.tldr: νPI uses proportional-integral control for Lagrange multiplier updates, empirically stabilizing constrained optimization while generalizing familiar momentum methods.

title: On PI Controllers for Updating Lagrange Multipliers in Constrained Optimization

abstract: GEneral Matrix Multiply (GEMM) is a central operation in deep learning and corresponds to a large chunk of the compute footprint. Therefore, improving its efficiency is an active topic of research. A popular strategy is the use of low bit-width integers to approximate the original matrix entries. This allows efficiency gains, but often requires sophisticated techniques to control the rounding error. In this work, we first verify that when the low bit-width restriction is removed, for a variety of Transformer-based models, integers are, in fact, sufficient for all GEMMs need – for both training and inference stages, and achieve parity (with floating point). No sophisticated techniques are needed. We find that while a large majority of entries in matrices (encountered in such models) can be easily represented by low bit-width integers, the existence of a few heavy hitter entries make it difficult to achieve efficiency gains via the exclusive use of low bit-width GEMMs alone. To address this issue, we develop a simple algorithm, Integer Matrix Unpacking (IM-Unpack), to unpack a matrix with large integer entries into a larger matrix whose entries all lie within the representable range of arbitrarily low bit-width integers. This allows equivalence with the original GEMM, i.e., the exact result can be obtained using purely low bit-width integer GEMMs. This comes at the cost of additional operations – we show that for many popular models, this overhead is quite small. Code is available at https://github.com/vsingh-group/im-unpack.

paragraphs: Matrix multiplication accounts for a large share of deep-learning computation. Low-bit integers can make it more efficient, but approximating matrix entries introduces rounding errors. The authors first find that, without a low-bit restriction, integer matrix multiplications achieve parity with floating-point computation during training and inference for a variety of Transformer models.

The remaining difficulty is that a few large entries require more bits even when most entries fit into a small integer range. IM-Unpack addresses these heavy hitters by expanding a matrix into a larger representation whose entries all fit within an arbitrarily low-bit integer range. Low-bit matrix multiplications can then recover the original integer multiplication exactly.

This exactness concerns the original integer matrix operation, avoiding additional approximation from forcing its large entries into the smaller range. The tradeoff is extra operations caused by unpacking. The authors report that this overhead is small for many popular models, suggesting a route to exploiting low-bit computation while preserving the original integer result.
summary.tldr: IM-Unpack expands integer matrices so arbitrarily low-bit multiplications can reproduce their original multiplication exactly, at an added computational cost.

title: IM-Unpack: Training and Inference with Arbitrarily Low Precision Integers

abstract: Gaussian smoothing combined with a probabilistic framework for denoising via the empirical Bayes formalism, i.e., the Tweedie-Miyasawa formula (TMF), are the two key ingredients in the success of score-based generative models in Euclidean spaces. Smoothing holds the key for easing the problem of learning and sampling in high dimensions, denoising is needed for recovering the original signal, and TMF ties these together via the score function of noisy data. In this work, we extend this paradigm to the problem of learning and sampling the distribution of binary data on the Boolean hypercube by adopting Bernoulli noise, instead of Gaussian noise, as a smoothing device. We first derive a TMF-like expression for the optimal denoiser for the Hamming loss, where a score function naturally appears. Sampling noisy binary data is then achieved using a Langevin-like sampler which we theoretically analyze for different noise levels. At high Bernoulli noise levels sampling becomes easy, akin to log-concave sampling in Euclidean spaces. In addition, we extend the sequential multi-measurement sampling of Saremi et al. (2024) to the binary setting where we can bring the "effective noise" down by sampling multiple noisy measurements at a fixed noise level, without the need for continuous-time stochastic processes. We validate our formalism and theoretical findings by experiments on synthetic data and binarized images.
originalAbstract: Gaussian smoothing combined with a probabilistic framework for denoising via the empirical Bayes formalism, i.e., the Tweedie-Miyasawa formula (TMF), are the two key ingredients in the success of score-based generative models in Euclidean spaces. Smoothing holds the key for easing the problem of learning and sampling in high dimensions, denoising is needed for recovering the original signal, and TMF ties these together via the score function of noisy data. In this work, we extend this paradigm to the problem of learning and sampling the distribution of binary data on the Boolean hypercube by adopting Bernoulli noise, instead of Gaussian noise, as a smoothing device. We first derive a TMF-like expression for the optimal denoiser for the Hamming loss, where a score function naturally appears. Sampling noisy binary data is then achieved using a Langevin-like sampler which we theoretically analyze for different noise levels. At high Bernoulli noise levels sampling becomes easy, akin to log-concave sampling in Euclidean spaces. In addition, we extend the sequential multi-measurement sampling of Saremi et al. (2024) to the binary setting where we can bring the "effective noise" down by sampling multiple noisy measurements at a fixed noise level, without the need for continuous-time stochastic processes. We validate our formalism and theoretical findings by experiments on synthetic data and binarized images.

paragraphs: Score-based generation in continuous spaces connects adding noise, sampling the smoothed distribution, and recovering the original signal through denoising. This paper develops a corresponding framework for binary data, whose coordinates take only two possible values. It uses Bernoulli noise to smooth distributions on the Boolean hypercube while retaining the binary structure of the problem.

The authors derive a formula linking a score function to the optimal denoiser under Hamming loss, which counts mismatched binary coordinates. They then construct a Langevin-like sampler for noisy binary data and analyze its behavior at different noise levels. At high Bernoulli noise levels, sampling becomes easier, paralleling a favorable sampling regime in continuous spaces.

The paper also extends sequential multi-measurement sampling to binary data. Multiple noisy measurements at a fixed noise level can lower the effective noise, avoiding a need for continuous-time stochastic processes. Experiments on synthetic datasets and binarized images validate the framework and theoretical findings, supporting a discrete version of the smoothing-and-denoising approach.
summary.tldr: Bernoulli smoothing and score-based denoising extend a continuous generative-modeling framework to sampling binary data.

title: Sampling Binary Data by Denoising through Score Functions

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been observed to process non-human-readable text sequences, such as jailbreak prompts, often viewed as a bug for aligned LLMs. In this work, we present a systematic investigation challenging this perception, demonstrating that unnatural languages - strings that appear incomprehensible to humans but maintain semantic meanings for LLMs - contain latent features usable by models. Notably, unnatural languages possess latent features that can be generalized across different models and tasks during inference. Furthermore, models fine-tuned on unnatural versions of instruction datasets perform on-par with those trained on natural language, achieving $49.71$ win rates in Length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 in average across various base models. In addition, through comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs process unnatural languages by filtering noise and inferring contextual meaning from filtered words. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/John-AI-Lab/Unnatural_Language.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes respond meaningfully to text that people find incomprehensible, including strings encountered in jailbreak prompts. This paper investigates such unnatural language as a source of usable model features. The question is whether these strings carry information that models can exploit beyond an isolated unusual response.

The authors find that features in unnatural language can generalize across different models and tasks during inference. They also fine-tune models on unnatural versions of instruction datasets and report performance comparable to training on natural-language versions. Across various base models, the reported average length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate is 49.71.

Their analysis attributes processing of these strings to filtering noise and inferring contextual meaning from the words that remain. This supplies an account of how apparently unreadable inputs can still support meaningful model behavior. Together, the transfer and fine-tuning findings challenge the idea that such behavior is only a defect, identifying usable semantic information in the unnatural-language constructions studied.
summary.tldr: The study finds transferable semantic features in human-unreadable text and comparable instruction-tuning performance using unnatural-language datasets.

title: Unnatural Languages Are Not Bugs but Features for LLMs

abstract: Deep State Space Models (SSMs), such as Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2024), have become powerful tools for language modeling, offering high performance and linear scalability with sequence length. However, the application of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods to SSM-based models remains largely underexplored. We start by investigating two fundamental questions on existing PEFT methods: (i) How do they perform on SSM-based models? (ii) Which parameters should they target for optimal results? Our analysis shows that LoRA and its variants consistently outperform all other PEFT methods. While LoRA is effective for linear projection matrices, it fails on SSM modules—yet still outperforms other methods applicable to SSMs, indicating their limitations. This underscores the need for a specialized SSM tuning approach. To address this, we propose Sparse Dimension Tuning (SDT), a PEFT method tailored for SSM modules. Combining SDT for SSMs with LoRA for linear projection matrices, we achieve state-of-the-art performance across extensive experiments.

paragraphs: Deep state-space models offer strong language-modeling performance with computation that scales linearly with sequence length. This paper asks how to adapt them using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, an area that has received less attention for these architectures. It examines both which existing methods work well and which parts of the model those methods should target.

The analysis finds that LoRA and its variants consistently outperform the other evaluated parameter-efficient methods. However, their effectiveness differs across components: LoRA works well for linear projection matrices but fails on the state-space modules themselves. Even there, it still outperforms the other applicable methods, highlighting a weakness in the available approaches to adapting those modules.

The authors introduce Sparse Dimension Tuning, a method tailored to state-space modules. They combine it with LoRA on the linear projection matrices, assigning different tuning methods to different architectural components. This combination achieves reported state-of-the-art performance across extensive experiments. The findings emphasize that choosing where and how to adapt parameters is central to effective fine-tuning of state-space models.
summary.tldr: Sparse Dimension Tuning adapts state-space modules while LoRA handles projection matrices, improving parameter-efficient fine-tuning in the reported experiments.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of State Space Models

abstract: Inverse problems aim to reconstruct unseen data from corrupted or perturbed measurements. While most work focuses on improving reconstruction quality, generalization accuracy and robustness are equally important, especially for safety-critical applications. Model-based architectures (MBAs), such as loop unrolling methods, are considered more interpretable and achieve better reconstructions. Empirical evidence suggests that MBAs are more robust to perturbations than black-box solvers, but the accuracy-robustness tradeoff in MBAs remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective training scheme for MBAs, called SGD jittering, which injects noise iteration-wise during reconstruction. We theoretically demonstrate that SGD jittering not only generalizes better than the standard mean squared error training but is also more robust to average-case attacks. We validate SGD jittering using denoising toy examples, seismic deconvolution, and single-coil MRI reconstruction. Both SGD jittering and its SPGD extension yield cleaner reconstructions for out-of-distribution data and demonstrates enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct unseen data from measurements that may be corrupted or perturbed. Model-based architectures organize this reconstruction around an iterative procedure, but good reconstruction quality alone does not settle questions about generalization and robustness. This paper studies a training strategy intended to improve those properties together.

SGD jittering injects noise at individual reconstruction iterations during training. The authors theoretically show better generalization than standard mean-squared-error training and greater robustness to average-case attacks. The stated robustness result concerns that attack setting, giving a specific meaning to the theoretical improvement rather than an unrestricted guarantee against every perturbation.

Experiments cover toy denoising, seismic deconvolution, and single-coil MRI reconstruction. Both SGD jittering and its SPGD extension produce cleaner reconstructions for out-of-distribution data and show enhanced resistance to adversarial attacks. These findings connect the theoretical analysis with several reconstruction settings, supporting iteration-wise noise injection as a simple way to improve how model-based architectures handle unfamiliar or perturbed measurements.
summary.tldr: Injecting noise during reconstruction training improves generalization and average-case robustness theoretically, with supporting results across three inverse-problem settings.

title: SGD Jittering: A Training Strategy for Robust and Accurate Model-Based Architectures

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated superior performance in a variety of graph mining and learning tasks. However, when node representations involve sensitive personal information or variables related to individuals, learning from graph data can raise significant privacy concerns. Although recent studies have explored local differential privacy (LDP) to address these concerns, they often introduce significant distortions to graph data, severely degrading private learning utility (e.g., node classification accuracy). In this paper, we present UPGNET, an LDP-based privacy-preserving graph learning framework that enhances utility while protecting user data privacy. Specifically, we propose a three-stage pipeline that generalizes the LDP protocols for node features, targeting privacy-sensitive scenarios. Our analysis identifies two key factors that affect the utility of privacy-preserving graph learning: feature dimension and neighborhood size. Based on the above analysis, UPGNET enhances utility by introducing two core layers: High-Order Aggregator (HOA) layer and the Node Feature Regularization (NFR) layer. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets indicate that UPGNET significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both privacy protection and learning utility.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can learn from information about individuals, making privacy protection important when node features contain sensitive data. Existing approaches using local differential privacy can substantially distort the graph data and reduce learning quality, including node-classification accuracy. UPGNET aims to preserve useful learning while protecting the information supplied by users.

The framework introduces a three-stage pipeline that generalizes local differential privacy protocols for node features. Its analysis identifies feature dimension and neighborhood size as two key influences on learning utility. These findings connect the privacy problem to how much information each node represents and the neighborhood structure through which graph learning operates.

The paper’s contribution combines analysis of what drives utility loss with architectural components designed to improve learning under the privacy framework.
summary.tldr: UPGNET improves private graph learning by addressing the effects of feature dimension and neighborhood size on utility.

title: Going Deeper into Locally Differentially Private Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recently, transformer-based models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across various computer vision tasks, including image classification, detection, and segmentation. However, their substantial parameter count poses significant challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments such as edge or mobile devices. Low-rank approximation (LRA) has emerged as a promising model compression technique, effectively reducing the number of parameters in transformer models by decomposing high-dimensional weight matrices into low-rank representations. Nevertheless, matrix decomposition inherently introduces information loss, often leading to a decline in model accuracy. Furthermore, existing studies on LRA largely overlook the quantization process, which is a critical step in deploying practical vision transformer (ViT) models. To address these challenges, we propose a robust LRA framework that preserves weight information after matrix decomposition and incorporates quantization tailored to LRA characteristics. First, we introduce a reparameterizable branch-based low-rank approximation (RB-LRA) method coupled with weight reconstruction to minimize information loss during matrix decomposition. Subsequently, we enhance model accuracy by integrating RB-LRA with knowledge distillation techniques. Lastly, we present an LRA-aware quantization method designed to mitigate the large outliers generated by LRA, thereby improving the robustness of the quantized model. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on the ImageNet dataset using various ViT-based models. Notably, the Swin-B model with RB-LRA achieved a 31.8% reduction in parameters and a 30.4% reduction in GFLOPs, with only a 0.03% drop in accuracy. Furthermore, incorporating the proposed LRA-aware quantization method reduced accuracy loss by an additional 0.83% compared to naive quantization.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be difficult to deploy on devices with limited resources because their weight matrices contain many parameters. Low-rank approximation compresses those matrices, but decomposition can discard information and reduce accuracy. The paper also addresses quantization, another deployment step whose interaction with low-rank compression has received insufficient attention.

The proposed framework uses reparameterizable branches and weight reconstruction to reduce information loss during low-rank approximation. It then combines this approach with knowledge distillation to improve accuracy. A separate quantization method accounts for the characteristics of low-rank approximation, specifically targeting the large outliers it can produce and making the quantized model more robust.

Experiments on ImageNet cover several Vision Transformer models. For Swin-B, the authors report 31.8% fewer parameters and a 30.4% reduction in GFLOPs with a reported accuracy drop of only 0.03%. Their quantization method further reduces accuracy loss by a reported 0.83% relative to naive quantization. These results support coordinating decomposition and quantization when compressing a model, since the first stage changes the weights that the second stage must handle.
summary.tldr: LRA-QViT coordinates low-rank compression and quantization to reduce Vision Transformer size and computation while preserving accuracy.

title: LRA-QViT: Integrating Low-Rank Approximation and Quantization for Robust and Efficient Vision Transformers

abstract: Abstract visual reasoning (AVR) involves discovering shared concepts across images through analogy, akin to solving IQ test problems. Bongard Problems (BPs) remain a key challenge in AVR, requiring both visual reasoning and verbal description. We investigate whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can solve BPs by formulating a set of diverse MLLM-suited solution strategies and testing $4$ proprietary and $4$ open-access models on $3$ BP datasets featuring synthetic (classic BPs) and real-world (Bongard HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld) images. Despite some successes on real-world datasets, MLLMs struggle with synthetic BPs. To explore this gap, we introduce Bongard-RWR, a dataset representing synthetic BP concepts using real-world images. Our findings suggest that weak MLLM performance on classical BPs is not due to the domain specificity, but rather comes from their general AVR limitations. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/pavonism/bongard-rwr

paragraphs: Bongard Problems test abstract visual reasoning by requiring a solver to discover concepts across images and express the relevant distinction verbally. This paper uses them to investigate whether multimodal language models can connect visual evidence with abstract concepts across different kinds of imagery.

The authors develop several solution strategies suited to these models and test four proprietary and four open-access models. The evaluation covers three datasets containing both synthetic and real-world images. Although models achieve some success on the real-world datasets, they struggle with classical synthetic Bongard Problems. That difference raises a question about whether unfamiliar image style or reasoning difficulty drives the failures.

To investigate, the authors introduce Bongard-RWR, which expresses concepts from synthetic problems using real-world images. Their findings suggest that the weakness on classical problems stems from general abstract visual reasoning limitations rather than domain specificity. The new dataset helps separate a problem’s visual presentation from its underlying concept, strengthening the investigation of what the models find difficult without making the explanation certain.
summary.tldr: Bongard evaluations suggest that multimodal models’ struggles reflect general abstract visual reasoning limitations rather than merely unfamiliar synthetic imagery.

title: Reasoning Limitations of Multimodal Large Language Models. A case study of Bongard Problems

abstract: Recently, forecasting future abnormal events has emerged as an important scenario to tackle realworld necessities. However, the solution of predicting specific future time points when anomalies will occur, known as Anomaly Prediction (AP), remains under-explored. Existing methods dealing with time series data fail in AP, focusing only on immediate anomalies or failing to provide precise predictions for future anomalies. To address AP, we propose a novel framework called Anomaly to Prompt (A2P), comprised of Anomaly-Aware Forecasting (AAF) and Synthetic Anomaly Prompting (SAP). To enable the forecasting model to forecast abnormal time points, we adopt a strategy to learn the relationships of anomalies. For the robust detection of anomalies, our proposed SAP introduces a learnable Anomaly Prompt Pool (APP) that simulates diverse anomaly patterns using signal-adaptive prompt. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of A2P over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to predict future anomalies.

paragraphs: Detecting an abnormal event as it happens differs from predicting the specific future time when it will occur. This paper focuses on that latter task, called anomaly prediction. The authors argue that existing time-series methods either concentrate on immediate anomalies or do not give sufficiently precise predictions of future abnormal points.

Their framework, Anomaly to Prompt, combines Anomaly-Aware Forecasting with Synthetic Anomaly Prompting. The forecasting component learns relationships involving anomalies so that it can predict abnormal time points. The prompting component uses a learnable Anomaly Prompt Pool to simulate diverse abnormal patterns through prompts adapted to the signal, supporting robust anomaly detection.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art methods and support the framework’s ability to forecast future anomalies. The contribution brings anomaly relationships directly into forecasting and uses synthetic patterns to broaden the anomaly behavior represented by the model. Its practical focus is timing: predicting upcoming abnormal points gives the task a more specific target than recognizing that a signal is already unusual.
summary.tldr: A2P combines anomaly-aware forecasting and synthetic anomaly prompts to predict when future abnormal events will occur.

title: When Will It Fail?: Anomaly to Prompt for Forecasting Future Anomalies in Time Series

abstract: It is widely believed that noise conditioning is indispensable for denoising diffusion models to work successfully. This work challenges this belief. Motivated by research on blind image denoising, we investigate a variety of denoising-based generative models in the absence of noise conditioning. To our surprise, most models exhibit graceful degradation, and in some cases, they even perform better without noise conditioning. We provide a mathematical analysis of the error introduced by removing noise conditioning and demonstrate that our analysis aligns with empirical observations. We further introduce a noise-unconditional model that achieves a competitive FID of 2.23 on CIFAR-10, significantly narrowing the gap to leading noise-conditional models. We hope our findings will inspire the community to revisit the foundations and formulations of denoising generative models.

paragraphs: Denoising generative models are commonly given information about the noise level they are handling. This paper questions whether that explicit conditioning is indispensable for successful generation. Inspired by blind image denoising, the authors investigate what happens when a variety of denoising-based generative models operate without noise conditioning.

Most models in their investigation deteriorate gradually rather than failing outright, and some perform better without the conditioning information. The authors also mathematically analyze the error introduced by removing it. That analysis agrees with their empirical observations, giving a theoretical account alongside the experiments rather than relying only on the surprising outcomes.

The paper further introduces a model without noise conditioning that reaches an FID of 2.23 on CIFAR-10, narrowing the gap to leading noise-conditioned models. The findings challenge a necessity claim: explicit noise information is not essential for every successful denoising generator examined here. They do not imply that removing conditioning improves every model, since the reported behavior includes both degradation and occasional improvement.
summary.tldr: Experiments and analysis show that many denoising generators remain effective without explicit noise conditioning.

title: Is Noise Conditioning Necessary for Denoising Generative Models?

abstract: One-Shot Federated Learning (FL) is a recent paradigm that enables multiple clients to cooperatively learn a global model in a single round of communication with a central server. In this paper, we analyze the One-Shot FL problem through the lens of Bayesian inference and propose FedBEns, an algorithm that leverages the inherent multimodality of local loss functions to find better global models.Our algorithm leverages a mixture of Laplace approximations for the clients’ local posteriors, which the server then aggregates to infer the global model. We conduct extensive experiments on various datasets, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms competing baselines that typically rely on unimodal approximations of the local losses.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning asks multiple clients to build a shared model with only one communication round with a central server. FedBEns approaches this problem through Bayesian inference. Its central idea is that a client's local learning problem can have multiple promising solutions, and the information sent to the server should preserve that variety.

The method represents each client's local posterior using a mixture of Laplace approximations. Each approximation captures a local region, while the mixture represents multiple regions together. The server aggregates these local posterior representations to infer a global model. This makes multimodality—the presence of multiple distinct possibilities—a feature used in aggregation, rather than reducing each client's contribution to a single mode.

Experiments across various datasets show FedBEns outperforming competing baselines that typically use unimodal local approximations. The finding supports retaining multiple local possibilities when forming a global model under a strict communication constraint. Its significance is specifically tied to the one-shot setting: the richer posterior representation helps the server combine client information within the single available round.
summary.tldr: FedBEns improves one-shot federated learning by combining Bayesian representations that preserve multiple promising solutions at each client.

title: FedBEns: One-Shot Federated Learning based on Bayesian Ensemble

abstract: This paper focuses on non-asymptotic confidence bounds (CB) for the optimal values of stochastic optimization (SO) problems. Existing approaches often rely on two conditions that may be restrictive: The need for a global Lipschitz constant and the assumption of light-tailed distributions. Beyond either of the conditions, it remains largely unknown whether computable CBs can be constructed. In view of this literature gap, we provide three key findings below: (i) Based on the conventional formulation of sample average approximation (SAA), we derive non-Lipschitzian CBs for convex SP problems under heavy tails. (ii) We explore diametrical risk minimization (DRM)—a recently introduced modification to SAA—and attain non-Lipschitzian CBs for nonconvex SP problems in light-tailed settings. (iii) We extend our analysis of DRM to handle heavy-tailed randomness by utilizing properties in formulations for training over-parameterized classification models.

paragraphs: This paper studies computable confidence bounds for the optimal value of an optimization problem involving randomness. The bounds are non-asymptotic, meaning they concern finite samples. Existing approaches often require a global Lipschitz constant controlling how sharply the objective changes, along with light-tailed randomness. The authors investigate what can be established beyond those restrictions.

The first result uses conventional sample average approximation to obtain bounds without a global Lipschitz requirement for convex problems with heavy-tailed randomness. The second studies diametrical risk minimization, a modification of sample average approximation, and obtains such bounds for nonconvex problems when randomness is light-tailed.

The third extends the diametrical risk minimization analysis to heavy-tailed settings by using properties of formulations for training over-parameterized classification models. These results cover different combinations of optimization structure and randomness. Their importance is that confidence assessment becomes available in the specified settings beyond familiar assumptions; the heavy-tailed nonconvex extension specifically draws on the structure of those classification formulations.
summary.tldr: The paper derives finite-sample confidence bounds for stochastic optimal values beyond global Lipschitz assumptions, including specified heavy-tailed settings.

title: Non-Asymptotic and Non-Lipschitzian Bounds on Optimal Values in Stochastic Optimization Under Heavy Tails

abstract: Machine learning models often perform well on tabular data by optimizing average prediction accuracy. However, they may underperform on specific subsets due to inherent biases and spurious correlations in the training data, such as associations with non-causal features like demographic information. These biases lead to critical robustness issues as models may inherit or amplify them, resulting in poor performance where such misleading correlations do not hold. Existing mitigation methods have significant limitations: some require prior group labels, which are often unavailable, while others focus solely on the conditional distribution $P(Y|X)$, upweighting misclassified samples without effectively balancing the overall data distribution $P(X)$. To address these shortcomings, we propose a latent score-based reweighting framework. It leverages score-based models to capture the joint data distribution $P(X, Y)$ without relying on additional prior information. By estimating sample density through the similarity of score vectors with neighboring data points, our method identifies underrepresented regions and upweights samples accordingly. This approach directly tackles inherent data imbalances, enhancing robustness by ensuring a more uniform dataset representation. Experiments on various tabular datasets under distribution shifts demonstrate that our method effectively improves performance on imbalanced data.

paragraphs: A tabular classifier can achieve strong average accuracy while failing on subsets where misleading training correlations no longer hold. Some robustness methods require group labels; others emphasize misclassified examples without directly balancing which kinds of inputs appear in the data. This paper targets that underlying imbalance through a learned reweighting scheme.

The method uses score-based models to capture the joint distribution of inputs and labels without additional prior information. It estimates sample density by comparing score vectors with those of neighboring data points. Examples in regions identified as underrepresented receive greater weight, so training gives those regions more influence.

The distinction matters because classification errors and underrepresentation are different signals. The proposed weights explicitly address uneven coverage of the data distribution rather than relying only on whether a prediction was wrong. Experiments on several tabular datasets under distribution shifts report improved performance on imbalanced data, supporting the use of learned density information to improve robustness without requiring prior group annotations.
summary.tldr: Score-based density estimates identify underrepresented tabular examples and increase their training weight to improve robustness under distribution shifts.

title: Latent Score-Based Reweighting for Robust Classification on Imbalanced Tabular Data

abstract: We propose MUltiway Dynamic Dense (MUDD) connections, a simple yet effective method to address the limitations of residual connections and enhance cross-layer information flow in Transformers. Unlike existing dense connection approaches with static and shared connection weights, MUDD generates connection weights dynamically depending on hidden states at each sequence position and for each decoupled input stream (the query, key, value or residual) of a Transformer block. MUDD connections can be seamlessly integrated into any Transformer architecture to create MUDDFormer. Extensive experiments show that MUDDFormer significantly outperforms Transformers across various model architectures and scales in language modeling, achieving performance of Transformers trained with 1.8x–2.4x compute. Notably, MUDDPythia-2.8B matches Pythia-6.9B in pretraining ppl and downstream tasks and even rivals Pythia-12B in five-shot settings, while adding only 0.23% parameters and 0.4% computation. Code in JAX and PyTorch and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/MUDDFormer.

paragraphs: MUDDFormer changes how information moves between Transformer layers. The paper targets limitations of residual connections and proposes dense connections whose weights adapt to the current hidden states. This makes cross-layer information flow responsive to what the network is processing at each sequence position.

The method generates separate connection weights for a block’s query, key, value, and residual input streams. Each stream can therefore receive its own dynamically weighted combination of cross-layer information. The authors present these connections as compatible with any Transformer architecture, allowing the same modification to be applied across different model designs.

Language-modeling experiments across architectures and scales report performance comparable to Transformers trained with 1.8 to 2.4 times as much compute. MUDDPythia-2.8B matches Pythia-6.9B on pretraining perplexity and downstream tasks, and rivals Pythia-12B in five-shot settings. The reported overhead is only 0.23% more parameters and 0.4% more computation. These comparisons suggest that more adaptive use of existing layers can deliver substantial gains with very small architectural overhead.
summary.tldr: MUDDFormer dynamically weights cross-layer connections for separate Transformer input streams, improving language-model performance with little added computation.

title: MUDDFormer: Breaking Residual Bottlenecks in Transformers via Multiway Dynamic Dense Connections

abstract: Recent advancements in Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have significantly improved performance in Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks through multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). However, existing methods still face challenges, such as the scarcity of knowledge with reasoning examples and erratic responses from retrieved knowledge. To address these issues, in this study, we propose a multimodal RAG framework, termed RCTS, which enhances LVLMs by constructing a Reasoning Context-enriched knowledge base and a Tree Search re-ranking method. Specifically, we introduce a self-consistent evaluation mechanism to enrich the knowledge base with intrinsic reasoning patterns. We further propose a Monte Carlo Tree Search with Heuristic Rewards (MCTS-HR) to prioritize the most relevant examples. This ensures that LVLMs can leverage high-quality contextual reasoning for better and more consistent responses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple VQA datasets, significantly outperforming In-Context Learning (ICL) and Vanilla-RAG methods. It highlights the effectiveness of our knowledge base and re-ranking method in improving LVLMs.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can help vision-language models answer visual questions by supplying external knowledge. Yet retrieved material may lack useful reasoning examples, and the resulting responses can be inconsistent. RCTS addresses both the content of the knowledge base and the selection of examples provided to the model.

The framework first enriches its knowledge base with reasoning patterns through a self-consistent evaluation mechanism. It then uses Monte Carlo Tree Search with heuristic rewards to re-rank examples and prioritize those most relevant to the question. These steps connect the availability of reasoning-rich material with a search procedure for choosing useful context.

Experiments on multiple visual question answering datasets report state-of-the-art performance and substantial improvements over in-context learning and vanilla retrieval-augmented generation. The results support the combined value of the enriched knowledge base and the re-ranking method. The broader significance is that retrieval quality depends on more than having related information available: in this framework, reasoning examples and their ordering help produce better and more consistent answers.
summary.tldr: RCTS improves visual question answering by enriching retrieved knowledge with reasoning examples and re-ranking them through heuristic-guided tree search.

title: Re-ranking Reasoning Context with Tree Search Makes Large Vision-Language Models Stronger

abstract: The isomorphism problem is a key challenge in both graph and hypergraph domains, crucial for applications like protein design, chemical pathways, and community detection. Hypergraph isomorphism, which models high-order relationships in real-world scenarios, remains underexplored compared to the graph isomorphism. Current algorithms for hypergraphs, like the 1-dimensional generalized Weisfeiler-Lehman test (1-GWL), lag behind advancements in graph isomorphism tests, limiting most hypergraph neural networks to 1-GWL’s expressive power. To address this, we propose the high-dimensional GWL (k-GWL), generalizing k-WL from graphs to hypergraphs. We prove that k-GWL reduces to k-WL for simple graphs, and thus develop a unified isomorphism method for both graphs and hypergraphs. We also successfully establish a clear and complete understanding of the GWL hierarchy of expressivity, showing that (k+1)-GWL is more expressive than k-GWL with illustrative examples. Based on k-GWL, we develop a hypergraph neural network model named k-HNN with improved expressive power of k-GWL, which achieves superior performance on real-world datasets, including a 6% accuracy improvement on the Steam-Player dataset over the runner-up. Our code is available at https://github.com/talence-zcq/KGWL.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of entities, making structural comparisons relevant to applications such as protein design and chemical pathways. Many hypergraph neural networks are limited by the distinguishing power of the one-dimensional generalized Weisfeiler–Leman test. This paper develops higher-dimensional versions, called k-GWL, to distinguish a richer range of hypergraph structures.

The authors prove that k-GWL becomes the established k-WL procedure when applied to simple graphs, giving a shared framework for graphs and hypergraphs. They also establish a hierarchy: moving from k-GWL to (k+1)-GWL increases expressive power. Here, greater expressivity concerns the ability to tell structures apart, and the paper supplies examples demonstrating the distinction.

The theory leads to k-HNN, a hypergraph neural network with the improved expressive power of k-GWL. Experiments show superior performance on real-world datasets, including a reported 6% accuracy improvement over the runner-up on Steam-Player. The contribution connects a formal account of structural distinguishability with a network architecture and evidence of practical predictive benefits.
summary.tldr: Higher-dimensional hypergraph tests establish an expressivity hierarchy and motivate a neural network with improved real-world performance.

title: Improved Expressivity of Hypergraph Neural Networks through High-Dimensional Generalized Weisfeiler-Leman Algorithms

abstract: The Machine Learning (ML) community has wit- nessed explosive growth, with millions of ML models being published on the Web. Reusing ML model components has been prevalent nowadays. Developers are often required to choose a license to publish and govern the use of their models. Popular options include Apache-2.0, OpenRAIL (Responsible AI Licenses), Creative Commons Licenses (CCs), Llama2, and GPL-3.0. Currently, no standard or widely accepted best practices ex- ist for model licensing. But does this lack of standardization lead to undesired consequences? Our answer is Yes. After reviewing the clauses of the most widely adopted licenses, we take the position that current model licensing practices are dragging us into a quagmire of legal noncom- pliance. To support this view, we explore the cur- rent practices in model licensing and highlight the differences between various model licenses. We then identify potential legal risks associated with these licenses and demonstrate these risks using examples from real-world repositories on Hug- ging Face. To foster a more standardized future for model licensing, we also propose a new draft of model licenses, ModelGo Licenses (MGLs), to address these challenges and promote better compliance. https://www.modelgo.li/

paragraphs: This position paper examines licensing problems created by widespread publication and reuse of machine-learning models. Developers choose among licenses such as Apache-2.0, OpenRAIL, Creative Commons, Llama2, and GPL-3.0, but the authors identify a lack of accepted standards or best practices for model licensing. They argue that this fragmented situation creates risks of legal noncompliance.

The paper reviews clauses in commonly used licenses, compares their differences, and investigates current licensing practices. It then uses examples from real repositories on Hugging Face to illustrate potential legal risks. This connects the argument about inconsistent practices to concrete model-sharing settings, rather than treating the choice of license as an isolated administrative decision.

The authors also propose ModelGo Licenses, a new draft intended to address the identified challenges and improve compliance. The contribution combines a review of existing approaches with a proposed route toward standardization. Its stated concern is that continued model reuse without clearer licensing practices can carry legal risks, while a more coherent framework could help developers govern that reuse.
summary.tldr: The authors identify compliance risks in fragmented model licensing and propose draft ModelGo Licenses as a route toward clearer practices.

title: Position: Current Model Licensing Practices are Dragging Us into a Quagmire of Legal Noncompliance

abstract: We study mechanism design for the budget-feasible procurement problem, a natural problem that arises when a buyer wants to procure goods or services from multiple strategic sellers who each have a cost to provide that service, the buyer has a value for each service procured, but is constrained by a budget. In contrast to prior work, which has focused on buyer value maximization for this problem, we solve for optimal and approximately-optimal mechanisms for the objectives of buyer utility (value of procured services minus payments), welfare (value minus production costs), and generalizations of the two. For welfare, we design a simple mechanism that obtains a constant-factor approximation for the prior-free (worst-case) setting. As prior-free mechanisms fail to provide any guarantee for utility, even for a single seller, we consider Bayesian settings, where the buyer has distributional knowledge over sellers’ costs. We first provide a utility-optimal mechanism that satisfies the buyer’s budget constraint in expectation, then we show how to modify the mechanism to satisfy the budget constraint ex-post, for every realization of seller costs, while still obtaining near-optimal utility guarantees. Finally, we generalize our mechanisms to other objectives.

paragraphs: A buyer with a limited budget must choose what to purchase from sellers who have their own production costs and act strategically. Maximizing the value of purchased services is only one possible objective. This paper also studies buyer utility, which subtracts payments from value, and welfare, which subtracts production costs.

For welfare, the authors design a simple mechanism with a constant-factor approximation guarantee in the prior-free, worst-case setting. Utility behaves differently: prior-free mechanisms cannot offer a guarantee even with one seller. The paper therefore studies utility when the buyer knows probability distributions over sellers’ costs, making that information central to the available guarantees.

In this Bayesian setting, the authors first construct a utility-optimal mechanism whose spending respects the budget in expectation. They then modify it to respect the budget for every realization of seller costs while retaining near-optimal utility guarantees. Extensions cover further objectives. These distinctions matter because average budget compliance and guaranteed compliance in every outcome impose different requirements on a purchasing mechanism.
summary.tldr: The paper designs budget-feasible purchasing mechanisms for welfare and buyer utility, with guarantees that depend on the objective and available cost information.

title: From Welfare to Utility: Generalized Objectives in Budget-Feasible Procurement

abstract: The Gaussian graphical model (GGM) is a useful tool to represent relationships of conditional dependence among variables. In many real-world applications, datasets often contain multiple related sub-populations, whose associated GGMs may have common structure, as well as large structural differences. In such cases, it is useful to recover common hub variables, which are the highly connected variables in the GGMs of all sub-populations. In this paper, we propose the Joint Inverse Components for Hub Detection (JIC-HD) method to recover the common hubs across multiple GGMs without the need to estimate all subpopulation GGMs. To this end, we introduce joint minimax eigenspaces, and show that these can be leveraged for the recovery of common hubs. We establish theoretical guarantees for the recovery of common hubs. Additionally, our numerical simulation studies confirm superior performance of our JIC-HD in detecting common hubs compared to the existing methods in the literature. Our method is especially advantageous when the multiple GGMs have both common and individual hubs across sub-populations. Finally, we analyze cancer gene-expression datasets and identify biologically meaningful common hub genes across cancer subtypes.
