paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models describe conditional dependence among variables. Related populations can share some relationships while differing substantially elsewhere. This paper focuses on common hubs: variables that are highly connected in every population’s graph, even when other highly connected variables are specific to individual populations.

The proposed Joint Inverse Components for Hub Detection method, JIC-HD, targets these shared hubs without first estimating every complete population graph. Its mathematical tool is a set of joint minimax eigenspaces, which the authors show can support common-hub recovery. They also establish theoretical guarantees for that recovery. This focuses the analysis on the shared structural feature of interest.

In numerical simulations, JIC-HD detects common hubs better than existing methods, with particular advantages when shared and population-specific hubs coexist. An application to cancer gene-expression datasets identifies biologically meaningful hub genes shared across cancer subtypes. The findings support direct common-hub estimation as a useful strategy when related datasets combine common organization with substantial individual differences.
summary.tldr: JIC-HD identifies highly connected variables shared across Gaussian graphical models without estimating every population’s full graph.

title: Identifying Common Hubs in Multiple Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Language models (LMs) tend to memorize portions of their training data and reproduce verbatim spans. When the underlying sources are sensitive or copyright-protected, such reproduction raises issues of consent and compensation for creators and compliance risks for developers. We propose Anchored Decoding, a plug-and-play inference-time method for suppressing verbatim reproduction: it enables decoding from any risky LM trained on mixed-license data by keeping generation in bounded proximity to a permissively trained safe LM. Anchored Decoding does so by adaptively allocating a user-chosen information budget over the generation trajectory and enforcing per-step constraints that yield a sequence-level guarantee, enabling a tunable risk–utility trade-off. To make Anchored Decoding practically useful, we introduce a new permissively trained safe model (TinyComma 1.8B), as well as Anchored-Byte Decoding, a byte-level variant of our method that enables cross-vocabulary fusion via the ByteSampler (Hayase et al., 2025) framework. Across six model pairs on long-form metrics for copying risk and utility, Anchored and Anchored-Byte Decoding define a new Pareto frontier, preserving near-original fluency and factuality while eliminating up to 75% of the measurable copying gap between the risky baseline and a safe reference, at a modest inference overhead.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce memorized training passages verbatim, creating concerns when those passages come from protected or sensitive sources. Anchored Decoding addresses this during generation by constraining a model trained on mixed-license material to remain within a bounded distance of a reference model trained on permissively licensed material. The method is designed to attach to an existing model at inference time.

A user selects an information budget, and the method distributes that budget adaptively across generation steps. Constraints at individual steps combine into a guarantee for the complete sequence. This gives users a way to adjust the trade-off between copying risk and output usefulness. The authors also introduce the permissively trained TinyComma 1.8B reference model and a byte-level variant that supports model pairs with different vocabularies.

Across six model pairs, the methods achieve improved measured risk–utility trade-offs while preserving nearly the original fluency and factuality. They close up to 75% of the measurable copying gap between a risky baseline and a safe reference, with modest inference overhead. That finding describes reduced measured copying relative to a reference, rather than complete elimination of reproduction.
summary.tldr: Anchored Decoding constrains generation using a permissively trained reference model to improve the trade-off between verbatim copying risk and output quality.

title: Anchored Decoding: Provably Reducing Copyright Risk for Any Language Model

abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) encode data as continuous coordinate-based functions parameterized by neural networks, shifting downstream tasks such as image recognition to operate on functional rather than discrete representations. Despite their increasing adoption, the adversarial robustness of INR-based classification pipelines remain largely underexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of adversarial robustness in INR-based classifiers. A key challenge is that generating an INR requires $\text{\emph{training}}$ a neural network for each input sample, resulting in an optimization-in-the-loop forward pass that renders standard gradient-based attacks computationally prohibitive. To address this, we design surrogate models that amortizes the INR-generation process, serving as a practical proxy for attacking INR-based classifiers. We also develop speed-up techniques that substantially reduce the training cost of the surrogate. We show that in contrast to recent work, INR-based classifiers are vulnerable: under adversarial input perturbations, classification accuracy collapses to near zero. Moreover, existing countermeasures designed to operate on discrete representations offer limited protection.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode an input as a neural network that maps coordinates to values. Classification then operates on this continuous representation. The paper investigates whether this change in representation provides protection against adversarial input perturbations, addressing a robustness question that has received relatively little systematic study.

Testing these pipelines is difficult because producing the representation requires training a separate network for each input. An attack that follows gradients through this process must contend with optimization inside the classifier’s forward computation. The authors develop surrogate models that approximate the representation-generation process, spreading its cost across inputs. They also introduce techniques that reduce the cost of training these surrogates.

Using this attack approach, the authors find that classification accuracy falls to nearly zero under adversarial perturbations in their study. Countermeasures developed for discrete representations provide limited protection. The findings challenge earlier robustness claims and show why expensive attack computation can obscure vulnerabilities: making a pipeline difficult to attack computationally does not establish that its representations resist adversarial changes.
summary.tldr: Surrogate attacks reveal severe adversarial vulnerabilities in classifiers that encode inputs as implicit neural representations.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Implicit Neural Representation-Based Classifiers

abstract: AI agents equipped with tool-calling capabilities are susceptible to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks. In this attack scenario, malicious commands hidden within untrusted content trick the agent into performing unauthorized actions. Existing defenses can reduce attack success but often suffer from the over-defense dilemma: they deploy expensive, always-on sanitization regardless of actual threat, thereby degrading utility and latency even in benign scenarios. We revisit IPI through a causal ablation perspective: a successful injection manifests as a dominance shift where the user request no longer provides decisive support for the agent’s privileged action, while a particular untrusted segment, such as a retrieved document or tool output, provides disproportionate attributable influence. Based on this signature, we propose CausalArmor, a selective defense framework that (i) computes lightweight, leave-one-out ablation-based attributions at privileged decision points, and (ii) triggers targeted sanitization only when an untrusted segment dominates the user intent. Additionally, CausalArmor employs retroactive Chain-of-Thought masking to prevent the agent from acting on “poisoned" reasoning traces. We present a theoretical analysis showing that sanitization based on attribution margins conditionally yields an exponentially small upper bound on the probability of selecting malicious actions. Experiments on AgentDojo and DoomArena demonstrate that CausalArmor matches the security of aggressive defenses while improving explainability and preserving utility and latency of AI agents.

paragraphs: Indirect prompt injection occurs when instructions inside untrusted material redirect an agent toward unauthorized actions. Defenses that sanitize everything can impose costs even on harmless requests. CausalArmor instead looks for a shift in what supports a privileged action: an untrusted passage becomes disproportionately influential while the user's request loses decisive influence.

At privileged decision points, the framework uses lightweight leave-one-out checks to estimate the contributions of different inputs. It triggers targeted sanitization when an untrusted segment dominates user intent. It also masks earlier reasoning traces affected by the injection, addressing the possibility that contaminated reasoning could continue influencing actions after the original content has been sanitized.

The theoretical analysis gives a conditional, exponentially small upper bound on malicious-action probability when sanitization uses attribution margins. This is a qualified guarantee, rather than an unconditional promise of protection. On AgentDojo and DoomArena, the method reportedly matches aggressive defenses in security while preserving agent utility and latency. Its central contribution is selective intervention guided by attributable influence, which also provides an explanation for why a particular segment required attention.
summary.tldr: CausalArmor selectively sanitizes untrusted content when attribution checks indicate that it dominates an agent's privileged decision.

title: CausalArmor: Efficient Indirect Prompt Injection Guardrails via Causal Attribution

abstract: Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) is a foundational pillar of physical-layer security, providing unclonable identity authentication and lightweight defense mechanisms for zero-trust wireless networks. Its practical deployment, however, often occurs in a source-free open-world (SF-OW) setting, characterized by a continuous influx of unregistered devices and privacy constraints that preclude the retention of historical data. In this paper, we formalize SF-OW RFFI task, which manifests a severe stability-plasticity dilemma: intrinsic signal similarity confuses new classes, while source absence precipitates catastrophic forgetting. To address this, we propose Incremental Orthogonal ETF (IO-ETF), a novel neural collapse-inspired framework utilizing output geometry to actively induce parameter separation and isolation. We further devise a Triple-Level Geometric Alignment (TLGA) strategy via semantic optimal transport, manifold progressive anchoring, and reliable subspace retention to stably align unlabeled streams to this geometric skeleton. Experiments on benchmarks demonstrate a superior trade-off between old-class retention and new-class discovery, offering a promising solution for secure access in dynamic networks.

The system must learn new device classes while preserving recognition of old ones, despite similar signals and the absence of earlier examples.

The proposed Incremental Orthogonal ETF framework organizes the model’s output geometry to encourage separation and isolation of parameters. Its design is inspired by neural collapse. The two components address the stability–plasticity trade-off: adapting to new devices can interfere with established knowledge, while preserving established knowledge can hinder discovery. Benchmark experiments report a superior balance between retaining old classes and discovering new ones. The contribution is a framework explicitly designed for this source-free, open-world setting, with geometric organization providing a common structure for learning from incoming signals without retaining the historical dataset.
summary.tldr: IO-ETF uses output geometry and multilevel alignment to balance new-device discovery with old-device retention when historical radio data cannot be stored.

title: Source-Free Open-World RF Fingerprint Identification

abstract: Multi-person human mesh recovery (HMR) from a single image is inherently ill-posed, as multiple 3D poses can produce identical 2D projections due to depth ambiguity. Most existing methods implicitly regress 3D translation from image features, which often leads to unreliable depth estimation. To address this issue, we propose a depth-guided multi-person HMR framework that explicitly models instance-level depth cues and integrates them into mesh recovery. Specifically, we first introduce an instance-aware depth estimator to predict per-person pelvis depths that serve as explicit 3D anchors, thereby decoupling depth estimation from mesh regression. Then, we design a geometry-anchored refinement decoder that uses these anchors to initialize each instance within a plausible 3D neighborhood, stabilizing mesh refinement under joint 2D-3D supervision. Finally, we adopt a single-stage joint training strategy to coordinate depth estimation and mesh recovery in a unified framework. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both mesh reconstruction accuracy and depth ordering.

paragraphs: Recovering several people’s three-dimensional body meshes from one image is ambiguous: different spatial arrangements can produce the same two-dimensional view. A particularly difficult part is estimating each person’s distance from the camera. This paper addresses that problem by making person-specific depth estimates an explicit input to mesh recovery.

The framework first predicts the depth of each person’s pelvis. These predictions act as three-dimensional anchors, separating depth estimation from the subsequent prediction of body meshes. A refinement decoder uses each anchor to place a person in a plausible spatial neighborhood before refining the mesh. This gives the refinement process a concrete geometric starting point under combined two-dimensional and three-dimensional supervision.

Although the framework separates the roles of depth prediction and mesh regression, it trains them together in a single stage so they can coordinate. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art mesh reconstruction accuracy and depth ordering. The stated findings support explicit depth anchoring as a useful way to improve both reconstructed body geometry and the relative placement of people.
summary.tldr: DGG-HMR uses explicit per-person depth anchors to improve multi-person body reconstruction and depth ordering from a single image.

title: DGG-HMR: Multi-Person Human Mesh Recovery with Depth-Guided Geometric Anchoring

abstract: Irregular Multivariate Time Series (IMTS) are common in practice, yet their irregular sampling complicates effective modeling. Existing approaches typically either (i) design specialized architectures that limit the reuse of proven Multivariate Time Series (MTS) models, or (ii) map IMTS onto regular temporal grids through interpolation, which may distort temporal dynamics by introducing artificial values. To address these limitations, we propose a new input-embedding-based approach. We identify that the key bottleneck lies not in the backbone architecture, but in conventional embedding layers that assume uniform sampling. In this work, we introduce QuITE (Query-Based Irregular Time Series Embedding), a simple yet effective plug-and-play embedding module for IMTS. QuITE employs learnable query tokens to aggregate irregular observations through a single self-attention layer, directly producing backbone-compatible latent representations without artificial value generation or architectural modification. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks show that QuITE consistently improves MTS models, yielding average relative gains of up to 54.7% in forecasting and 15.8% in classification across diverse datasets and backbone architectures.

paragraphs: Time-series models often expect observations at regular intervals, while practical multivariate data can arrive unevenly. Existing solutions either introduce specialized architectures or interpolate observations onto regular grids, potentially adding artificial values that distort temporal behavior. QuITE addresses this mismatch at the input-embedding stage.

The module uses learnable query tokens and a single self-attention layer to aggregate irregular observations into latent representations compatible with existing time-series backbones. This allows established models to receive irregular data without changing their architectures or inventing measurements between observed points. The design locates the adaptation at the interface between raw observations and the model's internal processing.

Across real-world forecasting and classification benchmarks, QuITE consistently improves the tested multivariate time-series models. Reported average relative gains reach 54.7% for forecasting and 15.8% for classification across datasets and architectures. These findings support the authors' diagnosis that conventional input embeddings are a key bottleneck. They also show why a small, reusable embedding module can broaden the usefulness of existing models.
summary.tldr: QuITE turns irregular observations into embeddings for existing time-series models without interpolation or backbone changes.

title: QuITE: Query-Based Irregular Time Series Embedding

abstract: Traditional instrumental variable (IV) estimators cannot accommodate more treatments than instruments, a limitation that is critical for high-dimensional, unstructured data like clinical treatment pathways. Current practice—applying unsupervised dimension reduction before IV estimation—suffers from substantial omitted treatment bias because the representation learning step ignores the instrument. We propose a novel framework that constructs treatment representations by explicitly incorporating instrumental variables. We prove that this instrument-guided approach ensures the identification of optimal outcome-prediction directions even with limited instruments. Validation on large-scale, semi-synthetic clinical data derived from a major hospital, along with other simulations, shows that our approach significantly outperforms conventional two-stage methods.

paragraphs: Traditional instrumental-variable estimators cannot handle more treatments than instruments, which becomes a serious obstacle when treatments are high-dimensional or unstructured. Clinical treatment pathways are one example. A common workaround compresses the treatment data before estimation, but that compression can discard information needed for the downstream instrumental-variable analysis.

The paper argues that unsupervised dimension reduction creates substantial omitted treatment bias because it ignores the instrument when deciding what to preserve. Its proposed framework instead learns treatment representations with instrumental variables explicitly included. This makes the representation-learning stage responsive to the information that the later estimation stage will actually use.

The authors prove identification of optimal outcome-prediction directions even when instruments are limited. This result concerns those predictive directions, rather than unrestricted recovery of every original treatment effect. Large-scale semi-synthetic clinical data derived from a major hospital, alongside other simulations, show significant improvements over conventional two-stage methods. The findings support coordinating treatment compression with the downstream identification problem instead of solving the two stages independently.
summary.tldr: Instrument-guided treatment representations improve downstream instrumental-variable regression when treatment dimensions exceed the available instruments.

title: Learning Treatment Representations for Downstream Instrumental Variable Regression

abstract: LLM self-explanations are often presented as a promising tool for AI oversight, yet their faithfulness to the model’s true reasoning process is poorly understood. Existing faithfulness metrics have critical limitations, typically relying on identifying unfaithfulness via adversarial prompting or detecting reasoning errors. These methods overlook the predictive value of explanations. We introduce Normalized Simulatability Gain (NSG), a general and scalable metric based on the idea that a faithful explanation should allow an observer to learn a model’s decision-making criteria, and thus better predict its behavior on related inputs. We evaluate 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight models, e.g., Gemini 3, GPT-5.2, and Claude 4.5, on 7,000 counterfactuals from popular datasets covering health, business, and ethics. We find self-explanations substantially improve prediction of model behavior (11-37% NSG). Self-explanations also provide more predictive information than explanations generated by external models, even when those models are stronger. This implies an advantage from self-knowledge that external explanation methods cannot replicate. Our approach also reveals that, across models, 5-15% of self-explanations are egregiously misleading. Despite their imperfections, we show a positive case for self-explanations: they encode information that helps predict model behavior.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a model’s explanation helps an observer predict how that model will behave on related inputs. This provides a positive test of explanations: they may communicate useful decision criteria even when other tests expose errors or inconsistencies. The authors introduce Normalized Simulatability Gain, or NSG, to measure this predictive contribution.

They evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight models using 7,000 counterfactual examples spanning health, business, and ethics. Self-explanations improve predictions of model behavior, with reported NSG values of 11–37%. They also provide more predictive information than explanations written by external models, including stronger ones. The authors interpret this advantage as evidence that models convey information about their own behavior that external explainers do not reproduce.

The results remain mixed at the level of individual explanations: across models, 5–15% are classified as egregiously misleading. The paper’s positive case is therefore specific. Self-explanations contain useful behavioral information, while their demonstrated predictive value coexists with serious failures that matter when using them for oversight.
summary.tldr: Self-explanations help predict LLM behavior better than external explanations in the reported evaluation, although a meaningful minority are seriously misleading.

title: A Positive Case for Faithfulness: LLM Self-Explanations Help Predict Model Behavior

abstract: Least privilege is a core security principle: grant each request only the minimum access needed to achieve its goal. Deployed language models almost never follow it, instead being exposed through a single API endpoint that serves all users and requests. This gap exists not because least privilege would be unhelpful—deployments would benefit greatly from reducing unnecessary capability exposure. The real obstacle is definitional and mechanistic: what does "access" mean inside a language model, and how can we enforce it without retraining or deploying multiple models? We take inspiration from least privilege in computer systems and define a class of models called least-privilege language models, where privilege is reachable internal computation during the forward pass. In this view, lowering privilege literally shrinks the model’s accessible function class (as opposed to denying access via learned policies). We formalize deployment-time control as a monitor–allocator–enforcer stack, separating (i) request-time signals, (ii) a decision rule that allocates privilege, and (iii) an inference-time mechanism that selects privilege. We then propose Nested Least-Privilege Networks, a shape-preserving, rank-indexed intervention that provides a smooth, reversible control knob. We show that this knob yields policy-usable privilege–utility frontiers and enables selective suppression of targeted capabilities with limited collateral degradation across various policies. Most importantly, we see this as a defense of a completely new deployment paradigm which challenges the premise that we can only have output-level control of language models.

paragraphs: Least privilege means giving a request only the access needed to accomplish its task. This paper brings that security principle inside language models by defining privilege as the internal computation reachable during a forward pass. Reducing privilege therefore reduces the set of functions the model can access, giving a concrete computational meaning to capability restriction.

Their proposed Nested Least-Privilege Networks use a shape-preserving intervention indexed by rank. The broader contribution is a deployment framework in which requests receive different computational access. It demonstrates a way to control capability exposure internally while measuring how those restrictions affect useful behavior.
summary.tldr: Least-privilege language models restrict reachable internal computation per request, enabling reversible capability control with measured utility tradeoffs.

title: No More, No Less: Least-Privilege Language Models

abstract: Estimating causal quantities traditionally relies on bespoke estimators tailored to specific assumptions. Recently proposed Causal Foundation Models (CFMs) promise a more unified approach by amortising causal discovery and inference in a single step. However, in their current state, they do not allow for the incorporation of any domain knowledge, which can lead to suboptimal predictions. We bridge this gap by introducing methods to condition CFMs on causal information, such as the causal graph or more readily available ancestral information. When access to complete causal graph information is too strict a requirement, our approach also effectively leverages partial causal information. We systematically evaluate conditioning strategies and find that injecting learnable biases into the attention mechanism is the most effective method to utilise full and partial causal information. Our experiments show that this conditioning allows a general-purpose CFM to match the performance of specialised models trained on specific causal structures. Overall, our approach addresses a central hurdle on the path towards all-in-one causal foundation models: the capability to answer causal queries in a data-driven manner while effectively leveraging any amount of domain expertise.

paragraphs: Causal Foundation Models aim to combine causal discovery and inference in one reusable model. However, the models considered here cannot incorporate domain knowledge, potentially weakening their predictions. This paper introduces ways to condition them on known causal relationships so that existing expertise can inform their answers.

The supplied knowledge can be a complete causal graph or ancestral information describing which variables lie upstream of others. The approach also accepts partial information, avoiding a requirement to know the entire causal structure. The authors compare conditioning strategies and find that learnable biases added to attention are the most effective way to use both full and incomplete knowledge.

In experiments, this conditioning allows a general-purpose causal model to match specialized models trained for particular causal structures. The result supports combining reusable causal inference with problem-specific expertise. Partial graphs are especially relevant to that goal because the method can make use of available relationships without requiring a complete account of the system before answering causal queries.
summary.tldr: Conditioning causal foundation models on full or partial causal knowledge lets a general-purpose model match specialized models in experiments.

title: Use What You Know: Causal Foundation Models with Partial Graphs

abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) under data contamination is critical for deploying unsupervised defect detection in industrial environments, where curating perfectly clean training sets is impractical. However, existing methods are sensitive to contamination, suffering significant performance degradation as the noise ratio increases. In this paper, we propose Memory-Distilled Selection (MeDS), a training algorithm based on data selection. MeDS constructs an ensemble of partial memories via random subsampling, where the resulting sparsity acts as a low-pass filter that captures nominal patterns across a wide range of noise ratios, enabling coarse-level identification of contaminated samples. The aggregated distances to the bootstrapped memories are then distilled into a reconstruction score network, which is subsequently fine-tuned on clean data filtered using scores from the distilled model, enabling fine-grained localization of anomalies. MeDS is robust across a wide range of noise ratios without requiring noise-ratio-specific hyperparameter tuning, achieving 99.16% image-level AUROC on MVTecAD at a 40% noise ratio, and attaining state-of-the-art performance on both VisA and Real-IAD under noisy settings. We thoroughly verify the efficacy of MeDS on industrial AD benchmarks under noisy data scenarios, accompanied by in-depth empirical analyses.

paragraphs: Industrial anomaly detectors often need to learn normal appearance from training sets that already contain defects. Such contamination can make anomalies harder to distinguish from ordinary examples. Memory-Distilled Selection, or MeDS, addresses this problem by selecting cleaner training data through a staged process.

MeDS first constructs several partial memories using random subsamples. The authors describe the resulting sparsity as a low-pass filter that retains nominal patterns across different contamination levels, supporting coarse identification of suspect samples. Distances to these memories are aggregated and distilled into a reconstruction score network. That network’s scores then filter data for further fine-tuning, enabling more precise localization of anomalies.

The method remains robust over a broad range of noise ratios without tuning hyperparameters separately for each ratio. It achieves 99.16% image-level AUROC on MVTecAD with 40% contamination and reports state-of-the-art results on noisy VisA and Real-IAD settings. The findings support a progression from coarse memory-based screening to refined localization, allowing industrial defect detection to work effectively with imperfectly curated training sets.
summary.tldr: MeDS combines subsampled memories, score distillation, and data filtering to detect industrial defects despite contaminated training data.

title: Memory-Distilled Selection for Noise-Robust Anomaly Detection

abstract: Determining the complexity, or Intrinsic Dimension (ID), of data is fundamental to efficient and interpretable representation learning. This is particularly challenging in multi-modal settings when trying to learn disentangled representations for shared and private information. Existing techniques leave a critical gap: they are often static, uni-modal, or in the case of contrastive methods, adapt only to the shared ID implicitly. We introduce Fidelity-Guided Rank Optimization (FiGuRO), a framework for approximating the ID of uni- and multi-modal data under constraints of model capacity and hyperparameters. FiGuRO learns the dimensions of low-rank projections using truncated singular value decomposition and an algorithm that determines when to reduce or increase dimension and in which latent space. Disentanglement of shared and private information arises as an emergent property of this optimization, eliminating the need for complex auxiliary loss functions. We demonstrate that FiGuRO outperforms existing ID estimation techniques and is more robust to hyperparameter changes. Across simulations and real-world data, FiGuRO captures distinct ID scales and varying subspace ratios, and decomposes shared and private information successfully. Furthermore, we show that FiGuRO can be applied to modern uni-modal pretrained models, enabling efficient, post-hoc disentanglement of multi-modal representations.

paragraphs: Intrinsic dimension describes the underlying complexity of data rather than simply counting its recorded features. In multimodal data, that complexity includes information shared across modalities and information private to each. FiGuRO estimates these dimensions within the constraints imposed by model capacity and hyperparameters, addressing approaches that are static or focus mainly on shared information.

Its optimization procedure decides when a representation should gain or lose dimensions and which latent space should change. It can also operate on modern pretrained unimodal models, enabling efficient post-hoc disentanglement when their representations are brought into a multimodal setting.
summary.tldr: FiGuRO adapts representation dimensions to estimate data complexity and separate shared from modality-specific information.

title: FiGuRO: Intrinsic Dimension Estimation for Multi-Modal Data

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at $\textit{decode time}$ rather than during $\textit{prefill}$. We propose $\textbf{DecodeShare}$, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

paragraphs: Language models use the same parameters for many tasks, but that does not reveal which internal computations are shared while generating answers. DecodeShare focuses specifically on decoding with cached attention states, distinguishing this stage from prefill, when the model initially processes the prompt.

The protocol identifies a compact subspace of hidden states that appears consistently across tasks during decoding. It then tests whether that subspace matters by removing it only at generation time. In the experiments, this intervention harms decision performance much more than equally budgeted interventions on random subspaces or subspaces identified from prefill. That comparison provides causal evidence for the importance of the discovered structure.

The findings also affect activation steering, which modifies internal model states to influence behavior. Common steering directions can overlap the shared decoding subspace. Projecting out that component separates its functional role from the remaining direction. The authors further find that evaluating steering during decoding gives a more reliable deployment signal than using prefill-based proxies.
summary.tldr: DecodeShare identifies a compact, shared decoding subspace whose removal strongly disrupts decisions and whose overlap matters for activation steering.

title: DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions

abstract: Vision–language pre-training (VLP) holds great promise for general-purpose medical AI by leveraging radiology reports as rich textual supervision, yet existing methods struggle with 3D CT imaging due to inefficient visual backbones and coarse semantic alignment. To address these issues, we propose a tailored VLP framework featuring three key components: (1) a CNN–ViT hybrid encoder that replaces ViT’s patch embedding with a 3D CNN backbone to efficiently capture local anatomical details while preserving global attention and compatibility with pre-trained cross-modal priors; (2) a disease-level contrastive learning mechanism using learnable query tokens to dynamically extract disease-specific semantics from full reports and align them with corresponding visual features, thereby disentangling distinct diseases within the same anatomical region; and (3) a diagnosis-aware prompt strategy that employs real clinical phrases and aggregated disease prototypes to bridge the pre-training–inference gap and enhance zero-shot diagnostic reliability. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on CT-RATE (84.4% AUC, +5.1%) and Rad-ChestCT (75.4% AUC, +5.4%), with even larger gains (+9.8% AUC) on a challenging 60-disease benchmark, and demonstrates strong transferability to radiology report generation, underscoring the generality and clinical utility of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops vision-language pretraining for three-dimensional CT scans using radiology reports as supervision. It addresses two problems: processing volumetric images efficiently and matching their visual information to disease-specific meanings in reports. Its hybrid encoder replaces a vision transformer's patch embedding with a 3D convolutional backbone, combining local anatomical detail with global attention and compatibility with pretrained cross-modal knowledge.

The training objective uses learnable query tokens to extract disease-specific information from full reports and align it with corresponding image features. This aims to separate diseases that occur within the same anatomical region. A diagnosis-aware prompting strategy then combines real clinical phrases with aggregated disease prototypes to better connect pretraining with zero-shot diagnosis.

The model reports state-of-the-art AUC results of 84.4% on CT-RATE and 75.4% on Rad-ChestCT, with stated gains of 5.1% and 5.4%. It reports a larger 9.8% AUC gain on a 60-disease benchmark and strong transfer to report generation. Together, the results support the value of combining efficient volumetric encoding with more precise disease-level alignment.
summary.tldr: A hybrid CT encoder and disease-specific report alignment improve zero-shot diagnostic performance and transfer to radiology report generation.

title: Disease-Centric Vision-Language Pretraining with Hybrid Visual Encoding for 3D Computed Tomography

abstract: Global ocean modeling is vital for climate science but struggles to balance computational efficiency with accuracy. Traditional numerical solvers are accurate but computationally expensive, while pure deep learning approaches, though fast, often lack physical consistency and long-term stability. To address this, we introduce HybridOM, a framework integrating a lightweight, differentiable numerical solver as a skeleton to enforce physical laws, with a neural network as the flesh to correct subgrid-scale dynamics. To enable efficient high-resolution modeling, we further introduce a physics-informed regional downscaling mechanism based on flux gating. This design achieves the inference efficiency of AI-based methods while preserving the accuracy and robustness of physical models. Extensive experiments on the GLORYS12V1 and OceanBench dataset validate HybridOM’s performance in two distinct regimes: long-term subseasonal-to-seasonal simulation and short-term operational forecasting coupled with the FuXi-2.0 weather model. Results demonstrate that HybridOM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining physical consistency, offering a robust solution for next-generation ocean digital twins.

summary.tldr: HybridOM combines a differentiable physical solver, learned subgrid corrections, and regional downscaling for efficient, physically consistent ocean modeling.

title: HybridOM: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Ocean Modeling with Efficient Spatial Downscaling

abstract: The hippocampus encodes space through a striking gradient of place field sizes along its dorsal-ventral axis, yet the principles generating this continuous gradient from discrete grid cell inputs remain unclear. We propose a unified theoretical framework establishing how multiscale hippocampal place fields arise from the frequency-dependent decay of grid cell projections. Functionally, this organization establishes an inductive bias in the population code, managing a fundamental trade-off between spatial precision and sample efficiency. Translating this insight to artificial neural networks, we incorporate a hippocampus-inspired positional embedding (HIPE) into the Transformer architecture to induce multi-scale representation. Experimental results confirm that this mechanism effectively improves data efficiency. Our work establishes a link between neural connectivity, activity patterns, and learning, suggesting a principled approach to utilizing multi-scale representations for sample-efficiency learning. Our codes are available at https://github.com/AIogry/relative_PE.

paragraphs: This paper connects a spatial organization in the hippocampus with data-efficient learning in artificial networks. Hippocampal place fields vary in size along the dorsal–ventral axis, but how a continuous size gradient arises from discrete grid-cell inputs remains unclear. The authors propose a theoretical account based on frequency-dependent decay in grid-cell projections.

Within that framework, the resulting multiscale population code creates an inductive bias that balances spatial precision against sample efficiency. Representations at different scales therefore have a functional role in learning, beyond describing the observed organization of spatial responses. The theory links patterns of connectivity to activity patterns and then to the tradeoff involved in learning from limited samples.

The authors translate this principle into a hippocampus-inspired positional embedding for Transformers, called HIPE. Its purpose is to induce multiscale representations within the architecture. Experiments show improved data efficiency with this mechanism. The work thus offers both a proposed explanation for biological organization and an artificial-network design that tests the learning value of the associated multiscale bias.
summary.tldr: A theory of hippocampal spatial scales inspires Transformer positional embeddings that improve data efficiency in experiments.

title: The Hippocampal Place Field Gradient: A Bio-inspired Framework Building Multiscale Representation for Better Sample Efficiency

abstract: The goal of quantization is to produce a compressed model whose output distribution is as close to the original model’s as possible. To do this tractably, most quantization algorithms minimize the immediate activation error of each layer as a proxy for the end-to-end error. However, this ignores the effect of future layers, making it a poor proxy. In this work, we introduce Yet Another Quantization Algorithm (YAQA), a new adaptive rounding algorithm that directly considers the error at the network’s output. YAQA introduces a series of theoretical results that culminate in the first end-to-end error bounds for quantization algorithms. First, we characterize the convergence time of adaptive rounding algorithms via the structure of their Hessian approximations. We then show that the end-to-end error can be bounded by the approximation’s cosine similarity to the true Hessian. This admits a natural Kronecker-factored approximation with corresponding near-optimal Hessian sketches. YAQA is provably better than GPTQ/LDLQ and empirically reduces the error by $\approx$ 30% over these methods. YAQA even achieves a lower error than quantization aware training. This translates to state of the art performance on downstream tasks, all while adding no inference overhead.

paragraphs: Quantization compresses a model, but the desired outcome is to preserve its final output distribution. Many methods instead minimize errors in each layer’s immediate activations. This paper argues that such local objectives can be misleading because subsequent layers determine how an intermediate error ultimately affects the prediction.

YAQA, an adaptive rounding algorithm, directly considers error at the network output. The theory first relates rounding convergence time to the structure of Hessian approximations, which describe how the objective curves around parameter settings. It then bounds end-to-end error using the cosine similarity between an approximate Hessian and the true Hessian. Empirically, YAQA reduces error by approximately 30% relative to those methods and even reports lower error than quantization-aware training. The improvements translate into state-of-the-art downstream performance without additional inference overhead, linking the theoretical objective to practical model preservation.
summary.tldr: YAQA uses curvature-aware adaptive rounding to control final-output quantization error and improve compressed-model performance without inference overhead.

title: Model-Preserving Adaptive Rounding

abstract: Single-cell RNA-seq profiles are high-dimensional, sparse, and unordered, causing autoregressive generation to impose an artificial ordering bias and suffer from error accumulation. To address this, we propose scDiVa, a masked discrete diffusion foundation model that aligns generation with the dropout-like corruption process by defining a continuous-time forward masking mechanism in token space. ScDiVa features a bidirectional denoiser that jointly models discrete gene identities and continuous values, utilizing entropy-normalized serialization and a latent anchor token to maximize information efficiency and preserve global cell identity. The model is trained via depth-invariant time sampling and a dual denoising objective to simulate varying sparsity levels while ensuring precise recovery of both identity and magnitude. Pre-trained on 59 million cells, scDiVa achieves strong transfer performance across major benchmarks, including batch integration, cell type annotation, and perturbation response prediction. These results suggest that masked discrete diffusion serves as a biologically coherent and effective alternative to autoregression.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles are sparse, high-dimensional, and unordered. Generating them autoregressively imposes an artificial sequence and can accumulate errors across generation steps. scDiVa instead uses masked discrete diffusion, with a continuous-time process that masks tokens in a way intended to align with dropout-like corruption in the data.

A bidirectional denoiser jointly models which genes are present and their continuous expression values. Entropy-normalized serialization supports information efficiency, while a latent anchor token preserves the cell’s global identity. Training combines depth-invariant time sampling with a dual denoising objective, exposing the model to different sparsity levels and teaching it to recover both gene identity and expression magnitude. These components link the corruption process to the two kinds of information that need reconstruction.

After pretraining on 59 million cells, scDiVa shows strong transfer performance on benchmarks for batch integration, cell type annotation, and perturbation response prediction. The results suggest that masked discrete diffusion is an effective and biologically coherent alternative to autoregression for these data. They connect the model’s representation and generation choices to the unordered, sparse structure of cellular profiles.
summary.tldr: scDiVa jointly reconstructs gene identities and expression values through masked diffusion, showing strong transfer across single-cell analysis tasks.

title: ScDiVa: Masked Discrete Diffusion for Joint Modeling of Single-Cell Identity and Expression

abstract: Code Large Language Models (CodeLLMs) have been widely adopted for Natural Language to Programming Language code generation, powering applications with large user bases. Their performance, however, varies sharply across programming languages (PLs) and is particularly suboptimal for low-resource PLs due to data scarcity, limiting their overall usability. In this work, we introduce CodeChemist, a simple yet effective, training-free test-time scaling framework that transfers the model’s functional knowledge from high-resource to low-resource PLs via synthesized test cases, without relying on external models. Specifically, CodeChemist first applies multi-temperature hedged sampling to generate a pool of candidate solutions in the low-resource PL and synthesizes a set of test inputs. It then estimates uncertainty: when uncertainty is low, it selects the output via in-language majority voting; otherwise, it constructs cross-lingual I/O test oracles by executing high-resource reference programs and selects the candidate with the highest pass rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CodeChemist significantly outperforms existing test-time scaling methods, improving code generation for both low-resource PLs (e.g., Lua) and complex-syntax PLs (e.g., C++, Java) without retraining.

paragraphs: Code models often perform unevenly across programming languages because training data is much scarcer for some languages. CodeChemist addresses this at generation time, using a model’s stronger functional knowledge in well-supported languages to help choose solutions in less-supported ones. It requires neither retraining nor an external model.

The framework first samples candidate solutions in the target language at multiple temperatures and synthesizes test inputs. It then estimates uncertainty to decide how to select a candidate. When uncertainty is low, it uses majority voting within the target language. When uncertainty is higher, it executes reference programs written in a high-resource language to construct input-output test oracles.

Those cross-language oracles let CodeChemist compare candidates by their behavior on shared inputs and select the one with the highest pass rate. Experiments report significant improvements over existing test-time scaling methods, including for Lua and for complex-syntax languages such as C++ and Java. The findings support transferring functional knowledge through executable tests, with uncertainty determining when that additional cross-language evidence is used.
summary.tldr: CodeChemist uses uncertainty-guided voting and tests derived from high-resource reference programs to improve code generation without retraining.

title: CodeChemist: Test-Time Scaling for Low-Resource Code Generation via Functional Knowledge Transfer

abstract: This paper studies the problem of graph out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, which aims to identify anomaly graphs out of a graph dataset. Prior efforts usually focus on the utilization of topological structures with unsupervised graph learning to foster typical pattern recognition, which overlooks the semantic structure preserved in contextually affine neighborhoods. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Contextual Affinity Exploration with Twin Concordance (CLINIC) for graph OOD detection. The core of CLINIC is to explore and exploit the contextual affinity of the graph data samples for discriminative graph representations. In particular, our CLINIC first builds a contextual affinity graph to depict the semantic structure in the hidden space. More importantly, we introduce high-order affinity to enhance geometric understanding of the structure by utilizing a meta-graph neural network. To enhance representation discriminability with high robustness, we introduce twin concordance learning, which not only minimizes the difference of affinity distributions across different views, but also encourages the consistency between contextually affinitive neighbors. Finally, we introduce a compression strategy to expand the decision boundary for enhanced separation between in-distribution and out-of-distribution graphs. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our CLINIC across ten real datasets in comparison to various baselines.

paragraphs: Graph out-of-distribution detection identifies entire graphs that differ from the typical graphs in a dataset. Earlier approaches often emphasize the connections inside each graph. CLINIC also examines relationships among graph samples, seeking semantic structure in groups of samples that are close in a learned representation. This supplies context beyond each graph’s own topology.

The method first builds a contextual affinity graph describing those relationships in hidden space. A meta-graph neural network then captures higher-order affinity to improve its understanding of the structure. Twin concordance learning encourages agreement in two ways: affinity distributions should align across different views, and contextually similar neighbors should have consistent representations. Together, these objectives aim to make graph representations more discriminative and robust.

CLINIC also introduces a compression strategy intended to expand the decision boundary and improve separation between familiar and anomalous graphs. Experiments across ten real datasets show better performance than the compared baselines. The reported findings support using relationships between graph samples alongside internal graph structure when learning to recognize unusual graphs.
summary.tldr: CLINIC improves graph anomaly detection by learning contextual relationships among graph samples and enforcing consistency across views and neighbors.

title: CLINIC: Towards High-quality Graph Out-Of-Distribution Detection

abstract: This paper studies optimization for a family of problems termed compositional entropic risk minimization, in which each data’s loss is formulated as a Log-Expectation-Exponential (Log-E-Exp) function. The Log-E-Exp formulation serves as an abstraction of the Log-Sum-Exponential (LogSumExp) function when the explicit summation inside the logarithm is taken over a gigantic number of items and is therefore expensive to evaluate. While entropic risk objectives of this form arise in many machine learning problems, existing optimization algorithms suffer from several fundamental limitations including non-convergence, numerical instability, and slow convergence rates. To address these limitations, we propose a geometry-aware stochastic algorithm, termed SCENT, for the dual formulation of entropic risk minimization cast as a min–min optimization problem. The key to our design is a stochastic proximal mirror descent (SPMD) update for the dual variable, equipped with a Bregman divergence induced by a negative exponential function that faithfully captures the geometry of the objective. Our main contributions are threefold: (i) we establish an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate of the proposed SCENT algorithm for convex problems; (ii) we theoretically characterize the advantages of SPMD over standard SGD update for optimizing the dual variable; and (iii) we demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of SCENT on extreme classification, partial AUC maximization, contrastive learning and distributionally robust optimization, where it consistently outperforms existing baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/Optimization-AI/SCENT.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine losses by exponentiating them, averaging the results, and then taking a logarithm. This Log-Expectation-Exponential structure generalizes a familiar logarithm-of-summed-exponentials calculation to settings where enumerating all contributing items is prohibitively expensive. The paper studies how to optimize these compositional entropic risk objectives, addressing failures of existing methods involving convergence, numerical stability, and speed.

Its central choice concerns how to update the dual variable: it uses stochastic proximal mirror descent with a Bregman divergence generated by a negative exponential function. This makes the update reflect the objective’s geometry, rather than applying an ordinary stochastic gradient step without that geometric adaptation.

For convex problems, the authors establish an O(1/√T) convergence rate and theoretically characterize advantages of the proposed dual update over standard SGD. Experiments cover extreme classification, partial AUC maximization, contrastive learning, and distributionally robust optimization, with consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The result connects a specific mathematical update design to effectiveness across several applications sharing this objective structure.
summary.tldr: SCENT uses geometry-aware stochastic updates to optimize compositional entropic risk objectives, with a convergence guarantee for convex problems and improvements across several applications.

title: A Geometry-Aware Efficient Algorithm for Compositional Entropic Risk Minimization

abstract: Symbol grounding (Harnad, 1990) describes how symbols such as words acquire their meanings by connecting to real-world sensorimotor experiences. Recent work has shown preliminary evidence that grounding may emerge in (vision-)language models trained at scale without using explicit grounding objectives. Yet, the specific loci of this emergence and the mechanisms that drive it remain largely unexplored. To address this problem, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that systematically traces how symbol grounding arises within the internal computations through mechanistic and causal analysis. Our findings show that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations and is implemented through the aggregate mechanism, where attention heads aggregate the environmental ground to support the prediction of linguistic forms. This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models), but not in unidirectional LSTMs. Our results provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that symbol grounding can emerge in language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.

paragraphs: Symbol grounding concerns how symbols such as words connect to experiences of the world. This paper investigates evidence that such connections can emerge inside language models without an explicit grounding objective. Its focus is mechanistic: where grounding appears in the computation and which internal operations support it.

The authors introduce a controlled evaluation framework combining mechanistic inspection with causal analysis. They find that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations. They describe an aggregate mechanism in which attention heads combine environmental grounding information to support prediction of linguistic forms, linking information about the environment to the model’s language output.

The phenomenon also appears in multimodal dialogue and across the tested Transformer and state-space architectures, but does not replicate in unidirectional LSTMs. That architectural distinction is part of the reported evidence, rather than a claim that grounding emerges in every model. Together, the behavioral and internal analyses support the possibility of emergent grounding in language models. They also motivate potential ways to predict and perhaps control generation reliability by understanding the computations that connect language to environmental information.
summary.tldr: Controlled causal analysis finds emergent symbol grounding concentrated in middle-layer computations across several tested model architectures.

title: The Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding in Language Models

abstract: Despite the rapid evolution of training paradigms, the decoder backbone of large vision–language models (LVLMs) remains fundamentally rooted in the residual-connection Transformer architecture. Therefore, deciphering the distinct roles of internal modules is critical for understanding model mechanics and guiding architectural optimization. While prior statistical approaches have provided valuable attribution-based insights, they often lack a unified theoretical basis. To bridge this gap, we propose a unified framework grounded in information theory and geometry to quantify the geometric and entropic nature of residual updates. Applying this unified framework reveals a fundamental functional decoupling: Attention acts as a subspace-preserving operator focused on reconfiguration, whereas FFNs serve as subspace-expanding operators driving semantic innovation. Strikingly, further experiments demonstrate that replacing learned attention weights with predefined values (e.g., Gaussian noise) yields comparable or even superior performance across a majority of datasets relative to vanilla models. These results expose severe misallocation and redundancy in current mechanisms, suggesting that state-of-the-art LVLMs effectively “get lost in attention” rather than efficiently leveraging visual context.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models rely on transformer decoders whose modules repeatedly update a shared representation through residual connections. This paper develops a framework using information theory and geometry to examine what those updates do. It seeks a common theoretical account of module behavior beyond statistical attribution alone.

The analysis finds a division of labor between attention and feed-forward networks. Attention primarily rearranges information while preserving its representational subspace. Feed-forward networks expand that subspace, contributing what the authors describe as semantic innovation. This distinction provides a way to examine whether computational effort in the architecture corresponds to meaningful changes in its representations.

The authors then replace learned attention weights with predefined alternatives, including Gaussian noise. Across a majority of the evaluated datasets, these replacements produce comparable or better performance than the original models. The result suggests substantial redundancy and misallocation in the examined attention mechanisms. Its scope is the reported models and evaluations: the evidence challenges how effectively their learned attention uses visual context, without establishing that attention is universally dispensable.
summary.tldr: A geometric and information-theoretic analysis finds attention redundancy in vision-language models, with predefined weights matching or improving many evaluated results.

title: Large Vision-Language Models Get Lost in Attention

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance in multi-image cross-modal retrieval, yet suffer from severe position bias, where predictions are dominated by input order rather than semantic relevance. Through empirical analysis, we identify a phenomenon termed Logit-Attention Divergence, in which output logits are heavily biased while internal attention maps remain well-aligned with relevant visual evidence. This observation reveals a fundamental limitation of existing logit-level calibration methods such as PriDe. Based on this insight, we propose a training-free, attention-guided debiasing framework that leverages intrinsic attention signals for instance-level correction at inference time, requiring only a minimal calibration set with negligible computational overhead. Experiments on MS-COCO-based benchmarks show that our method substantially improves permutation invariance and achieves state-of-the-art performance, enhancing accuracy by over 40% compared to baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/brightXian/LAD.

paragraphs: This paper examines why multimodal language models can choose images based on their position in an input sequence instead of their relevance. In multi-image retrieval, changing the order of candidate images should not change which image best matches the request. Severe position bias undermines that behavior even when the models otherwise perform strongly.

The authors identify a mismatch between output scores and internal attention. The scores used for predictions can be heavily biased by order, while attention remains aligned with relevant visual evidence. They call this Logit-Attention Divergence and use it to motivate a calibration method that draws on attention signals. The method corrects individual cases during inference, needs no training, and uses a minimal calibration set.

On benchmarks based on MS-COCO, the approach substantially improves consistency under reordered inputs and reports state-of-the-art performance, with accuracy improvements exceeding 40% over baselines. Computational overhead is described as negligible. The findings indicate that useful relevance information may already exist internally even when final prediction scores express a strong positional bias.
summary.tldr: Attention-guided calibration reduces image-order bias by using internal visual evidence that remains informative when output scores are biased.

title: Logit-Attention Divergence: Mitigating Position Bias in Multi-Image Retrieval via Attention-Guided Calibration

abstract: We propose a mathematically principled PDE gradient flow framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Exploiting the recent advances in the intersection of Monte Carlo sampling and statistical optimal transport, we show that our theoretical framework can be implemented as practical algorithms for sampling from worst-case distributions and, consequently, DRO. While numerous previous works have relied on dual reformulation techniques, we contribute a sound and complete gradient flow view based on SDEs or PDEs that can be used to construct new algorithms for general, potentially non-convex, losses. Without loss of generality, we solve a class of Wasserstein and entropy-regularized DRO problems using the recently-discovered Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao and Stein variational gradient flows. Notably, we also show some simple reductions of our framework recover exactly previously proposed popular DRO methods, and provide new insights into their theoretical limits and optimization dynamics of DRO. Numerical studies based on stochastic gradient descent on machine learning tasks provide empirical backing for our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains against unfavorable data distributions, making the construction of those distributions central to the problem. This paper develops a gradient-flow framework for doing so. It connects Monte Carlo sampling with statistical optimal transport to turn a mathematical description of how distributions evolve into practical procedures for sampling worst-case distributions.

The framework describes this evolution using stochastic or partial differential equations. Unlike approaches centered on dual reformulations, it offers a route to algorithms for general losses, including potentially nonconvex ones. The authors instantiate the approach for a class of Wasserstein and entropy-regularized problems using Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao and Stein variational gradient flows.

Some simplified versions of the framework exactly recover previously proposed DRO methods. This gives those methods a shared interpretation and exposes insights into their theoretical limits and optimization dynamics. Numerical studies using stochastic gradient descent on machine learning tasks support the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore both an algorithmic construction and a way to understand relationships among existing robust optimization procedures.
summary.tldr: A gradient-flow view of robust optimization yields worst-case distribution samplers and recovers existing methods as special cases.

title: Gradient Flow Sampler-based Distributionally Robust Optimization

abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for enabling quantum advantages, with decoding as a central algorithmic primitive. Owing to its importance and intrinsic difficulty, substantial effort has been made to QEC decoder design, among which neural decoders have recently emerged as a promising data-driven paradigm. Despite this progress, practical deployment remains hindered by a fundamental accuracy–latency tradeoff, often on the microsecond timescale. To address this challenge, here we revisit neural decoders for surface-code decoding under explicit accuracy–latency constraints, considering code distances up to $d=9$ (161 physical qubits). We unify and redesign representative neural decoders into five architectural paradigms and develop an end-to-end compression pipeline to evaluate their deployability and performance on FPGA hardware. Through systematic experiments, we reveal several previously underexplored insights: (i) near-term decoding performance is driven more by data scale than architectural complexity; (ii) appropriate inductive bias is essential for achieving high decoding accuracy; and (iii) INT4 quantization is a prerequisite for meeting microsecond-scale latency requirements on FPGAs. Together, these findings provide concrete guidance toward scalable and real-time neural QEC decoding.

paragraphs: Quantum error correction depends on decoding quickly enough to support ongoing computation. Neural decoders offer a data-driven approach, but accuracy alone is insufficient when the available response time is measured in microseconds. This paper evaluates surface-code neural decoders with explicit accuracy and latency constraints, considering code distances up to nine, corresponding to 161 physical qubits.

The authors organize and redesign representative decoders into five architectural paradigms. They also develop an end-to-end compression pipeline and evaluate the resulting models on FPGA hardware. This brings architectural design, compression, and actual deployment timing into the same comparison, making it possible to assess whether a model's predictive performance is compatible with the required execution speed.

The experiments find that near-term decoding performance depends more on data scale than architectural complexity, while suitable inductive bias remains essential for high accuracy. In the investigated FPGA setting, INT4 quantization is identified as a prerequisite for microsecond-scale latency. These findings provide practical guidance about where to invest effort: training data, appropriate structural assumptions, and aggressive numerical compression all influence whether neural decoding can operate within real-time constraints.
summary.tldr: An FPGA-focused study identifies data scale, suitable inductive bias, and INT4 quantization as key factors for accurate neural decoding at microsecond latency.

title: Rethink the Role of Neural Decoders in Quantum Error Correction

abstract: The key to building trustworthy large language models (LLMs) lies in endowing them with inherent uncertainty expression capabilities, thereby mitigating overconfident errors in high-stakes applications. However, existing RL paradigms such as GRPO often suffer from Advantage Bias due to binary decision spaces and static uncertainty rewards, inducing either excessive conservatism or overconfidence. To tackle this challenge, this paper unveils the root causes of reward hacking and overconfidence in current RL paradigms incorporating uncertainty-based rewards, based on which we propose the UnCertainty-Aware Policy Optimization (UCPO) framework. UCPO employs Ternary Advantage Decoupling to separate and independently normalize deterministic and uncertain rollouts, thereby eliminating advantage bias. Furthermore, a Dynamic Uncertainty Reward Adjustment mechanism adapts uncertainty weights in real-time according to model evolution and instance difficulty. Experimental results in mathematical reasoning and general tasks demonstrate that UCPO effectively resolves the reward imbalance, significantly improving the reliability of the model beyond their knowledge boundaries. The code is available at https://github.com/xzhouzeng/ucpo.

paragraphs: Teaching a language model to express uncertainty requires balancing useful caution against confident answering. The paper identifies advantage bias in reinforcement-learning approaches with binary decision spaces and fixed uncertainty rewards. These training signals can encourage excessive conservatism or overconfidence, undermining the intended benefit of rewarding uncertainty.

UCPO addresses the problem with Ternary Advantage Decoupling, separating deterministic and uncertain rollouts and normalizing their advantages independently. The authors describe this as eliminating the identified advantage bias. A second mechanism adjusts uncertainty reward weights dynamically according to the model's evolution and the difficulty of each instance.

Together, the mechanisms change both how sampled responses are compared during learning and how strongly uncertainty is rewarded. This allows the training signal to respond to changing capabilities and task difficulty. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and general tasks show that UCPO resolves the reported reward imbalance and significantly improves reliability beyond the model's knowledge boundaries. The findings support adaptive reward design and separated advantage computation as ways to train more appropriate expressions of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: UCPO improves uncertainty expression by separating advantage calculations and adapting uncertainty rewards to model capability and problem difficulty.

title: UCPO: Uncertainty-Aware Policy Optimization

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful controllers for interactive agents in complex environments, yet training them to perform reliable long-horizon decision making remains a fundamental challenge. A key difficulty lies in credit assignment: agents often receive delayed rewards only at the end of episodes. In this paper, we propose Q-Evolve, a self-evolving framework for LLM agents that unifies automatic process-reward labeling and policy learning within a principled in-distribution reinforcement learning paradigm. In each evolving iteration, our method learns an in-distribution critic from a hybrid off-policy dataset that combines expert demonstrations with agent-generated trajectories, stabilizing Bellman backups in sparse-reward settings via a weighted Implicit Q-Learning objective. The learned value function is then used to derive step-wise process rewards through advantage estimation, enabling dense and reliable supervision without environment backtracking or human annotation. Leveraging these signals, we perform behavior-proximal policy optimization that evolves the agent over the data used for process reward labeling, allowing iterative self-improvement without exacerbating distribution shift. We evaluate our method on AlfWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, showing Q-Evolve outperforms strong baselines in sample efficiency, robustness, and overall task performance. Our results demonstrate that stable agent self-evolution is achievable through the co-evolution of process-level supervision and policy, both grounded within a shared in-distribution learning loop.

paragraphs: Q-Evolve addresses credit assignment in agents that receive rewards only after completing a long interaction. A final outcome gives limited direct guidance about which earlier actions helped. The framework jointly develops a critic that supplies feedback on individual steps and a policy that learns from those signals, keeping both within a shared data distribution.

Each iteration trains the critic on a mixture of expert demonstrations and agent-generated trajectories. A weighted Implicit Q-Learning objective stabilizes value updates in the sparse-reward setting. The results support iterative improvement in which supervision and behavior evolve together. Grounding both updates in shared data is central to the approach's attempt to improve the agent without aggravating distribution shift.
summary.tldr: Q-Evolve jointly improves step-level reward supervision and agent policies through an in-distribution learning loop grounded in shared trajectory data.

title: Self-evolving LLM agents with in-distribution Optimization

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a practical way to adapt large models, yet under strict context limits, it remains unclear how to spend scarce tokens without being misled by noisy, redundant, or conflicting demonstrations. We address this gap by targeting token-budgeted context construction: how to select and compress demonstrations so the prompt carries maximal task-relevant signal with minimal predictive distortion. We propose RDCO, a deterministic, training-free optimizer that scores demonstrations by marginal task information per token, penalizes redundancy and prefix-conditioned conflicts, and finally compacts the selected context under a bounded predictive-divergence constraint to control drift. Across a 10-dataset ICL suite spanning classification and structured generation, RDCO achieves the best average performance (63.26 Acc. on classification and 60.26 EM on generation), improving over the strongest classification and generation baselines by 2.20 and 2.26 points, respectively, and improving the 10-task overall average by 4.94 points under the same budget. Our results suggest that viewing prompts as finite-capacity messages yields a principled and effective path to more reliable and token-efficient ICL.
