paragraphs: In-context learning adapts a model by placing demonstrations in its prompt, but a strict token budget limits how much guidance can fit. More examples are not automatically more useful when they repeat information or conflict. This paper treats prompt construction as selecting and compressing a finite-capacity message while preserving its task-relevant content.

The proposed RDCO optimizer is deterministic and requires no training. It scores each demonstration by the additional task information it contributes per token, while penalizing redundancy and conflicts conditioned on the existing prefix. After selection, it compacts the context subject to a bound on predictive divergence, controlling how much compression changes the predictive signal.

Across ten classification and structured-generation datasets, RDCO achieves average classification accuracy of 63.26 and generation exact match of 60.26. The reported improvements over the strongest respective baselines are 2.20 and 2.26 points, with a 4.94-point improvement in the ten-task overall average under the same budget. The findings support optimizing information density and compression jointly when prompt space is scarce.
summary.tldr: RDCO selects and compresses demonstrations by task information per token, improving in-context learning under a fixed prompt budget.

title: In-Context Learning as Rate–Distortion Optimization

abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is a must-acquire skill for modern foundation model systems to operate effectively and safely in the real world. Recent works have explored honing ToM via post-training; however, we show that such progress is confounded by a pervasive “shortcut” issue: tasks can reach up to 99% accuracy by simply exploiting spurious causal correlations, leading to a false sense of ToM. Motivated by this, we first develop a framework to systematically examine ToM datasets for shortcuts and provide guidance for future development. We find that questions reducible to pure state tracking, such as “belief,” are especially shortcut-prone compared to mind questions, such as “intention,” where reasoning beyond tracking is required. Using four shortcut-free datasets across three ToM contexts, we then comprehensively study whether Reinforcement Fine-Tuning with verifiable rewards and explicit reasoning chains, called Thinking-RFT, elevates ToM beyond Supervised Fine-Tuning, or SFT. Our key findings are as follows. First, Thinking-RFT effectively improves ToM in all scenarios, with a 6% improvement over SFT, particularly in complex higher-order reasoning, with a 10% improvement over SFT, and multimodal cases, with a 7% improvement over SFT. It also generalizes notably better to unseen domains and higher-order queries while being more robust to counterfactuals. Second, ToM benefits specifically from the joint effect of reasoning and RL: Thinking-RFT outperforms No-Thinking-RFT by 7% on average. Third, RFT works by learning to ground its reasoning on anchor cues, such as keywords and state changes, that correspond to causal factors. We believe our study is useful for developing effective and robust ToM post-training datasets and advancing critical ToM capabilities. Project code is available at: https://github.com/jkz-338/Robust-ToM-RL.git

paragraphs: A model can score highly on questions about another person's beliefs or intentions without reliably reasoning about their mind. This paper shows that spurious causal correlations can support accuracy as high as 99% on theory-of-mind tasks. It develops a framework for detecting such shortcuts and finds questions reducible to state tracking especially vulnerable.

The researchers then compare supervised fine-tuning with Thinking-RFT, which combines reinforcement learning, verifiable rewards, and explicit reasoning chains. They use four shortcut-free datasets spanning three theory-of-mind contexts. Thinking-RFT improves performance across the evaluated scenarios, with reported gains over supervised fine-tuning of 6% overall, 10% for complex higher-order reasoning, and 7% for multimodal cases.

Thinking-RFT also generalizes better to unseen domains and higher-order questions and shows greater robustness to counterfactuals. Its average 7% advantage over reinforcement fine-tuning without explicit thinking supports the joint contribution of reasoning and reinforcement learning. The analysis links improvement to reasoning grounded in causally relevant cues, including keywords and state changes, making shortcut-resistant evaluation central to interpreting the gains.
summary.tldr: Shortcut-resistant evaluations show that reinforcement fine-tuning with explicit reasoning improves theory-of-mind performance and generalization.

title: From Shortcuts to Reasoning: Robust Post-Training of Theory of Mind with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Biosignals acquired from different locations on the body often provide temporally ordered views of the same underlying physiological process. However, most existing self-supervised learning methods treat these signals as interchangeable views, overlooking the directional temporal dynamics that link them. A canonical example is the relationship between electrocardiography (ECG), which captures the electrical activation initiating each heartbeat, and photoplethysmography (PPG), which records the resulting peripheral pulse delayed by vascular dynamics. To capture this structured relationship, we introduce xMAE, a biosignal pretraining framework that leverages masked cross-modal reconstruction across temporally ordered biosignals as a training-time constraint to encourage physiologically meaningful timing structure in the learned representations. We show that pretraining with xMAE yields representations that outperform both unimodal and multimodal baselines on 15 of 19 downstream tasks, including cardiovascular outcome prediction, abnormal laboratory test detection, sleep staging, and demographic inference, while generalizing across devices, body locations, and acquisition settings. Further analysis suggests that the ECG–PPG timing structure is reflected in the learned PPG representations. Code is available at https://github.com/hzhou3/xMAE.

paragraphs: Different biosignals can observe successive stages of the same physiological event. ECG records the electrical activation that starts a heartbeat, while PPG measures the peripheral pulse after a delay shaped by vascular dynamics. Treating these signals as interchangeable views overlooks the directional timing relationship between them.

The proposed xMAE framework uses masked reconstruction across temporally ordered modalities during pretraining. Reconstructing missing information across signals acts as a training constraint that encourages representations to capture meaningful physiological timing. This makes the relationship between measurement sources part of the learning objective, rather than relying only on information within each signal or on generic multimodal similarity.

The learned representations outperform unimodal and multimodal baselines on fifteen of nineteen downstream tasks, including cardiovascular outcomes, abnormal laboratory tests, sleep stages, and demographic inference. The authors also report generalization across devices, body locations, and acquisition settings. Further analysis suggests that ECG–PPG timing is reflected in the learned PPG representations, supporting the intended role of ordered cross-modal reconstruction without claiming that every learned feature has a physiological interpretation.
summary.tldr: xMAE uses the temporal relationship between biosignals during pretraining to learn representations that improve many downstream prediction tasks.

title: Physiology-Aware Masked Cross-Modal Reconstruction for Biosignal Representation Learning

abstract: As LLM-based agents increasingly operate in high-stakes domains with real-world consequences, ensuring their behavioral safety becomes paramount. The dominant oversight paradigm, LLM-as-a-Judge, faces a fundamental dilemma: how can probabilistic systems reliably supervise other probabilistic systems without inheriting their failure modes? We argue that formal verification offers a principled escape from this dilemma, yet its adoption has been hindered by a critical bottleneck: the translation from natural language requirements to formal specifications. This paper bridges this gap by proposing , a neuro-symbolic framework that employs a bidirectional Formal-of-Thought architecture: LLMs serve as specification compilers that top-down decompose high-level human intent into atomic, verifiable constraints, then bottom-up prove compliance using Dafny specifications and Z3 Satisfiability modulo theories solving, which produces mathematical guarantees rather than probabilistic scores. We validate across three benchmarks spanning behavioral safety, multi-domain constraint adherence, and agentic upward deception detection. Experiments on 7 agent models demonstrate that achieves an average improvement of 16.6% over LLM-as-a-Judge baselines, enables weak-to-strong generalization where a 7B judge achieves over 90% accuracy detecting deception from 72B agents, and provides near-linear safety improvement through iterative refinement.

paragraphs: Using a language model to judge another agent raises a reliability problem: the judge can inherit the same kinds of probabilistic failures as the system it supervises. FormalJudge combines language models with formal verification to address this problem. Its central focus is translating human requirements into specifications that symbolic tools can check.

The framework follows a bidirectional Formal-of-Thought process. A language model first breaks high-level intent into small, verifiable constraints. Compliance is then established from the bottom up using Dafny specifications and the Z3 satisfiability solver. The resulting mathematical guarantees concern the formal specifications being checked, giving the oversight process a different basis from a model-generated confidence score.

Across three benchmarks and seven agent models, the authors report an average 16.6% improvement over LLM-as-a-Judge baselines. A 7B judge also exceeds 90% accuracy when detecting deception from 72B agents, demonstrating weak-to-strong generalization in that evaluation. Iterative refinement produces near-linear safety improvement, supporting the framework’s use as a repeated process for strengthening agent oversight.
summary.tldr: FormalJudge translates human requirements into formal constraints and checks agent compliance with symbolic verification.

title: FormalJudge: A Neuro-Symbolic Paradigm for Agentic Oversight

abstract: We study linear seriation from noisy point clouds: given samples from an unknown one-dimensional curve embedded in $\mathbb{R}^d$, recover their latent order along the curve, up to reversal. Unlike much of the seriation literature, which starts from a precomputed similarity matrix, this setting retains ambient coordinates and therefore local geometric information. We propose STAGE, a geometric ordering method that estimates local tangent directions by neighborhood PCA, resolves their sign ambiguity through a graph-wide $\mathbb{Z}_2$ synchronization step, and constructs signed local displacement estimates by projecting ambient differences onto the oriented tangents. These increments are then integrated into a global scalar embedding through an inhomogeneous least-squares problem, equivalently a Laplacian linear system with a nonzero right-hand side, and the final order is obtained by sorting the embedding. We prove a finite-sample Kendall’s $\tau$ recovery bound that makes explicit the roles of curvature, noise, neighborhood scale, sampling density, and graph connectivity. Empirically, STAGE gives accurate and fast order recovery on high-dimensional synthetic curves, compares favorably with spectral seriation, 1D UMAP, 1D t-SNE, Recanati’s method, LTSA, and SABRE, and produces meaningful pseudotime orderings on single-cell RNA-seq datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the order of noisy points sampled from an unknown one-dimensional curve in a higher-dimensional space. The order is recoverable up to reversal. Unlike methods that begin with a similarity matrix, STAGE uses the original coordinates to retain information about the curve’s local geometry.

STAGE estimates local tangent directions using neighborhood principal component analysis. Because each estimated tangent can point in either direction, a graph-wide synchronization step makes their orientations consistent. The method projects neighboring point differences onto these oriented tangents to estimate signed displacements, then integrates them through a least-squares system into one scalar coordinate per point. Sorting those coordinates gives the recovered order.

A finite-sample Kendall’s tau bound describes how recovery depends on curvature, noise, neighborhood scale, sampling density, and graph connectivity. Experiments show accurate, fast ordering on high-dimensional synthetic curves and favorable comparisons with several existing methods. The method also produces meaningful pseudotime orderings for single-cell RNA-seq data, connecting its geometric construction to an application involving latent progression.
summary.tldr: STAGE aligns local curve directions and integrates their displacements to recover a global ordering of noisy points.

abstract: We present a new method to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of a submanifold M in ℝᵈ from random samples. The method is based on the convergence rates of a certain U-statistic on the manifold. We solve at least partially the question of the choice of the scale of the data. Moreover the proposed method is easy to implement, can handle large data sets and performs very well even for small sample sizes. We compare the proposed method to two standard estimators on several artificial as well as real data sets.

Moreover the proposed method is easy to implement, can handle large data sets and performs very well even for small sample sizes. We compare the proposed method to two standard estimators on several artificial as well as real data sets.

paragraphs: Data represented by many coordinates may lie on a structure with fewer underlying dimensions. This paper proposes a method for estimating that intrinsic dimension from random samples of a submanifold in a higher-dimensional space. The target is the dimension of the structure containing the observations, rather than simply the number of coordinates used to record them.

The estimator relies on convergence rates of a particular U-statistic defined on the manifold. Its statistical behavior supplies information about the underlying dimension. The authors also address the choice of data scale, reporting a partial solution to that question. This matters because scale selection is part of making the dimensionality estimation procedure usable.

The method is described as easy to implement, capable of handling large datasets, and effective even with small samples. Comparisons involve two standard estimators and both artificial and real data. These results support the proposed estimator's practical usefulness, while the claim about resolving scale choice remains explicitly partial.
summary.tldr: A dimension estimator uses a manifold U-statistic's convergence rates and partially addresses the problem of choosing data scale.

title: Intrinsic dimensionality estimation of submanifolds in Rd

abstract: We introduce a novel active learning algorithm for classification of network data. In this setting, training instances are connected by a set of links to form a network, the labels of linked nodes are correlated, and the goal is to exploit these dependencies and accurately label the nodes. This problem arises in many domains, including social and biological network analysis and document classification, and there has been much recent interest in methods that collectively classify the nodes in the network. While in many cases labeled examples are expensive, often network information is available. We show how an active learning algorithm can take advantage of network structure. Our algorithm effectively exploits the links between instances and the interaction between the local and collective aspects of a classifier to improve the accuracy of learning from fewer labeled examples. We experiment with two real-world benchmark collective classification domains, and show that we are able to achieve extremely accurate results even when only a small fraction of the data is labeled.

We experiment with two real-world benchmark collective classification domains, and show that we are able to achieve extremely accurate results even when only a small fraction of the data is labeled.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when examples form a network and connected examples tend to have correlated labels. Such dependencies create an opportunity: information about one example can help classify others through their links. The practical motivation is that obtaining labels can be expensive even when the network connecting the examples is already available.

The authors introduce an active learning algorithm that uses this network structure when learning from selected labeled examples. Its design accounts for the interaction between local classification and collective classification, which uses dependencies across linked instances. The central idea is that the value of labeled data should be considered in the context of the connected prediction problem.

Experiments cover two real-world benchmark domains for collective classification. The authors report very high accuracy with only a small fraction of examples labeled. These results support the usefulness of incorporating links into active learning in the evaluated settings, showing how network information can help make a limited supply of labels more effective.
summary.tldr: An active learning algorithm uses network links and collective classification to achieve high accuracy from relatively few labeled examples.

title: Active Learning for Networked Data

abstract: We propose to combine two approaches for modeling data admitting sparse representations: on the one hand, dictionary learning has proven effective for various signal processing tasks. On the other hand, recent work on structured sparsity provides a natural framework for modeling dependencies between dictionary elements. We thus consider a tree-structured sparse regularization to learn dictionaries embedded in a hierarchy. The involved proximal operator is computable exactly via a primal-dual method, allowing the use of accelerated gradient techniques. Experiments show that for natural image patches, learned dictionary elements organize themselves in such a hierarchical structure, leading to an improved performance for restoration tasks. When applied to text documents, our method learns hierarchies of topics, thus providing a competitive alternative to probabilistic topic models.

We thus consider a tree-structured sparse regularization to learn dictionaries embedded in a hierarchy. The involved proximal operator is computable exactly via a primal-dual method, allowing the use of accelerated gradient techniques. paragraphs: The paper combines dictionary learning with structured sparsity to represent data using a hierarchy of dictionary elements. Dictionary learning supplies elements that can represent signals sparsely, while structured sparsity models dependencies among those elements. The authors bring the two together through a tree-structured regularizer.

This formulation creates an optimization problem whose proximal operator can be computed exactly using a primal-dual method. That exact computation allows accelerated gradient techniques to be used. The optimization result is central to the modeling proposal because it provides a practical way to learn dictionaries subject to the hierarchical sparse structure.

For natural image patches, experiments show that the learned dictionary elements organize into a hierarchy and that this leads to improved restoration performance. Applied to text, the method learns topic hierarchies and is reported as a competitive alternative to probabilistic topic models. Together, these results show the approach serving both signal restoration and the organization of document topics, with a shared mechanism for learning structured sparse representations.
summary.tldr: Tree-structured sparse dictionary learning uses an exact proximal computation to learn hierarchies for image restoration and text topics.

title: Proximal Methods for Sparse Hierarchical Dictionary Learning

abstract: Linear support vector machines ({\sc svm}s) have become popular for solving classification tasks due to their fast and simple online application to large scale data sets. However, many problems are not linearly separable. For these problems kernel-based {\sc svm}s are often used, but unlike their linear variant they suffer from various drawbacks in terms of computational and memory efficiency. Their response can be represented only as a function of the set of support vectors, which has been experimentally shown to grow linearly with the size of the training set. In this paper we propose a novel locally linear {\sc svm} classifier with smooth decision boundary and bounded curvature. We show how the functions defining the classifier can be approximated using local codings and show how this model can be optimized in an online fashion by performing stochastic gradient descent with the same convergence guarantees as standard gradient descent method for linear {\sc svm}. Our method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art whilst being significantly faster than competing kernel {\sc svm}s. We generalise this model to locally finite dimensional kernel {\sc svm}.

paragraphs: Linear support vector machines are appealing for large datasets because they are simple and fast to apply, but a single linear boundary cannot separate every classification problem. Kernel SVMs address nonlinear structure at a computational and memory cost. Their predictions depend on support vectors, whose number has been observed experimentally to grow with training-set size.

The paper proposes a locally linear SVM with a smooth decision boundary and bounded curvature. Local codings approximate the functions defining the classifier, allowing the model to represent nonlinear decisions through local linear structure. The authors also show how to train it online using stochastic gradient descent, with the same convergence guarantees as the standard gradient-descent method for linear SVMs.

The reported results combine classification performance comparable to leading methods with substantially faster operation than competing kernel SVMs. This makes the contribution a practical attempt to retain useful nonlinear behavior while reducing the cost associated with kernel classifiers. The paper also generalizes the construction to locally finite-dimensional kernel SVMs.
summary.tldr: Locally linear SVMs provide smooth nonlinear decision boundaries with online training and reported speed advantages over competing kernel SVMs.

title: Locally Linear Support Vector Machines

abstract: We propose a method for learning similarity-preserving hash functions that map high-dimensional data onto binary codes. The formulation is based on structured prediction with latent variables and a hinge-like loss function. It is efficient to train for large datasets, scales well to large code lengths, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
originalAbstract: We propose a method for learning similarity-preserving hash functions that map high-dimensional data onto binary codes. The formulation is based on structured prediction with latent variables and a hinge-like loss function. It is efficient to train for large datasets, scales well to large code lengths, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to turn high-dimensional data into compact binary codes while preserving similarity. Each learned hash function contributes to a representation made of binary values. The aim is for this compact representation to retain useful information about which original data items resemble one another.

The authors formulate the learning problem as structured prediction with latent variables and a hinge-like loss. This treats code learning as a prediction problem with an explicit loss criterion. The latent variables are part of the formulation, allowing the learning procedure to work with quantities that are not simply supplied as observed target values.

The method is reported to train efficiently on large datasets and to scale well as code lengths increase. It also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings connect the similarity-preservation objective to two practical demands: learning from substantial amounts of data and supporting larger binary representations. The contribution is a learned hashing method that addresses those computational demands alongside predictive quality.
summary.tldr: A latent structured-prediction formulation learns similarity-preserving binary hashes efficiently for large datasets and longer codes.

title: Minimal Loss Hashing for Compact Binary Codes

abstract: Traditionally, multitask learning (MTL) assumes that all the tasks are related. This can lead to negative transfer when tasks are indeed incoherent. Recently, a number of approaches have been proposed that alleviate this problem by discovering the underlying task clusters or relationships. However, they are limited to modeling these relationships at the task level,which may be restrictive in some applications. In this paper, we propose a novel MTL formulation that captures task relationships at the feature-level. Depending on the interactions among tasks and features, the proposed method construct different task clusters for different features, without even the need of pre-specifying the number of clusters. Computationally, the proposed formulation is strongly convex, and can be efficiently solved by accelerated proximal methods. Experiments are performed on a number of synthetic and real-world data sets. Under various degrees of task relationships, the accuracy of the proposed method is consistently among the best. Moreover, the feature-specific task clusters obtained agree with the known/plausible task structures of the data.

Recently, a number of approaches have been proposed that alleviate this problem by discovering the underlying task clusters or relationships. However, they are limited to modeling these relationships at the task level,which may be restrictive in some applications. In this paper, we propose a novel MTL formulation that captures task relationships at the feature-level. Depending on the interactions among tasks and features, the proposed method construct different task clusters for different features, without even the need of pre-specifying the number of clusters. Computationally, the proposed formulation is strongly convex, and can be efficiently solved by accelerated proximal methods. Experiments are performed on a number of synthetic and real-world data sets. Under various degrees of task relationships, the accuracy of the proposed method is consistently among the best. Moreover, the feature-specific task clusters obtained agree with the known/plausible task structures of the data.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can suffer when it shares information between tasks that are not meaningfully related. Discovering task clusters helps address this problem, but assigning one relationship structure to whole tasks can still be restrictive. This paper instead allows relationships to vary by feature, so tasks can be grouped differently for different parts of their models.

The proposed formulation constructs feature-specific task clusters from interactions between tasks and features. It does not require the number of clusters to be specified beforehand. This makes sharing more flexible: a relationship found for one feature need not dictate how tasks relate for every other feature. The formulation is strongly convex and can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal methods.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets examine different degrees of task relatedness. The method’s accuracy is consistently among the best in those evaluations, rather than being claimed as uniformly best. Its learned feature-specific clusters also agree with known or plausible task structures, suggesting that the flexible relationships can provide interpretable information alongside predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A strongly convex multitask method learns different task clusters for different features without requiring a preset cluster count.

title: Convex Multitask Learning with Flexible Task Clusters
